chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.x:
**Period:** first quarter (1/01 to 31/03), $\frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$ of a year. The fixed assets were bought on 31/12 of the previous year, so they are used during the **whole** quarter.

The exercise trains the distinction of [Slide 8]: a **revenue** is recorded when the sale is made, whether or not it is collected; an **expense** when the good or service is received or consumed, whether or not it is paid. Collections and payments are the cash side of the same operations.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: classification of every operation
chunks.x:
| Operation | Revenue / expense of Q1 | Collection / payment in Q1 | Pending at 31/3 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sales | Revenue 1,930 | Collection $1{,}930 - 315 = 1{,}615$ | Receivable 315 |
| Salaries | Expense 450 | Payment $450 - 75 = 375$ | Salaries payable 75 |
| Materials (all consumed) | Expense 700 | Payment $700 - 125 = 575$ | Supplier payable 125 |
| Energy | Expense 230 | Payment 0 | Energy payable 230 |
| Fixed assets | Depreciation 30 | 0 | Net value $2{,}900 - 30$ |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.x:
For each asset, with no residual value given:

$$D_{\text{quarter}} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{\text{Years of life}} \times \frac{3}{12}$$

| Asset | Annual depreciation | Quarter |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Factory building | $1{,}000 / 25 = 40$ | $40 / 4 = 10.0$ |
| Office building | $1{,}500 / 50 = 30$ | $30 / 4 = 7.5$ |
| Machinery | $300 / 10 = 30$ | $30 / 4 = 7.5$ |
| Transport equipment | $100 / 5 = 20$ | $20 / 4 = 5.0$ |
| **Total** | **120** | **30.0** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.x:
- **Income (revenues):** the sales invoiced, **1,930 m.u.**
- **Expenses:** $450 + 700 + 230 + 30 = $ **1,410 m.u.** (so the profit of the quarter is $1{,}930 - 1{,}410 = 520$ m.u.).
- **Collections:** $1{,}930 - 315 = $ **1,615 m.u.**
- **Payments:** $(450 - 75) + (700 - 125) + 0 = 375 + 575 = $ **950 m.u.** Depreciation is not a payment.
- **Investments of the quarter:** **0 m.u.** The fixed assets (total $1{,}000 + 1{,}500 + 300 + 100 = 2{,}900$ m.u.) were acquired on 31/12 of the previous year, before the quarter began. If the question is read as "the investment the company works with", the answer is that 2,900 m.u.; state the reading you use in the exam.
- **Depreciation:** **30 m.u.**

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.h: Step 3. Part (b): only half of the materials consumed
chunks.x:
Only the material **consumed** is an expense [Slide 8, Slide 10]: $700 / 2 = 350$ m.u. The other 350 m.u. stay in the warehouse as **inventory**, a current asset [Slide 14].

| Magnitude | (a) | (b) | Change |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Income | 1,930 | 1,930 | 0 |
| Expenses | 1,410 | $450 + 350 + 230 + 30 = 1{,}060$ | −350 |
| Profit | 520 | 870 | +350 |
| Collections | 1,615 | 1,615 | 0 |
| Payments | 950 | 950 | 0 |
| Inventory at 31/3 | 0 | 350 | +350 |
| Depreciation | 30 | 30 | 0 |

Payments do not change: the company **paid** for what it **bought** (575 of the 700), regardless of how much it **used**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.x:
- **Profit is not cash:** in (a) the profit is 520 while the net cash generated is $1{,}615 - 950 = 665$. The difference, $665 - 520 = 145$, is explained item by item: $+30$ (depreciation, an expense without payment) $+75 + 125 + 230$ (expenses not yet paid) $- 315$ (revenue not yet collected) $= 145$.
- **Part (b)** raises the profit by 350 without any extra cash: unconsumed material is an asset, not an expense.
- **Check of depreciation:** the annual total 120 times $\frac{1}{4}$ gives 30.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 1 - Accrual vs Cash Basis and Linear Depreciation
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, pp. 1-2
Part (a) coincides with the key: income 1,930; collections 1,615; payments 950; expenses 1,410; depreciation 30; investments 0. In part (b) the key also states that revenue, collections and payments do not change and that the unused material appears as inventory.

Erratum in the official solution (part b)
The key gives total expenses of 1,124 for part (b), but its own items add to $450 + 350 + 230 + 30 = 1{,}060$. That is the value obtained above, and the only one consistent with a profit that rises by exactly the 350 of material that was not consumed.

**Back to:** Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.x: The JUGA S.A. firm is started with a shareholders' contribution of 60,000 €. Of those, 30,000 € are paid in and deposited in a bank account, and the remaining 30,000 € correspond to the transfer of a patent. With the cash of the bank account, raw materials are purchased for 10,500 € and machinery for 15,000 €. Detail the balance sheet at the start of operations.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.x:
- The capital contributed is **60,000 €**: 30,000 € in money and 30,000 € in kind (a patent).
- The purchases are paid **with the bank account** (no debt is created).
- It is the **start** of operations: nothing has been produced or sold yet, so there are no revenues or expenses and no income statement.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: effect of each operation on the balance sheet
chunks.x:
| Operation | Assets | Liabilities | Equity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Money contributed | Bank +30,000 | | Capital +30,000 |
| Patent contributed | Patent +30,000 | | Capital +30,000 |
| Raw materials bought | Raw materials +10,500; bank −10,500 | | |
| Machinery bought | Machinery +15,000; bank −15,000 | | |

Each row keeps Assets = Liabilities + Equity [Slide 12]: the contributions increase both sides; the purchases only change the composition of the assets.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.x:
- **Patent:** non-current asset [Slide 15].
- **Machinery:** non-current asset (equipment) [Slide 15].
- **Raw materials:** inventory, a current asset [Slide 14]; not consumed yet, so not an expense.
- **Bank:** cash, a current asset [Slide 14].
- **Share capital:** contributed capital [Slide 17].

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.h: Step 3. Balance sheet at the start of operations
chunks.x:
| Assets | € | Liabilities and equity | € |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Patent | 30,000 | Share capital | 60,000 |
| Machinery | 15,000 | **Equity** | **60,000** |
| **Non-current assets** | **45,000** | **Liabilities** | **0** |
| Raw materials | 10,500 | | |
| Bank | 4,500 | | |
| **Current assets** | **15,000** | | |
| **Total assets** | **60,000** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **60,000** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.x:
- **Balance:** $45{,}000 + 15{,}000 = 60{,}000 = 60{,}000 + 0$.
- **Typical mistake:** keeping the bank at 30,000 € while also adding the machinery and the raw materials gives assets of 85,000 € against 60,000 € of equity. Spending cash on an asset never changes the total.
- **Financial structure** [Slide 36]: the company is financed 100% with equity ($L/E = 0$).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 2 - JUGA SA Opening Balance Sheet
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, p. 3
The balance sheet coincides with the key in every line: bank 4,500; patent 30,000; machinery 15,000; raw materials 10,500; share capital 60,000; total 60,000. The bank movements (+30,000, −15,000, −10,500) are the same.

- **Balance:** $14{,}500 + 19{,}500 = 34{,}000 = 14{,}000 + 3{,}000 + 17{,}000$.
- **Financial structure** [Slide 36]: liabilities $L = 3{,}000 + 17{,}000 = 20{,}000$, equity $E = 14{,}000$, $E + L = 34{,}000$:

$$\%E = \frac{14{,}000}{34{,}000} = 41.2\%, \qquad \%L = \frac{20{,}000}{34{,}000} = 58.8\%, \qquad \frac{L}{E} = \frac{20{,}000}{14{,}000} = 1.43$$

 The company has more debt than equity, and most of it (17,000 of 20,000) is due within the year: by [Slide 36], a high leverage indicates higher risk to shareholders.
- **Typical mistakes:** retained earnings are equity, not a liability; accounts receivable (owed **to** the company) are an asset, accounts payable (owed **by** the company) a liability.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 3 - Libbys Company Balance Sheet Classification
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, p. 4
The balance sheet coincides with the key in every block: current assets 19,500; non-current assets 14,500; current liabilities 17,000; non-current liabilities 3,000; owners' equity 14,000; total 34,000. The key asks only for the balance sheet, so the leverage figures in Phase 4 are an addition based on Slide 36.

**Back to:** Business Management MOC

**Related notes:** Concept - Method to Build the Income Statement and Balance Sheet · Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.x:
Prepare the income statement for Hawkins Partners using the following figures (in euros), knowing that the applicable corporate tax rate is 30%:

| # | Item | € | # | Item | € |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- | ---: |
| 1 | Initial inventory | 600 | 6 | Interests from the long-term debt | 5,500 |
| 2 | Purchase of goods (sold 100%) | 84,000 | 7 | Wages and salaries | 12,700 |
| 3 | Rental costs | 1,000 | 8 | Water, gas and electricity | 1,200 |
| 4 | Property sold to another company (income) | 10,500 | 9 | Sales | 130,800 |
| 5 | Interests received by the company | 15,200 | 10 | Inventory at the end of the period | 500 |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.h: Phase 1 — Setup: what each figure is
chunks.x: The statement mixes the three kinds of income-statement lines of [Slide 9]: items of the primary operation (sales, goods, wages, rent, utilities), **non-operating items** (interests, the sale of property) [Slide 11], and the tax. It also gives the initial and final **inventory**, which adjust the cost of goods sold.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: classification of every item
chunks.x:
| Item | Line of the income statement |
| :--- | :--- |
| 9. Sales | Sales revenue |
| 1, 2, 10. Inventories and purchases | Cost of goods sold |
| 3, 7, 8. Rent, wages, utilities | Operating expenses [Slide 10] |
| 4. Property sold (income) | Non-operating item: gain on the sale of property [Slide 11] |
| 5. Interests received | Non-operating item: interest revenue [Slide 8, Slide 11] |
| 6. Interests on long-term debt | Non-operating item: interest expense [Slide 11] |
| Tax 30% | Income taxes [Slide 11] |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.x:
The goods sold are those available (initial inventory + purchases) minus those still in stock at the end:

$$\text{COGS} = 600 + 84{,}000 - 500 = 84{,}100 \text{ €}$$

The inventory fell by $600 - 500 = 100$ €: those 100 € of goods were also sold, so they add to the purchases.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.x:
| Line | Computation | € |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Sales revenue | | 130,800 |
| − Cost of goods sold | Step 1 | 84,100 |
| **= Gross profit** | $130{,}800 - 84{,}100$ | **46,700** |
| − Wages and salaries | | 12,700 |
| − Rental costs | | 1,000 |
| − Water, gas and electricity | | 1,200 |
| **= Income from operations** | $46{,}700 - 14{,}900$ | **31,800** |
| + Gain on property sold | | 10,500 |
| + Interests received | | 15,200 |
| − Interests on long-term debt | | 5,500 |
| **= Income before taxes** | $31{,}800 + 10{,}500 + 15{,}200 - 5{,}500$ | **52,000** |
| − Income taxes (30%) | $0.30 \times 52{,}000$ | 15,600 |
| **= Net income** | $52{,}000 - 15{,}600$ | **36,400** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.x:
- **Non-operating items add 20,200 €** ($10{,}500 + 15{,}200 - 5{,}500$): almost 39% of the income before taxes does not come from the primary operation, which is why the slides separate them [Slide 11].
- **The tax base** is the income before taxes (52,000), not the income from operations [Slide 11].
- **Reading of item 4:** the statement labels the 10,500 € as income from the property sold; no book value of the property is given, so the whole amount is taken as the gain on the sale.
- **Check:** $130{,}800 + 10{,}500 + 15{,}200 = 156{,}500$ of revenues and gains; $84{,}100 + 14{,}900 + 5{,}500 = 104{,}500$ of expenses; $156{,}500 - 104{,}500 = 52{,}000$.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 4 - Hawkins Partners Income Statement and Inventories
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, p. 5
Cost of goods sold 84,100 (purchases 84,000 plus the inventory variation of 100), operating expenses 14,900, interests received 15,200, interests paid 5,500, income before taxes 52,000, tax 15,600 and net income 36,400 coincide with the key.

Discrepancy with the official solution (EBIT)
The key includes the 10,500 € of the property sold (labelled "Income from rentals") in the income from operations, so its EBIT is 42,300 €. Here the amount is shown below EBIT, as a non-operating gain, following the definition of Slide 11 (gains and losses on the sale of equipment and investments). Both layouts give the same income before taxes (52,000 €) and the same net income (36,400 €); only the EBIT subtotal changes: 31,800 € here and 42,300 € in the key. For an exam marked against this key, expect EBIT = 42,300 €.

**Back to:** Business Management MOC

**Related notes:** Concept - Method to Build the Income Statement and Balance Sheet · Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
Prepare the income statement of a company with the following information for 2017:
- Gross sales during the year reached 2,002 million €. The company's trade policy gives a 3% discount to its Type A customers, those whose annual purchases from the company exceed 120 million €. Type A customers account for 40% of sales. Assume total sales = gross sales − discount.
- Purchases of raw materials amounted to 962 million €.
- The workforce consists of 7,800 employees. The average salary is 30,000 € per year, and the average spending on Social Security is 30% of the salary.
- Payments for other operating expenses amounted to 457 million €.
- In recent years the company has invested a total of 1,200 million € in fixed assets with an average lifespan of 10 years (linear depreciation, no residual value).
- The company obtained an international loan of 225 million € in 2015, at 6% interest along the whole year; the whole principal will be repaid in 2020.
- The corporate tax rate is 30%. The company has agreed to a dividend of 50%.
- Assume no change in stocks of raw materials or finished products during the year.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
All amounts are expressed in **millions of euros (M€)**. Salaries are given per employee in €, so they must be converted: $1 \text{ M€} = 10^6$ €.

**Hypotheses:**
1. "No change in stocks" means initial inventory = final inventory, so $\text{COGS} = \text{Purchases}$.
2. The 120 M€ threshold only defines who is a Type A customer; the statement already says these customers make 40% of the sales, so the discount applies to that 40%.
3. The loan principal is not an expense: only its interest enters the income statement [Slide 11].
4. The dividend of 50% is applied to the **net income** [Slide 23].

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: line of each item
chunks.x:
| Item | Line |
| :--- | :--- |
| Gross sales − discount | Sales revenue (net) |
| Raw materials (no stock change) | Cost of goods sold |
| Salaries + Social Security | Operating expense |
| Other operating expenses | Operating expense |
| Depreciation of fixed assets | Operating expense [Slide 10] |
| Interest on the loan | Non-operating item [Slide 11] |
| Tax 30% | Income taxes |
| Dividend 50% | Distribution of net income (not an expense) |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
$$\text{Type A sales} = 0.40 \times 2{,}002 = 800.8 \text{ M€}, \qquad \text{Discount} = 0.03 \times 800.8 = 24.024 \text{ M€}$$

$$\text{Net sales} = 2{,}002 - 24.024 = 1{,}977.976 \text{ M€}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
$$\text{Salaries} = 7{,}800 \times 30{,}000 = 234{,}000{,}000 \text{ €} = 234 \text{ M€}$$

$$\text{Social Security} = 0.30 \times 234 = 70.2 \text{ M€}, \qquad \text{Personnel} = 234 + 70.2 = 304.2 \text{ M€}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
| Line | Computation | M€ |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Net sales | Step 1 | 1,977.976 |
| − Cost of goods sold (raw materials) | | 962.000 |
| **= Gross profit** | $1{,}977.976 - 962$ | **1,015.976** |
| − Personnel | Step 2 | 304.200 |
| − Other operating expenses | | 457.000 |
| − Depreciation | Step 3 | 120.000 |
| **= Income from operations** | $1{,}015.976 - 881.2$ | **134.776** |
| − Interest expense | Step 3 | 13.500 |
| **= Income before taxes** | $134.776 - 13.5$ | **121.276** |
| − Income taxes (30%) | $0.30 \times 121.276$ | 36.383 |
| **= Net income** | $121.276 - 36.3828$ | **84.893** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.h: Step 5. Distribution of the net income [Slide 23]
chunks.x:
$$\text{Dividends} = 0.50 \times 84.8932 = 42.447 \text{ M€}, \qquad \text{Retained earnings} = 84.8932 - 42.4466 = 42.447 \text{ M€}$$

Pay-out 50%, self-financing 50%.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
- **Applying the discount to all the sales** would deduct $0.03 \times 2{,}002 = 60.06$ M€ instead of 24.024: the 40% restriction matters.
- **The loan repayment in 2020** does not appear in 2017: repaying principal is a payment that is never an expense.
- **Exact values:** income taxes 36.3828 M€ and net income 84.8932 M€ (shown rounded to three decimals in the table).
- **Dividends** come after taxes and are not an expense: the income statement ends at the net income, and the 50/50 split is shown separately.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 5 - Corporate Income Statement, Taxes and Dividends
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, p. 6
Every line coincides with the key: discount 24.024; net sales 1,977.976; cost of goods sold 962; personnel 304.2; other operating expenses 457; depreciation 120; EBIT 134.776; interest 13.5; income before taxes 121.276; tax 36.3828; net income 84.8932; dividends 42.4466 and retained earnings 42.4466 (all in M€).

**Back to:** Business Management MOC

**Related notes:** Concept - Method to Build the Income Statement and Balance Sheet · Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
Company X was incorporated on 1/01/2017 with a subscription of shares worth 100 m.u., fully paid in cash. On 1/01/2017 it bought, with cash: a) an area (land) for 20 m.u.; b) equipment with a life of 10 years (straight-line depreciation) and a purchase price of 20 m.u.; c) raw materials for 20 m.u.

The company hires an employee for a total annual cost (salaries, Social Security, etc.) of 10 m.u. per year. This employee processes half of the raw material and sells it for a total of 50 m.u. Sales are the same every day of the year. The average collection period is 3 months.

The single tax rate on the profits of the company is 30% (paid on 31/12/2017). The company follows a strict self-financing strategy.

1. Prepare the balance sheet at 31/12/2017, justifying and explaining the intermediate calculations.
2. Explain how the accounting statements would change if, instead of 100%, the shareholders had paid only 90% of the 100 m.u. subscribed.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
**Period:** calendar year 2017. **Closing:** 31/12/2017.

**Hypotheses:**
1. The employee's cost is paid during the year.
2. Land has no useful life given and is not depreciated; the equipment has no residual value given (zero).
3. **Strict self-financing** [Slide 23]: the whole net income is retained (pay-out 0%).
4. The tax is paid on 31/12, so no tax liability remains.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: classification of every operation
chunks.x:
| Operation | Income statement 2017 | Cash 2017 | Open at 31/12/2017 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Capital | — | +100 | Share capital 100 |
| Land | — | −20 | Land 20 |
| Equipment | Depreciation 2 | −20 | Equipment $20 - 2$ |
| Raw materials | COGS 10 (half consumed) | −20 | Inventory 10 |
| Employee | Personnel 10 | −10 | — |
| Sales | Revenue 50 | +37.5 | Receivables 12.5 |
| Tax | 8.4 | −8.4 | — |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.h: Step 1. Depreciation and cost of goods sold
chunks.x: $$D = \frac{20 - 0}{10} = 2 \text{ m.u.}, \qquad \text{COGS} = \frac{20}{2} = 10 \text{ m.u.}, \qquad \text{Inventory} = 20 - 10 = 10 \text{ m.u.}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.h: Step 2. Receivables from the collection period
chunks.x:
Sales are spread evenly over the year and customers pay 3 months after buying. At 31/12 the sales of the last 3 months are still unpaid:

$$\text{Receivables} = 50 \times \frac{3}{12} = 12.5 \text{ m.u.}, \qquad \text{Collected} = 50 - 12.5 = 37.5 \text{ m.u.}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
| Line | Computation | m.u. |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Sales revenue | | 50.0 |
| − Cost of goods sold | Step 1 | 10.0 |
| **= Gross profit** | | **40.0** |
| − Personnel | | 10.0 |
| − Depreciation | Step 1 | 2.0 |
| **= Income from operations = income before taxes** | no interest | **28.0** |
| − Income taxes (30%) | $0.30 \times 28$ | 8.4 |
| **= Net income** | $28 - 8.4$ | **19.6** |

All 19.6 is retained (strict self-financing).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
| Assets | m.u. | Liabilities and equity | m.u. |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Land | 20.0 | Share capital | 100.0 |
| Equipment ($20 - 2$) | 18.0 | Retained earnings (net income 2017) | 19.6 |
| **Non-current assets** | **38.0** | **Equity** | **119.6** |
| Inventory (raw materials) | 10.0 | **Liabilities** | **0** |
| Accounts receivable | 12.5 | | |
| Cash | 59.1 | | |
| **Current assets** | **81.6** | | |
| **Total assets** | **119.6** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **119.6** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
The shareholders **subscribed** 100 m.u. but **paid in** only $0.90 \times 100 = 90$ m.u. The remaining 10 m.u. is capital not yet paid (uncalled capital): the shareholders still owe it to the company.

- **Income statement:** **no change**. Revenues and expenses do not depend on how the capital was paid; there is no interest involved. Net income stays 19.6.
- **Cash:** 10 m.u. less: $59.1 - 10 = 49.1$ m.u. All the purchases (60) can still be paid in cash, since the company receives 90.
- **Equity:** the contributed capital is what the stockholders actually provided [Slide 13, Slide 17], so the subscribed capital is shown minus the unpaid part: $100 - 10 = 90$.

| Assets | m.u. | Liabilities and equity | m.u. |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| **Non-current assets** | **38.0** | Subscribed capital | 100.0 |
| Inventory | 10.0 | − Uncalled capital (unpaid by shareholders) | (10.0) |
| Accounts receivable | 12.5 | Retained earnings | 19.6 |
| Cash | 49.1 | **Equity** | **109.6** |
| **Current assets** | **71.6** | **Liabilities** | **0** |
| **Total assets** | **109.6** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **109.6** |

Both totals fall by exactly the 10 m.u. not paid.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
- **Balance:** $38 + 81.6 = 119.6 = 100 + 19.6$ (requirement 1); $38 + 71.6 = 109.6 = 90 + 19.6$ (requirement 2).
- **Equity bridge:** equity = capital paid + net income retained: $100 + 19.6$ and $90 + 19.6$.
- **Profit vs cash:** after the purchases of 1/01, the cash generated during the year is $37.5 - 10 - 8.4 = 19.1$, while the profit is 19.6. Reconciliation: $19.6 + 2 + 10 - 12.5 = 19.1$, that is, profit + depreciation (expense, never a payment) + materials consumed (expense whose payment was made on 1/01 with the purchase) − sales not collected yet.
- **Presentation note:** some textbooks show the 10 m.u. owed by shareholders as an asset instead of deducting it from capital; then both totals stay at 119.6. The deduction used here is the one consistent with "contributed capital" in [Slide 17]. Both readings give the same net equity provided (109.6) and leave the income statement unchanged.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Exercise 6 - Company X Full Cycle Balance Sheet and Uncalled Capital
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Financial Statements_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, pp. 7-8
Requirement 1 coincides with the key: sales 50; cost of goods sold 10; personnel 10; depreciation 2; EBIT 28; tax 8.4; net income 19.6; cash 59.1; receivables 12.5; inventory 10; land 20; equipment 18; total assets 119.6. The key does not solve requirement 2 (90 % paid in), so that part of the solution is not covered by it.

**Back to:** Business Management MOC

**Related notes:** Concept - Method to Build the Income Statement and Balance Sheet · Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x: The financial director of CIRCONSA is working on its financial statements (balance sheet and income statement) as of 30 June 2015. It has the balance of the company as of 31 December 2014 and the following operations that took place from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2015. The company sells a certain product.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
- **i.** During the semester the company sold 1,200 units at 20 m.u./unit (every month the same amount, 200 u.). Customers pay 30 days after the sale. A very important customer (30% of the sales), who bought an equal amount each month, was given a 10% discount on its purchases.
- **ii.** During the semester 1,000 units were purchased (40% in the first quarter and 60% in the second) at 12 m.u./u. Suppliers are paid at 90 days.
- **iii.** At 31/12/2014 there is a stock of 200 units valued at 12 m.u./u.
- **iv.** During the first quarter of 2015 the taxes and the outstanding supplier balances of the previous year were paid.
- **v.** During the first quarter of 2015 the customer debt outstanding from the previous year was collected, except 300 m.u. from a customer who requested to defer payment until July 2016.
- **vi.** Personnel expenses were 350 m.u./month (plus 150 for Social Security) and general expenses 300 m.u./month. Personnel and Social Security are paid in the month in which they occur; overheads two months after.
- **vii.** On 1/04/2015 a renting contract (3 years) for computer equipment was signed with a specialised company, 400 m.u. per month, with payment at 120 days (payment at the end of each month).
- **viii.** On 1/04/2015 a patent was bought for 2,400 m.u., to be paid on 1/07/2015. It is amortised in 4 years.
- **ix.** On 1/02/2015 a credit of 2,000 m.u. was obt

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
ained, to be returned a year later with 12% annual interest; interest and principal are paid on 1/02/2016.
- **x.** At 31/12/2014 the company had only one machine, bought on 1/07/2014, amortised linearly with a residual value of 20%.
- **xi.** On 1/02/2015 a capital increase (fully paid, no issue premium) of 10,000 m.u. was made. The same day a new machine costing 12,000 m.u. was bought: 8,000 paid in cash and the remainder on 1/07/2015. It is amortised in 4 years with zero residual value.
- **xii.** Assume a 20% corporate tax, recorded in the balance at 30/06/2015 as "taxes to pay".

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
**Balance sheet at 31/12/2014 (m.u.):** current assets 5,400 (cash 1,200; accounts receivable 1,800; inventory 2,400); non-current assets 450 (machinery 500; accumulated depreciation 50); current liabilities 800 (unpaid taxes 350; suppliers 450); owners' equity 5,050 (retained earnings 850; paid-in capital 4,200); total 5,850.

**Question:** calculate the balance sheet and the profit and loss account of CIRCONSA at 30 June 2015.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.h: Phase 1 — Setup: data, timeline and hypotheses
chunks.x:
**Period:** 1/01/2015 to 30/06/2015, **6 months**. **Closing instant:** 30/06/2015. Every monthly figure is multiplied by the months it applies inside this window.

| Date | Event |
| :--- | :--- |
| Jan-Mar | Sales 200 u./month; purchases 400 u. (Q1); payment of 2014 taxes and suppliers; collection of 2014 receivables except 300 |
| 1/02 | Credit 2,000 received; capital increase 10,000; machine 2 bought (8,000 paid) |
| 1/04 | Renting starts (400/month); patent bought (2,400, payable 1/07) |
| Apr-Jun | Sales 200 u./month; purchases 600 u. (Q2) |
| 30/06 | **Closing** |
| 1/07 | Payment of patent and of the 4,000 left on machine 2 (after the closing) |

**Hypotheses** (all read from the statement):
1. Sales are uniform (200 u./month) and collected 30 days later, so at 30/06 only **June's sales** are uncollected.
2. Q1 purchases are paid 90 days later, inside the semester; **Q2 purchases** are still unpaid at 30/06.
3. Overheads are paid two months later: January-April are paid, **May and June** are unpaid.
4. The renting is paid at 120 days: none of the April-June instalments has been paid at 30/06.
5. Simple interest, prorated by months. Tax: 20% of income before taxes, left unpaid.
6. Machine 1: its useful life is not given; it is deduced from the opening balance (Phase 3, Step 5).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: classification of every operation
chunks.x:
The three questions of the method (income statement? cash? open balance item at 30/06?) applied to each operation:

| Op. | Income statement (6 months) | Cash in (+) / out (−) | Open at 30/06 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| i. Sales | Net sales 23,280 | +19,400 (Jan-May) | Receivables 3,880 (June) |
| ii-iii. Purchases and stock | COGS 14,400 | −4,800 (Q1) | Inventory 0; suppliers 7,200 (Q2) |
| iv. 2014 taxes and suppliers | — | −350 − 450 | — |
| v. 2014 receivables | — | +1,500 | Long-term receivable 300 |
| vi. Personnel + SS | 3,000 | −3,000 | — |
| vi. Overheads | 1,800 | −1,200 (Jan-Apr) | Overheads payable 600 |
| vii. Renting | 1,200 | 0 | Renting payable 1,200 |
| viii. Patent | Amortisation 150 | 0 | Patent 2,400 − 150; patent payable 2,400 |
| ix. Credit | Interest 100 | +2,000 | Credit 2,000; interest payable 100 |
| x. Machine 1 | Depreciation 50 | 0 | Machine 500 − 100 |
| xi. Capital increase | — | +10,000 | Capital +10,000 |
| xi. Machine 2 | Depreciation 1,250 | −8,000 | Machine 12,000 − 1,250; debt 4,000 |
| xii. Tax | 266 | 0 | Taxes payable 266 |

Each figure is derived in Phase 3.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
Gross sales per month: $200 \times 20 = 4{,}000$ m.u. The important customer buys 30% of them, so its discount per month is

$$0.30 \times 4{,}000 \times 0.10 = 120 \text{ m.u./month}$$

Net sales per month: $4{,}000 - 120 = 3{,}880$ m.u. Over the semester:

$$\text{Net sales} = 6 \times 3{,}880 = 23{,}280 \text{ m.u.} \quad (= 24{,}000 - 720)$$

Collections at 30 days: the sales of January to May are collected by 30/06 ($5 \times 3{,}880 = 19{,}400$); June's sales are still owed: **receivables 3,880**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.h: Step 2. Purchases, stock and cost of goods sold (ops. ii, iii)
chunks.x:
Units: initial stock 200 + purchases 1,000 = 1,200 available; 1,200 sold, so the ending stock is 0 units. All units cost 12 m.u., so

$$\text{COGS} = \text{Initial inventory} + \text{Purchases} - \text{Ending inventory} = 2{,}400 + 12{,}000 - 0 = 14{,}400 \text{ m.u.}$$

Purchases: Q1 $= 0.40 \times 1{,}000 \times 12 = 4{,}800$, paid at 90 days (inside the semester); Q2 $= 0.60 \times 1{,}000 \times 12 = 7{,}200$, **unpaid at 30/06**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
Paid in Q1: taxes 350 and suppliers 450 (cash −800; both liabilities disappear). Collected in Q1: $1{,}800 - 300 = 1{,}500$. The remaining 300 is due in July 2016, more than one year after 30/06/2015, so it becomes a **non-current receivable** [Slide 15].

None of these affects the income statement: they settle revenues and expenses of 2014.

chunks.h: Step 4. Personnel, overheads and renting (ops. vi, vii)
chunks.x:
- Personnel + Social Security: $6 \times (350 + 150) = 3{,}000$, all paid.
- Overheads: $6 \times 300 = 1{,}800$ of expense; paid two months later, so January-April are paid ($4 \times 300 = 1{,}200$) and May-June are owed: **600 payable**.
- Renting: April, May, June, $3 \times 400 = 1{,}200$ of expense; paid at 120 days, nothing paid by 30/06: **1,200 payable**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.h: Step 5. Fixed assets: depreciation and amortisation (ops. viii, x, xi)
chunks.x:
**Machine 1.** Cost 500, residual value $0.20 \times 500 = 100$, depreciable base $500 - 100 = 400$. The opening accumulated depreciation is 50 for the 6 months from 1/07/2014 to 31/12/2014, so the annual depreciation is $50 \times \frac{12}{6} = 100$ and the useful life is $\frac{400}{100} = 4$ years. For the semester:

$$D_1 = \frac{500 - 100}{4} \times \frac{6}{12} = 50 \text{ m.u.}, \qquad \text{accumulated} = 50 + 50 = 100$$

**Machine 2.** Bought 1/02, used 5 months (February-June), zero residual value:

$$D_2 = \frac{12{,}000 - 0}{4} \times \frac{5}{12} = 1{,}250 \text{ m.u.}$$

**Patent.** Bought 1/04, used 3 months:

$$A = \frac{2{,}400}{4} \times \frac{3}{12} = 150 \text{ m.u.}$$

Total depreciation and amortisation: $50 + 1{,}250 + 150 = 1{,}450$ m.u. None of it is a payment.

Payments: machine 2, 8,000 paid in cash; the other 4,000 and the whole patent (2,400) are due on 1/07/2015, one day after the closing, so they are **current liabilities** at 30/06.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
Received 1/02 (cash +2,000), returned on 1/02/2016, within one year of 30/06/2015: **current liability**. Interest from 1/02 to 30/06 (5 months), paid only in 2016:

$$I = 2{,}000 \times 0.12 \times \frac{5}{12} = 100 \text{ m.u.} \quad \text{(expense and interest payable)}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
- **Balance:** $13{,}700 + 20{,}180 = 33{,}880 = 16{,}114 + 17{,}766$.
- **Equity bridge:** equity grows from 5,050 to 16,114, that is $+11{,}064 = 10{,}000$ (capital increase) $+ 1{,}064$ (net income).
- **Profit is not cash:** the semester earns 1,064 but cash grows by $16{,}300 - 1{,}200 = 15{,}100$, mostly because of the capital increase (10,000), the credit (2,000) and the many expenses still unpaid (suppliers, renting, overheads, interest, taxes). In the opposite direction, 8,000 of cash went into a machine whose expense this semester is only 1,250.
- **Limiting case:** if June's sales had been collected, cash would be 3,880 higher and receivables zero, but net income would not change: revenue is recognised when the sale is made [Slide 8].
- **Exam traps:** (1) the 1/07 debts are liabilities at 30/06, not payments; (2) the 300 deferred to July 2016 is non-current; (3) machine 2 is depreciated 5 months and the patent 3 months, not 6; (4) the life of machine 1 must be deduced from the opening balance.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Additional_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, pp. 6-8
The income statement and the cash account coincide with the key: net sales 23,280; cost of goods sold 14,400; personnel 3,000; general expenses 1,800; renting 1,200; EBITDA 2,880; depreciation and amortisation 1,450; EBIT 1,430; interest 100; income before taxes 1,330; tax 266; net income 1,064; collections 34,100; cash 16,300; total 33,880. The key writes the depreciation of machine 1 as $(500 - 100)/8$, that is, 8 half-years, the same 4-year life deduced above.

Discrepancy with the official solution (the 300 deferred to July 2016)
The key shows accounts receivable of 4,180, which includes the 300 due in July 2016, so it counts them as a current asset (current assets 20,480; non-current assets 13,400). Here they are a non-current receivable, because they fall due more than one year after 30/06/2015 (Slide 15), so receivables are 3,880 + 300 (current assets 20,180; non-current assets 13,700). Total assets, liabilities and equity are the same in both.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 1 - Circonsa Balance Sheet and Income Statement
chunks.x:
Erratum in the official solution
The key's payments column adds to 16,800, but its items add to $450 + 3{,}000 + 1{,}200 + 4{,}800 + 350 + 8{,}000 = 17{,}800$, which gives the cash of 16,300 that it does show. The capital increase in the equity block reads 1,000 instead of 10,000 (only 10,000 gives equity of 16,114), and the labels of the interest payable (100) and the tax payable (266) are swapped.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
Three entrepreneurs established INFOPYMES on 1/01/2016 to provide on-line information services for small and medium enterprises, start-ups and potential entrepreneurs.

- The computer equipment, worth 100,000 €, was acquired on 1/01/2016 and will be paid to suppliers after three months, on 1/04/2016. Useful life 5 years (until 31/12/2020), linear depreciation, no residual value.
- On-line consultations brought revenues of 300,000 € in 2016.
- Rented premises: 1,000 €/month from 1/01/2016. Salaries and Social Security of the permanent employees: 5,000 €/month. Electricity, phone, etc.: 500 €/month.
- Variable wages of the additional staff for the on-line consultations: 174,000 € in 2016.
- The partners contributed an initial capital of 100,000 €. A bank granted a loan of 100,000 € at 10% yearly interest for 5 years (1/01/2016 to 31/12/2020). Each 31 December the company returns 20,000 € and pays the interest (10%) on the loan value at the beginning of each year.
- Results are declared at 23:59 on 31 December (after all payments and receipts, including interest, wages, Social Security, etc.), and the corporation tax of 30% on the profits is paid immediately. Dividends of 40% of the profits after taxes are distributed, and the final balance is drawn at 24:00.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x: **Required:** (1) the income statement for 2016; (2) assuming the tax has been paid and the dividends distributed, the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31/12/2016; (3) the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31/12/2017, assuming no new investments in 2017 and that the retained earnings and the cash balance at the end of 2017 remained unchanged with respect to 2016; (4) the ROA and ROE ratios in 2017.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.h: Phase 1 — Setup: data, timeline and hypotheses
chunks.x:
| Item | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Capital | 100,000 € (1/01/2016) |
| Loan | 100,000 € at 10%; 20,000 € returned each 31/12; interest on the balance at the start of each year |
| Equipment | 100,000 €, bought 1/01/2016, paid 1/04/2016, 5 years, no residual value |
| Revenues 2016 | 300,000 € |
| Fixed monthly costs | Rent 1,000; permanent staff 5,000; utilities 500 (€/month) |
| Variable wages 2016 | 174,000 € |
| Tax | 30% of profits, paid at 23:59 on 31/12 |
| Dividends | 40% of profit after taxes, paid at 23:59 on 31/12 |

**Hypotheses:**
1. The statement says the results are declared "after having made all payments and receipts", so the 300,000 € of revenues are **collected** and all 2016 costs are **paid** within 2016.
2. The balance is drawn at 24:00, **after** paying tax, interest, the 20,000 € instalment and dividends: none of them remains as a liability.
3. For 2017 the statement gives no operating data; we assume the **same revenues and operating costs as in 2016**, which is the only reading that lets requirement 4 be computed. With retained earnings unchanged, the whole 2017 profit must have been paid out as dividends (shown in Phase 3).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.h: Phase 2 — Frames: classification of every operation (2016)
chunks.x:
| Operation | Income statement 2016 | Cash 2016 | Open at 24:00 on 31/12/2016 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Capital | — | +100,000 | Capital 100,000 |
| Loan | — | +100,000 | Loan 80,000 (after the instalment) |
| Equipment | Depreciation 20,000 | −100,000 (on 1/04) | Equipment 100,000 − 20,000 |
| Revenues | 300,000 | +300,000 | — |
| Rent, staff, utilities, variable wages | 252,000 | −252,000 | — |
| Interest | 10,000 | −10,000 | — |
| Instalment | — | −20,000 | (reduces the loan) |
| Tax | 5,400 | −5,400 | — |
| Dividends | — (distribution) | −5,040 | Retained earnings 7,560 |

The equipment is bought on credit on 1/01 and paid on 1/04: between those dates it is a debt to the supplier, but at 31/12 that debt no longer exists.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
$$D = \frac{100{,}000 - 0}{5} \times \frac{12}{12} = 20{,}000 \text{ €/year}$$

$$I_{2016} = 100{,}000 \times 0.10 = 10{,}000 \text{ €} \quad \text{(loan value at the beginning of 2016)}$$

chunks.x:

Distribution [Slide 23]: dividends $= 0.40 \times 12{,}600 = 5{,}040$ €; retained earnings (self-financing) $= 12{,}600 - 5{,}040 = 7{,}560$ €.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
The loan after the first instalment is $100{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 80{,}000$ €. The instalment due on 31/12/2017 (20,000 €) is within one year, so it is a **current liability**; the other 60,000 € are long-term [Slide 16].

| Assets | € | Liabilities and equity | € |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Equipment | 100,000 | Capital | 100,000 |
| − Accumulated depreciation | (20,000) | Retained earnings | 7,560 |
| **Non-current assets** | **80,000** | **Equity** | **107,560** |
| Cash | 107,560 | Long-term bank loan | 60,000 |
| **Current assets** | **107,560** | Short-term bank loan (due 31/12/2017) | 20,000 |
| **Total assets** | **187,560** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **187,560** |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
Item by item:
- **Equipment:** no new investment; two years of depreciation, $2 \times 20{,}000 = 40{,}000$; net value $100{,}000 - 40{,}000 = 60{,}000$ €.
- **Loan:** second instalment paid, $80{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 60{,}000$ €: 20,000 € current (due 31/12/2018) and 40,000 € long-term.
- **Cash and retained earnings:** unchanged by statement: 107,560 € and 7,560 €.
- **Capital:** unchanged, 100,000 €.

| Assets | € | Liabilities and equity | € |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Equipment | 100,000 | Capital | 100,000 |
| − Accumulated depreciation | (40,000) | Retained earnings | 7,560 |
| **Non-current assets** | **60,000** | **Equity** | **107,560** |
| Cash | 107,560 | Long-term bank loan | 40,000 |
| **Current assets** | **107,560** | Short-term bank loan (due 31/12/2018) | 20,000 |
| **Total assets** | **167,560** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **167,560** |

**Is the statement consistent?** With the 2016 operations repeated (hypothesis 3), 2017 gives:

$$I_{2017} = 80{,}000 \times 0.10 = 8{,}000, \quad \text{IBT} = 28{,}000 - 8{,}000 = 20{,}000, \quad T = 0.30 \times 20{,}000 = 6{,}000, \quad \text{NI} = 14{,}000$$

Retained earnings unchanged means dividends $= 14{,}000$ € (a 100% pay-out). Cash then moves by $+300{,}000 - 252{,}000 - 8{,}000 - 20{,}000 - 6{,}000 - 14{,}000 = 0$, so the cash is indeed unchanged: the two conditions of the statement are compatible.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
Definitions not in the Topic 3 slides
The Topic 3 deck in `sources/` does not define ROA and ROE, but the problem asks for them. The standard definitions used here are $\text{ROA} = \dfrac{\text{Income from operations}}{\text{Total assets}}$ (the return of the economic structure) and $\text{ROE} = \dfrac{\text{Net income}}{\text{Equity}}$ (the return to the owners). Check them against your class notes: if your lecturer defines ROA with net income instead, the value is $14{,}000 / 167{,}560 = 8.36\%$.

$$\text{ROA}_{2017} = \frac{28{,}000}{167{,}560} = 0.1671 = 16.71\%$$

$$\text{ROE}_{2017} = \frac{14{,}000}{107{,}560} = 0.1302 = 13.02\%$$

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
- **Balances:** $80{,}000 + 107{,}560 = 187{,}560 = 107{,}560 + 60{,}000 + 20{,}000$ (2016) and $60{,}000 + 107{,}560 = 167{,}560 = 107{,}560 + 40{,}000 + 20{,}000$ (2017).
- **What changes between the two years:** both sides shrink by 20,000 €: the asset loses 20,000 € of value through depreciation, and the loan falls by the 20,000 € instalment, which in cash terms was financed by the cash generated (depreciation is an expense that is not a payment).
- **Leverage** [Slide 36]: $L/E = 80{,}000/107{,}560 = 0.74$ in 2016 and $60{,}000/107{,}560 = 0.56$ in 2017; the company becomes less indebted each year.
- **ROE < ROA here:** the return to the owners is lower than the return of the assets because interest and taxes are deducted from the numerator; the equity base being smaller than total assets is not enough to compensate.
- **Exam traps:** (1) the loan instalment is a payment, never an expense; (2) at 24:00 no tax or dividend liability remains; (3) the current part of the loan (next instalment) must be separated from the long-term part.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 2 - Infopymes Full Cycle Financial Statements and ROA ROE
chunks.x:
Official solution, `T3_Additional_SOLUTIONS.pdf`, pp. 12-14
Requirements 1 and 2 coincide with the key in every figure: EBIT 28,000; interest 10,000; income before taxes 18,000; tax 5,400; net income 12,600; dividends 5,040; retained earnings 7,560; cash 107,560; equipment net 80,000; total 187,560; bank loan 20,000 current and 60,000 long term; equity 107,560.
The key does not solve requirement 3 (balance sheet at 31/12/2017) nor requirement 4 (ROA and ROE), so Steps 5 and 6 above are not covered by it.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 3 - Wifinet Internet Provider Accounting Cycle and Dividends
chunks.x:
Wifinet S.L. was incorporated on 1/01/2016 with a registered capital of 6,003 m.u., to provide wireless Internet on the Alicante coast.

**Fiscal year 2016.** It took a bank loan of 2,000 m.u. at 5% annual interest (payable at the end of each year), the principal being repayable in 2019. It invested 5,371 m.u. in technical equipment with a life of 20 years; at the end of 2016 it recorded an accumulated depreciation of 26 m.u. for those assets. It also invested 206 m.u. in licence fees by 31/12/2016, to use certain technologies for 5 years. It spent 636 m.u. on financial shares of other companies. Most of 2016 was devoted to building the network and business started only in the last two months. At the end of 2016 the balance sheet reflected a **loss of 340 m.u.** and **cash in hand and bank of 1,476 m.u.**

In 2017 the results were positive, but the company decided not to distribute dividends and to retain all its profits to reduce the loss of the previous year.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 3 - Wifinet Internet Provider Accounting Cycle and Dividends
chunks.x:
**Fiscal year 2017.**
- Internet and VOIP: 5,000 customers on average, with an average revenue of 0.032 m.u./month per client in subscription fees. Additionally, 46 m.u. of on-line sales of other products. At the end of 2017 customers owed 164 m.u.
- Stocks were exhausted at the end of 2016. Purchases of materials to be installed in customers' homes: 680 m.u., of which 560 m.u. paid immediately and the rest deferred to the following year. The 2017 sales consumed half of the purchased goods.
- Staff costs: 559 m.u., paid in full in 2017. Supplies and outside services: 312 m.u., paid.
- Other administrative expenses: 300 m.u., 60% of them deferred to the following year.
- Corporation tax: 30%, payable in the first quarter of 2018.

**Required:** (1) the income statement for 2017; (2) the balance sheet at 31/12/2017; (3) which balance-sheet items change, and by how much, if a dividend of 20% of net profit is paid at 24:00 on 31/12/2017; (4) the same if the dividend of 20% is decided before the end of 2017 and paid on 30/06/2018.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 3 - Wifinet Internet Provider Accounting Cycle and Dividends
chunks.h: Phase 1 — Setup: data, timeline and hypotheses
chunks.x:
**Period:** calendar year 2017. **Closing:** 31/12/2017. The 2016 data serve only to build the **opening balance** of 2017.

**Hypotheses:**
1. The licences were bought at the very end of 2016, so they start to be amortised in 2017 (no 2016 amortisation is given).
2. The equipment was depreciated only 26 m.u. in 2016 (part of the year); in 2017 it is used the whole year.
3. Interest is paid at the end of each year, so no interest payable remains; the loan is due in 2019, more than one year after 31/12/2017: **long-term** [Slide 16].
4. The financial shares are a long-term investment (non-current asset) [Slide 15]; they produce no revenue in the data.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 4 - Cemed Mediterranean Pottery Manufacturing and Supplier Discount
chunks.x:
- CEMED was created on 1/01/2016 by three partners, each contributing 7 m.u., fully in cash.
- On 1/02/2016 it bought a piece of land worth 10 m.u., paying 50% in cash and leaving 50% to be paid one year later. On the same date it bought the factory building, paying 6 m.u. in cash and financing this amount with a mortgage at 5% annual interest for ten years. The factory is amortised over 20 years, linearly, with zero residual value. Each 31 December the company returns 10% of the mortgage principal plus the interest accrued in the year.
- On 1/04/2016 it obtained an additional bank loan of 5 m.u. at 6% annual interest, returning 20% of the principal each semester for the next 2½ years (first repayment on 1/10/2016, second on 1/04/2017, and so on). Interest is paid semiannually, calculated on the amount actually due in that semester, the day after the end of the semester.
- With this loan, on the same date, it bought machinery for 3 m.u. with 60 days payment delay; useful life 10 years, straight-line, zero residual value.
- On 1/07/2016 it acquired 150 tons of raw material at 0.03 m.u./ton. Half of it was used in producing the products sold. 60% of the total cost is paid to the supplier at 90 days; the other 40% remains unpaid at the end of the year.
- Sales revenue: 50 m.u., of which only 70% had been collected at 31/12/2016.
- Personnel plus Social Security: 0.8 m.u., paid in

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 4 - Cemed Mediterranean Pottery Manufacturing and Supplier Discount
chunks.x:
full in 2016.
- Corporation tax: 30%, settled by calendar year and paid on 15/01/2017.
- The company keeps 40% of annual net profits as reserves; the dividends are paid on 31/12/2016.

In which case is the profit higher, and why?

chunks.t: Problem - T3 Extra 4 - Cemed Mediterranean Pottery Manufacturing and Supplier Discount
chunks.x:
- **Balance:** $18.5 + 45.4197 = 63.9197 = 33.8702 + 6.8 + 23.2495$; requirement 2: both sides fall by 0.02475.
- **In which case is the profit higher?** With the **discount**. The discount lowers the cost of the material; the price paid for it is giving up 90 days of **trade credit** [Slide 35], and trade credit has no explicit interest in this problem, so losing it costs nothing in the income statement: it only advances a payment that in both cases falls inside 2016.
- **Why only half of the saving reaches the profit:** only half of the material was consumed. The other half of the saving is in the lower value of the inventory and will reach the income statement when that stock is used.
- **Debt structure** [Slide 36]: liabilities $6.8 + 23.2495 = 30.0495$, equity 33.8702, so $L/E = 0.89$.
- **Exam traps:** (1) the mortgage finances the building: cash +6 and −6 on the same day; (2) the loan interest of October-December is accrued but unpaid; (3) the current part of each loan is what is due before 31/12/2017; (4) the land is not depreciated; (5) taxes are payable on 15/01/2017, so they are a liability, while dividends were paid.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 1 - Capitalization of a Deferred Debt
chunks.x: One person, Mr. Smith, is able to invest his available liquid capital at a 5 percent rate per year. Currently, another person, Mr. Martinez, must pay Mr. Smith the amount of USD 1,000, but he is going through a period of scarce liquidity and asks him to wait. How much money will Mr. Smith require if it is delayed a year? What if it is a two-year delay? What if it were three years of deferment?

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 1 - Capitalization of a Deferred Debt
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $C_0$ | debt today | 1,000 |
| $i$ | rate at which Mr. Smith can invest | 5% per year |
| $n$ | years of delay | 1, 2, 3 |

Mr. Smith must receive the amount that, invested at 5%, equals having the 1,000 today: the future (capitalized) value with compound interest,

$$C_n = C_0\,(1 + i)^n$$

This is the capitalization rule used in the key; the course decks on disk do not state it.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 1 - Capitalization of a Deferred Debt
chunks.h: Step 1. One, two and three years
chunks.x:
$$\begin{aligned} C_1 &= 1{,}000 \times 1.05 = 1{,}050 \\ C_2 &= 1{,}000 \times 1.05^2 = 1{,}000 \times 1.1025 = 1{,}102.50 \\ C_3 &= 1{,}000 \times 1.05^3 = 1{,}000 \times 1.157625 = 1{,}157.63 \end{aligned}$$

Each year the interest is earned on the previous year's balance, so the yearly increase grows: 50, then 52.50, then 55.13.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 1 - Capitalization of a Deferred Debt

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x:
Límite S.A. has 1,200 millions to invest in this period. Applying the criterion of recovery or payback, indicate which investment project is preferred and why.

| Project | Initial outlay | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Q5 | Q6 |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| X | 1,200 | −200 | 300 | 500 | 200 | 400 | 400 |
| Y | 1,200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 |
| Z | 1,000 | 125 | 125 | 250 | 250 | 250 | 250 |

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x: Cash flows in millions, one per year. The **payback** (recovery) period is the time the cumulative cash flows take to equal the initial outlay; the shorter, the better. Within a year the flow is taken as uniform.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x:
- X recovers its 1,200 exactly at the end of year 5: **5 years**.
- Y recovers its 1,200 at the end of year 6: **6 years**.
- Z recovers its 1,000 exactly at the end of year 5: **5 years**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x: Y is the worst. X and Z tie at 5 years, so the payback criterion alone does not separate them. Two remarks help: Z needs 200 million less, which stays available to the company, and X has a negative flow in the first year that must be financed. Beyond year 5, X returns 400 in year 6 against 250 for Z; payback ignores those flows.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 3 - Limite Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x:
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, p. 2): payback X = 5 years and Y = 6 years agree; the key prefers X "even if it generates negative cash flow in the first year".

Discrepancy with the official solution
The key gives Z a payback of **5 years and 10 months**. With the outlay of the statement (1,000) the cumulative flow reaches 1,000 exactly at the end of year 5 (table above), so the payback is 5 years. The key's figure is what an outlay of 1,200 would give: $5 + (1{,}200 - 1{,}000)/250 = 5.8$ years, about 5 years and 10 months. With the stated data X and Z tie, and the key's preference for X is not supported by payback alone.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 4 - Maximum Investment from the IRR
chunks.x: What is the maximum amount we should invest in a project at time 0 if the estimated annual cash inflow is €30,000 over a period of 4 years starting from year 1? Assume that the estimated internal rate of return is 8%.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 4 - Maximum Investment from the IRR
chunks.x:
Cash inflows $CF_1 = \dots = CF_4 = 30{,}000$ €; IRR 8%. The **net present value** of a project with outlay $I_0$ is

$$NPV = -I_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1 + k)^t}$$

and the **internal rate of return** is the rate that makes $NPV = 0$. The maximum outlay is the one that leaves the NPV at zero when discounted at 8%: any higher outlay would give a return below 8%.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 4 - Maximum Investment from the IRR
Problem - T3 NPV 4 - Maximum Investment from the IRR
chunks.x:
- **Check with the annuity factor:** $30{,}000 \times \dfrac{1 - 1.08^{-4}}{0.08} = 30{,}000 \times 3.312127 = 99{,}363.81$ €. ✓
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, pp. 2-3): $I_0 = 99{,}363.81$ €. Same result.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T3 Investment Selection NPV and IRR

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x:
Consider these projects (cash flows in euros) and answer the questions:

| Project | C0 | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 | C5 |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | −1,000 | +1,000 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| B | −2,000 | +1,000 | +1,000 | +4,000 | +1,000 | +1,000 |
| C | −3,000 | +1,000 | +1,000 | 0 | +1,000 | +1,000 |

a) If the interest rate is 10%, which projects have a positive NPV? b) Calculate the payback period for each project. c) Which project(s) would be accepted by a company that uses the payback period model if the maximum period is three years?

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x: $NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{5} C_t/(1.10)^t$ with the discount factors $1.1^{-1} = 0.909091$, $1.1^{-2} = 0.826446$, $1.1^{-3} = 0.751315$, $1.1^{-4} = 0.683013$, $1.1^{-5} = 0.620921$. Payback: the time the cumulative flows take to recover the outlay.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
chunks.h: Step 3. Part (c): maximum payback of three years
chunks.x: A and B are accepted, C is rejected. The payback model accepts A although its NPV is negative and rejects C although its NPV is positive, because it ignores the time value of money and the flows after the cut-off. Between the two accepted projects, the NPV favours B.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 5 - NPV and Payback of Three Projects
chunks.x:
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, p. 3): $NPV_A = -90.91$, $NPV_B = 4{,}044.7$, $NPV_C = 39.47$; payback 1, 2 and 4 years; A and B accepted, and B chosen by NPV. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T3 Investment Selection NPV and IRR

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 6 - NPV from a Known IRR
chunks.x: Assuming an interest rate of 7%, consider a three-year investment period generating a positive cash flow of €10,000 per year with an internal rate of return of 10%. Calculate the NPV of this investment.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 6 - NPV from a Known IRR
chunks.x: $CF_1 = CF_2 = CF_3 = 10{,}000$ €, IRR 10%, discount rate $k = 7\%$. The outlay $I_0$ is not given: it follows from the IRR, the rate at which the NPV is zero. Then the NPV is computed at 7%.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 6 - NPV from a Known IRR
Problem - T3 NPV 6 - NPV from a Known IRR
Problem - T3 NPV 6 - NPV from a Known IRR
chunks.x:
- **Check:** at $k = $ IRR the NPV would be zero; a lower rate gives a positive NPV, as found.
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, pp. 3-4): $I_0 = 24{,}868$ € and $NPV = 1{,}375$ €. Same results. The key also adds a part (b), not in the statement: at $k = 9\%$ the NPV is smaller but still positive, since $9\% < 10\%$; its value is $1{,}374.64 - 930.21 = 444.43$ €.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
chunks.x:
You want to rank, in order of preference, according to the criterion of NPV, the investment projects with initial payments and cash flows generated in the different years of their duration, listed in the table below:

| Project | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Year 4 | Year 5 | Initial outlay |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 2,000 | 2,000 | 3,500 | 3,500 | 3,500 | 10,000 |
| B | 2,000 | 2,000 | 4,000 | 4,000 | 4,000 | 11,000 |
| C | 3,000 | 3,000 | 4,000 | 4,000 | 4,000 | 12,000 |
| D | 2,000 | 2,000 | 15,000 | — | — | 13,000 |
| E | 2,000 | 3,000 | 5,000 | 5,000 | 5,000 | 14,000 |
| F | 4,000 | 4,000 | 4,500 | 4,500 | 4,500 | 15,000 |

The required profitability is the same for all projects (10 percent). Which projects should be undertaken by an individual who has 40,000 euros to invest if they cannot be repeated?

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
chunks.x: Net cash flows in euros, discount rate 10% with the factors $0.909091$, $0.826446$, $0.751315$, $0.683013$, $0.620921$ for years 1 to 5. $NPV = -I_0 + \sum CF_t/1.1^t$.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
chunks.x: Taking the projects in order of NPV: D (13,000), then C (12,000, total 25,000), then F (15,000, total 40,000). The budget is used exactly, so the individual undertakes **D, C and F**, with a total NPV of $1{,}740.80 + 1{,}427.61 + 1{,}190.77 = 4{,}359.18$ €.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 7 - Ranking Projects by NPV with a Budget
chunks.x:
- **Check of the budget choice:** no four projects fit in 40,000 € (the four cheapest cost 46,000 €), and every other set of three that fits gives less: D + C + B (36,000 €) 3,860.48 €, D + C + E (39,000 €) 3,742.18 €, D + F + A (38,000 €) 3,596.02 €.
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, pp. 4-5): NPVs 664.45, 692.07, 1,427.61, 1,740.8, 573.77 and 1,190.77 with the same ranking, and D, C and F selected. Same results.
