chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 8 - Gofres IRR Against the Cost of Capital
chunks.x: The director of the financial department of GOFRES, S.A. raises the possibility of investing in a project with a profitability of 8.5%. GOFRES, S.A. is funded 30% with equity capital, whose cost is estimated at 15%, and the rest with external funds, with an average cost of 8%. What would be your advice to this executive: to carry out the project or not to invest, and why? How does your answer change if you were offered another investment project with a yield of 18.5%?

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 8 - Gofres IRR Against the Cost of Capital
chunks.x:
| Source | Share | Cost |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Equity | 30% | 15% |
| Liabilities (external funds) | 70% | 8% |

The cost of capital is the weighted average cost, $K_{WACC} = K_{EQ}\,\frac{E}{E+L} + K_L\,\frac{L}{E+L}$ [Slide 37 of Topic 3]. A project creates value when its return is above that cost (profitability > cost, Slide 5 of Topic 3).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 8 - Gofres IRR Against the Cost of Capital
chunks.x:
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, p. 5): $K = 0.3 \times 0.15 + 0.7 \times 0.08 = 10.1\%$; reject at 8.5%, accept at 18.5%. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T3 Investment Selection NPV and IRR

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
chunks.x:
Company OSOPANDA, S.L. is considering an investment, for which it has two offers. The first offer (Project A) has an initial payment of €16,653 and generates cash flows of €6,500 and €13,000 during the first and second years (two-year period), respectively. The second offer (Project B) means a much higher initial payment, €71,428. It will end in a year, and it is expected to generate a positive cash flow of €76,428 by the end of that year. Answer the following questions and account for your answers:

a) Which project would the company choose if it uses the payback period model?

b) Analyze both alternatives in terms of internal rate of return (IRR).

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
chunks.x:
| Project | $I_0$ (€) | $CF_1$ (€) | $CF_2$ (€) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 16,653 | 6,500 | 13,000 |
| B | 71,428 | 76,428 | — |

Payback with flows spread evenly over each year (30-day months). IRR: the rate that makes $NPV = 0$. The **Fisher rate** is the discount rate at which both projects have the same NPV.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
chunks.x:
A recovers 6,500 in year 1; the remaining $16{,}653 - 6{,}500 = 10{,}153$ € come from the 13,000 of year 2 after $10{,}153/13{,}000 = 0.781$ years $= 9.37$ months: **1 year, 9 months and 11 days** (0.37 × 30 days), recovered during the 12th day.

B recovers 71,428 out of 76,428 after $71{,}428/76{,}428 = 0.9346$ years $= 11.21$ months: **11 months and 6 days** (0.21 × 30), recovered during the 7th day.

B has the shorter payback, so the payback model chooses **B**.

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
chunks.h: Step 4. Fisher rate and the decision by the cost of capital

chunks.t: Problem - T3 NPV 9 - Osopanda Payback, IRR and Fisher Rate
chunks.x:
- **Check of $r_A$:** $6{,}500/1.1 + 13{,}000/1.21 = 5{,}909.09 + 10{,}743.80 = 16{,}652.89 \approx 16{,}653$. ✓
- **Check against the official key** (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, p. 6): payback A "1 year, 9 months and days (12...)" and B "11 months and 7 days", B preferred; IRR(A) ≈ 10%, IRR(B) ≈ 7%; Fisher rate ≈ 5% (0.0507); B below 5%, A between 5% and 10%, neither above 10%. Same results; the key counts the day in which the outlay is recovered (12th and 7th), which is why it gives one day more than the completed days above.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T3 Investment Selection NPV and IRR

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 1 - Price Equal to Variable Cost
chunks.x: A company's annual fixed costs are €2,000. The variable cost per unit equals its selling price, which is €2. What is the break-even point?

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 1 - Price Equal to Variable Cost
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $FC$ | annual fixed costs | 2,000 € |
| $P$ | selling price per unit | 2 €/unit |
| $VC$ | variable cost per unit | 2 €/unit |

The break-even point is the volume at which the profit is zero [Slide 36], and with the unit margin $m = P - VC$ it is $Q_0 = FC/m$ [Slide 37].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 1 - Price Equal to Variable Cost
chunks.x:
$$Q_0 = \frac{FC}{m} = \frac{2{,}000}{0} \to \infty$$

The division has no finite result: no volume makes the profit zero. Writing the profit for any volume shows why,

$$\text{Profit} = Q\,m - FC = Q \times 0 - 2{,}000 = -2{,}000 \ \text{€}$$

Every unit sold brings in exactly what it costs, so nothing is left to cover the fixed costs: the company loses 2,000 € a year whatever it sells.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 1 - Price Equal to Variable Cost
chunks.x:
- **Meaning:** a break-even point only exists when $m > 0$. With $m = 0$ the profit line is horizontal at $-FC$ and never reaches zero.
- **Units:** €/(€/unit) = units.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 3): the key also obtains $Q^* = 2{,}000/(2 - 2) = \infty$ and concludes that the solution makes no economic sense, because the company will never cover its fixed costs. Same result.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.x:
A company has a unit margin of €5.

a) Assuming that the manufacturing of 500 physical units produces a loss of €500, calculate the break-even point.

b) Represent graphically the situation of this company assuming that the maximum capacity of the plant is 900 physical units. What is the maximum profit that can be obtained?

c) Calculate the degree of operating leverage of this company for a production and sales volume of 900 physical units and interpret this result.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $m$ | unit margin | 5 €/unit |
| $B(500)$ | profit at 500 units | −500 € |
| $Q_{max}$ | maximum capacity | 900 units |

The profit is $B = Q\,m - FC$ [Slide 39], the break-even point $Q^* = FC/m$ [Slide 37] and the operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slide 40]. Production equals sales, so $Q$ is both.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.h: Step 1. Part (a): fixed costs and break-even point
chunks.x:
The fixed costs are the only unknown in the profit at 500 units:

$$\begin{aligned} B(500) &= 500\,m - FC \\ -500 &= 500 \times 5 - FC = 2{,}500 - FC \\ FC &= 2{,}500 + 500 = 3{,}000 \ \text{€} \end{aligned}$$

Then

$$Q^* = \frac{FC}{m} = \frac{3{,}000}{5} = 600 \ \text{units}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.h: Step 2. Part (b): graph and maximum profit
chunks.x:
The profit line is $B(Q) = 5\,Q - 3{,}000$, valid between 0 and the capacity of 900 units. It starts at $-3{,}000$ € (only the fixed costs) and crosses zero at 600 units. The line grows with $Q$, so the maximum profit is at the capacity limit:

$$B_{max} = B(900) = 900 \times 5 - 3{,}000 = 4{,}500 - 3{,}000 = 1{,}500 \ \text{€}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.h: Step 3. Part (c): operating leverage at 900 units
chunks.x:
$$OL_{900} = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - FC} = \frac{900 \times 5}{900 \times 5 - 3{,}000} = \frac{4{,}500}{1{,}500} = 3$$

**Interpretation:** a 1% change in sales changes the profit by 3% [Slide 40]. The company is at full capacity and cannot sell more, so only a fall in sales is possible: each 1% fall below 900 units cuts the profit by 3%.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 2 - Break-Even from a Loss and Full Capacity
chunks.x:
- **Check with the BEP form** [Slide 42]: $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*) = 900/(900 - 600) = 3$, the same value.
- **Check of (a):** $B(600) = 600 \times 5 - 3{,}000 = 0$.
- **Units:** $FC$ in €, $Q^*$ in units, OL dimensionless.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, pp. 3-4): $FC = 3{,}000$ €, $q^* = 600$ units, maximum profit 1,500 € and $AO = 3$, with the same reading for a decrease in sales. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.x:
A company manager who wants to market a new product has to choose between two alternative production processes A and B. In both cases the selling price of the product is €20.

| | Process A | Process B |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Fixed costs | 40,000 | 20,000 |
| Unit variable costs | 13 | 15 |

a) Assuming that the expected level of production and sales is 10,000 physical units, decide the most convenient process according to the break-even analysis and the graphic representation.

b) If process B resulted in a higher quality product with a selling price of €25, how would this affect the choice of the most convenient process?

c) If the rise in price of the product obtained with process B (€25) caused a drop in sales from 10,000 to 6,000 physical units, which production process would the company choose?

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.x:
| Magnitude | Process A | Process B |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Price $P$ (€/unit) | 20 | 20 |
| Fixed costs $FC$ (€) | 40,000 | 20,000 |
| Variable cost $VC$ (€/unit) | 13 | 15 |
| Unit margin $m = P - VC$ (€/unit) | 7 | 5 |

Profit $B = Q\,m - FC$, break-even point $Q^* = FC/m$ [Slide 37] and operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slide 40], the index of operating risk [Slide 41].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.h: Step 1. Part (a): profit, break-even point and leverage at 10,000 units
chunks.x:
$$\begin{aligned} B_A &= (20 - 13) \times 10{,}000 - 40{,}000 = 70{,}000 - 40{,}000 = 30{,}000 \ \text{€} \\ B_B &= (20 - 15) \times 10{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 50{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 30{,}000 \ \text{€} \end{aligned}$$

Both processes give the same profit. The break-even points are

$$Q^*_A = \frac{40{,}000}{7} = 5{,}714.3 \ \text{units} \qquad Q^*_B = \frac{20{,}000}{5} = 4{,}000 \ \text{units}$$

and the operating leverages at 10,000 units

$$OL_A = \frac{70{,}000}{30{,}000} = 2.33 \qquad OL_B = \frac{50{,}000}{30{,}000} = 1.67$$

With the same profit, process **B** is chosen: its break-even point is lower, so 10,000 units are farther from it, and its leverage (operating risk) is lower. A fall in sales would hurt A's profit more.

The two profit lines cross where $7\,Q - 40{,}000 = 5\,Q - 20{,}000$, that is $2\,Q = 20{,}000$ and $Q = 10{,}000$ units: below that volume B gives more profit, above it A does. The expected volume is exactly the crossing point.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.h: Step 2. Part (b): process B sold at €25
chunks.x:
The new unit margin of B is $m_B = 25 - 15 = 10$ €/unit, twice the old one. At 10,000 units:

$$B_B = 10 \times 10{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 80{,}000 \ \text{€} \qquad Q^*_B = \frac{20{,}000}{10} = 2{,}000 \ \text{units} \qquad OL_B = \frac{100{,}000}{80{,}000} = 1.25$$

Process A is unchanged (30,000 €, $OL_A = 2.33$). B now gives more profit with less operating risk: **B** is chosen with even more reason.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.h: Step 3. Part (c): B at €25 but only 6,000 units sold
chunks.x:
$$B_B = (25 - 15) \times 6{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 60{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 40{,}000 \ \text{€}$$

Process A, which keeps the price of 20 € and the 10,000 units, still gives 30,000 €. Since $40{,}000 > 30{,}000$, the company still chooses **B**. Its leverage is $OL_B = 60{,}000/40{,}000 = 1.5$, also below A's 2.33.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 3 - Choosing Between Two Production Processes
chunks.x:
- **Check of the crossing:** at 10,000 units both lines give 30,000 €, as found in (a).
- **Units:** profits in €, break-even points in units, OL dimensionless.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, pp. 4-5): profits 30,000 € for both processes, $AO_A = 2.33$, $AO_B = 1.66$ (1.67 rounded up here), B chosen in (a), (b) and (c), with 40,000 € > 30,000 € in (c). Same results.

Discrepancy with the official solution
Two sentences of the key do not match its own numbers. In (a) it says that "A has a lower break-even point than B"; in fact $Q^*_A = 40{,}000/7 = 5{,}714$ units is **higher** than $Q^*_B = 4{,}000$ units, which is why B carries less risk, as the key itself concludes. In (b) it says the price rise increases "the unit margin by 5%"; the margin goes up by 5 € (from 5 to 10 €/unit, a 100% increase). The choices of the key are not affected.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
Given the following information: selling price €10; variable cost per unit €3; fixed costs €1,000.

a) How many units must be sold to start making a profit?

b) What would the profit be if the company sold 200 units?

c) What is the degree of operating leverage for 200 units sold?

d) Will the degree of operating leverage vary if there is a 50 unit increase in sales?

e) Will the degree of operating leverage vary if there is a 10% rise in price (for 200 units)?

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $P$ | selling price | 10 €/unit |
| $VC$ | variable cost per unit | 3 €/unit |
| $FC$ | fixed costs | 1,000 € |
| $m$ | unit margin, $P - VC$ | 7 €/unit |

Break-even point $Q^* = FC/m$ [Slide 37], profit $B = Q\,m - FC$ and operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slides 39-40].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
$$Q^* = \frac{FC}{P - VC} = \frac{1{,}000}{10 - 3} = \frac{1{,}000}{7} = 142.86 \ \text{units}$$

Units are whole, so at 142 units the profit is still negative ($142 \times 7 - 1{,}000 = -6$ €) and at 143 it becomes positive ($143 \times 7 - 1{,}000 = 1$ €): the company starts making a profit from **143 units**.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
$$OL_{200} = \frac{200 \times 7}{200 \times 7 - 1{,}000} = \frac{1{,}400}{400} = 3.5$$

A 1% change in sales changes the profit by 3.5%.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
$$OL_{250} = \frac{250 \times 7}{250 \times 7 - 1{,}000} = \frac{1{,}750}{750} = 2.33$$

Yes, it varies: it falls from 3.5 to 2.33, because the volume has moved away from the break-even point [Slide 42].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
The new price is $10 \times 1.10 = 11$ €/unit, so $m = 11 - 3 = 8$ €/unit and

$$OL = \frac{200 \times 8}{200 \times 8 - 1{,}000} = \frac{1{,}600}{600} = 2.67$$

Yes, it varies: it falls from 3.5 to 2.67. The higher margin lowers the break-even point to $1{,}000/8 = 125$ units, so 200 units are now farther from it.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 4 - Leverage After a Change in Volume or Price
chunks.x:
- **Check with the BEP form** [Slide 42]: (c) $200/(200 - 142.86) = 3.5$; (d) $250/(250 - 142.86) = 2.33$; (e) $200/(200 - 125) = 2.67$.
- **Units:** $Q^*$ in units, profit in €, OL dimensionless.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 5): $q^* \approx 143$ units, profit 400 €, $AO = 3.5$, $2.33$ and $2.66$ (2.67 rounded up here), with the same explanation (the volume moves away from the break-even point; the price changes the break-even point). Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
A visit to a company has provided the following information:

- If the company produced and sold 300 physical units, it would make a profit of €56.
- If the company produced and sold 160 physical units, it would make zero profit.
- The company forecasts sales of 500 physical units.

Calculate the company's fixed costs, the forecast profit, its safety margin and the degree of operating leverage.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
| Observation | Volume $Q$ (units) | Profit $B$ (€) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 300 | 56 |
| 2 (break-even point) | 160 | 0 |
| Forecast | 500 | ? |

The profit is linear in the volume, $B = Q\,m - FC$ [Slide 39]; the margin of safety is $Q - Q^*$ in units, $(Q - Q^*)\,m$ in monetary units and $(Q - Q^*)/Q^*$ in percentage [Slide 43]; the leverage is $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slide 40].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
Subtracting the two observations removes the fixed costs:

$$\begin{aligned} B(300) - B(160) &= (300\,m - FC) - (160\,m - FC) = (300 - 160)\,m \\ 56 - 0 &= 140\,m \\ m &= \frac{56}{140} = 0.4 \ \text{€/unit} \end{aligned}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
$$MS = Q - Q^* = 500 - 160 = 340 \ \text{units}$$

In monetary units, $MS = 340 \times 0.4 = 136$ €, and as a percentage of the break-even volume, $MS = 340/160 = 2.125$, that is 212.5%.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
$$OL_{500} = \frac{500 \times 0.4}{500 \times 0.4 - 64} = \frac{200}{136} = 1.47$$

A 1% change in sales changes the profit by 1.47%.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 5 - Cost Structure from Two Observations
chunks.x:
- **Check with observation 1:** $300 \times 0.4 - 64 = 120 - 64 = 56$ €. ✓
- **Check with the BEP form** [Slide 42]: $OL = 500/(500 - 160) = 1.47$. ✓
- **Note:** above the break-even point the margin of safety in m.u. equals the profit (136 €), since $(Q - Q^*)\,m = Q\,m - FC$.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 6): $m = 0.4$ €/unit, $FC = 64$ €, forecast profit 136 €, $MS = 340$ units, $AO = 1.47$. Same results; the key gives the margin of safety in units only.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 6 - Leverage from the Break-Even Point Alone
chunks.x: On the financial pages of a Spanish newspaper it was recently announced that a manufacturing company specialized in certain automotive components had sold 100,000 units of its product last year, well above its break-even point, set at 20,000 physical units approximately. What is the degree of operating leverage for this company?

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 6 - Leverage from the Break-Even Point Alone
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $Q$ | units sold | 100,000 units |
| $Q^*$ | break-even point | 20,000 units |

Price, costs and margin are not given. The form of the leverage that uses only the two volumes is the one of Slide 42.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 6 - Leverage from the Break-Even Point Alone
chunks.h: Step 1. The leverage in terms of the break-even point
chunks.x:
From $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slide 40] and $Q^* = FC/m$, so $FC = Q^*\,m$ [Slide 37]:

$$OL = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - Q^*\,m} = \frac{m\,Q}{m\,(Q - Q^*)} = \frac{Q}{Q - Q^*}$$

The unit margin cancels.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 6 - Leverage from the Break-Even Point Alone
chunks.x:
$$OL = \frac{100{,}000}{100{,}000 - 20{,}000} = \frac{100{,}000}{80{,}000} = 1.25$$

A 1% change in sales changes the profit by 1.25%. Being far above the break-even point, the company has a leverage close to 1, a low operating risk.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 6 - Leverage from the Break-Even Point Alone
chunks.x:
- **Limit:** as $Q$ grows far beyond $Q^*$, $OL \to 1$; as $Q$ approaches $Q^*$ from above, $OL \to \infty$ [Slide 42]. 1.25 fits a volume five times the break-even point.
- **Units:** units/units, dimensionless.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 6): $AO = 100{,}000/(100{,}000 - 20{,}000) = 1.25$, obtained by the same substitution. Same result.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 7 - Sumun Break-Even Point and Leverage
chunks.x:
We have the following data corresponding to a certain product manufactured by Sumun S.A.:

- Unit margin: €10
- Annual sales volume: 2,000 units
- Annual fixed costs: €1,000

Calculate: a) the break-even point of this product; b) its degree of operating leverage.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 7 - Sumun Break-Even Point and Leverage
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $m$ | unit margin | 10 €/unit |
| $Q$ | annual sales | 2,000 units |
| $FC$ | annual fixed costs | 1,000 € |

Break-even point $Q^* = FC/m$ [Slide 37], operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ [Slide 40].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 7 - Sumun Break-Even Point and Leverage
chunks.x:
$$OL_{2000} = \frac{2{,}000 \times 10}{2{,}000 \times 10 - 1{,}000} = \frac{20{,}000}{19{,}000} = 1.05$$

A 1% change in sales changes the profit by about 1.05%: with sales twenty times the break-even point, the profit moves almost in proportion to the sales.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 7 - Sumun Break-Even Point and Leverage
chunks.x:
- **Check with the BEP form** [Slide 42]: $2{,}000/(2{,}000 - 100) = 2{,}000/1{,}900 = 1.05$. ✓
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 7): $q^* = 100$ units and $AO = 20{,}000/19{,}000 = 1.05$. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
chunks.x:
Company ENIR, S.A., a black cigarette manufacturer, has not obtained profits during year 2008. It was established two years before and its maximum production capacity amounts to 11 million packs per year. Analyzing its management, we know that in 2008, the company produced 10 million packs, with financial costs relative to its external financing of €300,000, fixed costs of commercialization and administration of €1,000,000 and other fixed costs of €1,700,000. The selling price was €1.3 per pack, which was established by the Government, as this is an industry regulated by the State.

For the following year 2009 and, maintaining the same facilities, the company expects an increase of 15% in its fixed costs, as well as a decrease of 1% in the variable cost per unit. Calculate:

a) The break-even point for year 2009.

b) Considering these plans, is it possible that the company obtains profits? Account for your answer.

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
chunks.x:
| Magnitude | 2008 | 2009 |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Capacity (packs) | 11,000,000 | 11,000,000 |
| Volume $Q$ (packs) | 10,000,000 | ? |
| Price $P$ (€/pack) | 1.3 | 1.3 |
| Fixed costs $FC$ (€) | 3,000,000 | +15% |
| Variable cost $VC$ (€/pack) | unknown | −1% |

**Reading of the statement (the same as the official key):** "has not obtained profits" is read as a profit of exactly zero in 2008, so 10 million packs was the break-even point of 2008; and the financial costs of 300,000 € are counted among the fixed costs:

$$FC_{2008} = 300{,}000 + 1{,}000{,}000 + 1{,}700{,}000 = 3{,}000{,}000 \ \text{€}$$

Break-even condition: profit $= Q\,(P - VC) - FC = 0$ [Slides 36-37].

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
chunks.h: Step 1. Variable cost per pack in 2008

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
chunks.h: Step 4. Part (b): can the company make a profit?
chunks.x:
No. The break-even point (11,129,032 packs) is above the maximum capacity of the facilities (11,000,000 packs), and the price is fixed by the Government. Even working at full capacity the company loses money:

$$B(11{,}000{,}000) = 11{,}000{,}000 \times 0.31 - 3{,}450{,}000 = 3{,}410{,}000 - 3{,}450{,}000 = -40{,}000 \ \text{€}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4 Exercise 8 - ENIR Break-Even Point Beyond Capacity
chunks.x:
- **Check of Step 1:** $10{,}000{,}000 \times (1.3 - 1.0) - 3{,}000{,}000 = 0$. ✓
- **Units:** €/(€/pack) = packs.
- **Check against the official key** (BEP OL Statements Solutions.pdf, p. 7): $FC = 3{,}000{,}000$ €, $VC = 1.0$ €/unit, $FC_{2009} = 3{,}450{,}000$ €, $VC_{2009} = 0.99$ €, break-even point 11,129,032 units, and no profit possible because the maximum volume is 11,000,000. Same results; the key calls the packs "bottles" in its last sentence.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x:
The following table presents data concerning the demand for Product X:

| Point | Price | Quantity |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| A | 25 | 0 |
| B | 20 | 20 |
| C | 15 | 40 |
| D | 10 | 60 |
| E | 5 | 80 |
| F | 0 | 100 |

A) Draw the demand curve. B) What is elasticity? C) What is the sign of the coefficient of elasticity? D) Calculate the price elasticity at the mid-point of each interval.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x:
Six points of the demand of product X, equally spaced: from one point to the next the price falls by 5 € and the quantity rises by 20 units.

The price elasticity is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2). Between two points the percentages are taken with respect to the **midpoint** of the interval, as the statement asks:

$$E_d = \frac{\Delta Q / \bar Q}{\Delta P / \bar P}, \qquad \bar Q = \frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2}, \quad \bar P = \frac{P_1 + P_2}{2}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x: Each step of $-5$ € in price adds 20 units, so the slope is constant and the points lie on a straight line. Through A (0, 25): $P = 25 - \frac{5}{20}\,Q = 25 - Q/4$, or $Q = 100 - 4P$.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x: Elasticity is the sensitivity of the quantity demanded to a change in the price of the good, with both changes expressed in relative terms (%) (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2; Slide 17).

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x: **Negative.** By the law of demand, when the price falls the quantity demanded rises, and vice versa: $\Delta Q$ and $\Delta P$ always have opposite signs. The absolute value is used to classify the demand.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.h: Step 4. Part (D): midpoint elasticity of each interval
chunks.x:
In every interval $\Delta Q = +20$ and $\Delta P = -5$. For A-B, $\bar Q = (0 + 20)/2 = 10$ and $\bar P = (25 + 20)/2 = 22.5$:

$$E_{AB} = \frac{20/10}{-5/22.5} = \frac{2}{-0.2222} = -9$$

The same computation for the other intervals:

| Interval | $\bar Q$ | $\bar P$ | $\Delta Q/\bar Q$ | $\Delta P/\bar P$ | $E_d$ | Demand |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| A-B | 10 | 22.5 | 2.0000 | −0.2222 | −9.00 | elastic |
| B-C | 30 | 17.5 | 0.6667 | −0.2857 | −2.33 | elastic |
| C-D | 50 | 12.5 | 0.4000 | −0.4000 | −1.00 | unit elastic |
| D-E | 70 | 7.5 | 0.2857 | −0.6667 | −0.43 | inelastic |
| E-F | 90 | 2.5 | 0.2222 | −2.0000 | −0.11 | inelastic |

Along a straight demand line the slope is constant, but the elasticity is not: it falls in absolute value as we move down the line, because $\bar P/\bar Q$ falls. The demand is elastic on the upper half, unit elastic at the middle (Q = 50, P = 12.5) and inelastic on the lower half.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 1 - Demand Curve and Midpoint Elasticities
chunks.x:
- **Point form:** with $dQ/dP = -4$, the point elasticity $E_d = -4\,P/Q$ at the midpoint of C-D is $-4 \times 12.5/50 = -1$, matching the table.
- **Units:** both ratios are dimensionless.
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, pp. 1-2): the same demand curve; elasticity as the sensitivity of quantity to price in relative terms; negative sign by the law of demand; midpoint elasticities −9, −2.33, −1, −0.43 and −0.11. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 2 - Quantity Sold After a Price Rise
chunks.x: The price elasticity of demand of a certain good is 2 and we are currently selling 100 units at a price of 20 €. How many units will be sold at a price of 21 €? Show your answer with the respective calculations.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 2 - Quantity Sold After a Price Rise
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $\lvert E_d \rvert$ | price elasticity (absolute value) | 2 |
| $Q_1$, $P_1$ | current quantity and price | 100 units, 20 € |
| $P_2$ | new price | 21 € |
| $x$ | units sold at 21 € | unknown |

Price elasticity $E_d = (\%\Delta Q)/(\%\Delta P)$, negative by the law of demand (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2). Two ways of taking the percentages give two estimates.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 2 - Quantity Sold After a Price Rise
chunks.h: Step 1. Estimate with the initial values as base (Slide 17)
chunks.x:
$$\%\Delta P = \frac{21 - 20}{20} = 5\% \qquad \%\Delta Q = E_d \cdot \%\Delta P = -2 \times 5\% = -10\%$$

$$x = 100 \times (1 - 0.10) = 90 \ \text{units}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 2 - Quantity Sold After a Price Rise
chunks.h: Step 2. Exact value with the midpoint of the change
chunks.x:
Taking the elasticity at the midpoint of the change from $P = 20$ to $P = 21$ and from $Q = 100$ to $Q = x$:

$$\frac{(x - 100) \big/ \frac{x + 100}{2}}{(21 - 20) \big/ \frac{21 + 20}{2}} = -2$$

The price part is $1/20.5$, so

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{2\,(x - 100)}{x + 100} \cdot 20.5 &= -2 \\ \frac{41\,(x - 100)}{x + 100} &= -2 \\ 41x - 4{,}100 &= -2x - 200 \\ 43x &= 3{,}900 \\ x &= \frac{3{,}900}{43} = 90.70 \ \text{units} \end{aligned}$$

At 21 € about **90.7 units** are sold (90 units in the simpler estimate).

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 2 - Quantity Sold After a Price Rise
chunks.x:
- **Check of the midpoint value:** $\Delta Q/\bar Q = (90.70 - 100)/95.35 = -0.0975$ and $\Delta P/\bar P = 1/20.5 = 0.0488$; the ratio is $-2.00$. ✓
- **Meaning:** demand is elastic ($\lvert E_d \rvert = 2 > 1$), so the 5% price rise lowers sales by about 10% and revenue falls from $20 \times 100 = 2{,}000$ € to $21 \times 90.70 = 1{,}904.7$ €.
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, p. 2): about 90 units in rough numbers, and $x = 3{,}900/43 = 90.697$ units with the midpoint formula. Same result; $3{,}900/43 = 90.6977$, which the key truncates to 90.697 and is rounded here to 90.70.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 3 - Mini Laptop Elasticity and Revenue
chunks.x:
A company selling mini laptops is marketing a particular laptop in a market where demand corresponds to the expression $Q_d = 25000 - 40p$. This company is considering increasing the selling price of the mini laptop and would like to know what impact the increase in price will have on the total income.

a. Calculate the value of this elasticity considering the current price of its mini laptop is 500 m.u.

b. In view of the above result, state with appropriate reasons whether the firm should increase its price and the effect that total income will have due to this price increase.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 3 - Mini Laptop Elasticity and Revenue
chunks.x:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $Q_d(p)$ | demand | $25{,}000 - 40\,p$ |
| $p$ | current price | 500 m.u. |

Point price elasticity $E_d = \dfrac{dq}{dp}\cdot\dfrac{p}{q}$ (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2), and the relation between elasticity and income of p. 3.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 3 - Mini Laptop Elasticity and Revenue
chunks.x:
The derivative of the demand is $dq/dp = -40$, so

$$E_d = \frac{dq}{dp}\cdot\frac{p}{q} = -40 \times \frac{500}{5{,}000} = -4$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 3 - Mini Laptop Elasticity and Revenue
chunks.h: Step 3. Part (b): should the firm raise the price?
chunks.x: $\lvert E_d \rvert = 4 > 1$: the demand is **elastic**. A price rise of 1% lowers the quantity sold by about 4%, so total income ($p \cdot q$) **falls** (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3). The firm should **not** raise the price; if anything, a price cut would raise income.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 3 - Mini Laptop Elasticity and Revenue
chunks.x:
- **Check with the revenue function:** $I(p) = p\,(25{,}000 - 40\,p)$, so $dI/dp = 25{,}000 - 80\,p$, which at $p = 500$ is $25{,}000 - 40{,}000 = -15{,}000 < 0$: income falls when the price rises. ✓
- **Check with a small change:** at $p = 501$, $q = 4{,}960$ and $I = 2{,}484{,}960$ m.u., below $I(500) = 2{,}500{,}000$ m.u. ✓
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, p. 3): $q = 5{,}000$ units, $\eta = -40 \times 500/5{,}000 = -4$, demand elastic, and a price rise would lower total revenue. Same results.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 4 - Quantity Change After a Price Cut
chunks.x:
If a producer lowers the prices by 20% in a given good, knowing that the elasticity of demand with respect to price is 1.5, how much do you estimate the quantity demanded will vary (as a percentage)?

a) 15% b) 30% c) 45% d) 5%

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 4 - Quantity Change After a Price Cut
chunks.x: Price change $\%\Delta P = -20\%$; price elasticity $\lvert E_d \rvert = 1.5$. From the definition $E_d = \%\Delta Q / \%\Delta P$ (Slide 17; topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2), $\%\Delta Q = E_d \cdot \%\Delta P$.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 4 - Quantity Change After a Price Cut
chunks.x:
With the sign of the law of demand, $E_d = -1.5$:

$$\%\Delta Q = E_d \cdot \%\Delta P = (-1.5) \times (-20\%) = +30\%$$

The quantity demanded rises by **30%**: answer **b)**.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 4 - Quantity Change After a Price Cut
chunks.h: Step 2. Why the other options are wrong
chunks.x:
- a) 15% would need $\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.75$.
- c) 45% would need $\lvert E_d \rvert = 2.25$, or a 30% price cut.
- d) 5% would need $\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.25$, an inelastic demand.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 4 - Quantity Change After a Price Cut
chunks.x:
- **Meaning:** demand is elastic ($1.5 > 1$), so the quantity changes more, in percentage, than the price.
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, p. 3): answer b), $20\% \times 1.5 = 30\%$. Same answer.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 5 - Elastic Demand and Revenue
chunks.x:
When the price elasticity of demand for a normal good is relatively elastic:

a) A reduction in the price of the good involves obtaining a higher income by the offerer.
b) A reduction in the price of the good involves obtaining a lower income by the offerer.
c) A reduction of prices does not alter the amount of income by the offerer.
d) None of the other answers is correct.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 5 - Elastic Demand and Revenue
chunks.x: "Relatively elastic" means $\lvert E_d \rvert > 1$ (Slide 17). The seller's income is $I = P \cdot Q$; its reaction to a price change is given by the table of topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 5 - Elastic Demand and Revenue
chunks.h: Step 1. Effect of a price cut on income
chunks.x:
With elastic demand, a 1% fall in price raises the quantity demanded by more than 1%. In $I = P \cdot Q$ the rise of $Q$ outweighs the fall of $P$, so income **rises** (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3). Answer **a)**.

A short numerical illustration with $\lvert E_d \rvert = 2$: a 5% price cut raises the quantity by about 10%, and income changes by the factor $0.95 \times 1.10 = 1.045$, a 4.5% rise.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 5 - Elastic Demand and Revenue
chunks.h: Step 2. Why the other options are wrong
chunks.x:
- b) describes **inelastic** demand ($\lvert E_d \rvert < 1$), where a price cut lowers income.
- c) describes **unit elastic** demand ($\lvert E_d \rvert = 1$), where income does not change.
- d) is wrong because a) is correct.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 5 - Elastic Demand and Revenue
chunks.x:
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, p. 3): answer a). Same answer.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 6 - Substitute Goods from Cross Effects
chunks.x:
If when the price of a good "X" is reduced, an increase is induced in the quantity demanded of good "X" itself, as well as a decrease in the quantity demanded of good "Y", we say that "X" and "Y" are:

a) Complementary b) Substitutes c) Normal goods d) None of the previous

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 6 - Substitute Goods from Cross Effects
chunks.x: The price of X falls, the demand for X rises and the demand for Y falls. The **cross elasticity** $E_{YX} = \%\Delta Q_Y / \%\Delta P_X$ is positive for substitutes and negative for complements (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 5).

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 6 - Substitute Goods from Cross Effects
chunks.h: Step 1. Sign of the cross elasticity
chunks.x:
The price of X falls ($\%\Delta P_X < 0$) and the quantity of Y falls ($\%\Delta Q_Y < 0$):

$$E_{YX} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_Y}{\%\Delta P_X} = \frac{(-)}{(-)} > 0$$

A positive cross elasticity means **substitutes**: answer **b)**. In words, X became cheaper and buyers moved from Y to X (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 5).

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 6 - Substitute Goods from Cross Effects
chunks.h: Step 2. Why the other options are wrong
chunks.x:
- a) Complementary goods would see the demand for **both** rise when the price of X falls.
- c) "Normal good" describes the reaction of a good to the buyers' income, not to the price of another good, and the statement gives no income change.
- d) is wrong because b) is correct.

chunks.t: Problem - T5 Exercise 6 - Substitute Goods from Cross Effects
chunks.x:
- **Check against the official key** (PED Exercises SOL.pdf, p. 4): answer b). Same answer.

**Back to:** Problem Set - T5 Price Elasticity of Demand

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x: SkyCourier S.L. delivers medicines by drone to villages in the Pyrenees. It rents a hangar from a local farmer, employs twelve pilots and technicians, and was financed by investors who bought its shares. Each month it charges the regional health service and several pharmacies for the deliveries. In 2025 the families of the valley spent part of their wages on SkyCourier's new home-delivery service, and the company paid its first dividend to its shareholders.

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x: A business transforms inputs into outputs [Slides 3-4]. The classic factors are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x:
- Output: a service (drone delivery), not a good.
- Land: the hangar site; labour: pilots and technicians; capital: drones, equipment and the investors' money; entrepreneurship: the founders who coordinate and bear the risk.

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x:
SkyCourier's **output** is a **service**, the delivery of medicines and parcels. Its **inputs** are the factors of production [Slides 3-4]:

| Factor | In SkyCourier |
| :--- | :--- |
| Land (natural resources) | The rented hangar site |
| Labour | The twelve pilots and technicians |
| Capital | Drones, charging stations, software; the money provided by investors |
| Entrepreneurship | The founders who bring the other factors together and take the risk |

The business activity is precisely the transformation of these inputs into the delivery service.

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x: Every exchange has two sides that run in opposite directions [Slide 11]. Households own the factors and are the units of consumption [Slide 7].

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x:
- Factor market: households deliver land, labour and capital; SkyCourier pays rent, wages and dividends.
- Goods and services market: SkyCourier delivers the service; households pay for it.
- Real and financial flows run in opposite directions; what the firm keeps is its profit.

chunks.t: SkyCourier: real and financial flows of a drone-delivery start-up
chunks.x:
The circular flow of income links firms and households through two markets [Slides 5-11]:

| Market | Real flow | Financial flow (opposite direction) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Factor market** | Households → SkyCourier: the hangar (land), work (labour), savings invested in shares (capital) | SkyCourier → households: rent to the farmer, wages to the staff, dividends to the shareholders |
| **Market of goods and services** | SkyCourier → households: the delivery service | Households → SkyCourier: the price of the deliveries, paid out of their wages |

The flows close a circle: the wages paid by SkyCourier return to it, in part, when the families buy its home-delivery service. The **real flows** are the factors and the service; the **financial flows** are their monetary compensation, running the other way [Slide 11]. What SkyCourier keeps after paying all the factors is its **profit**, from which the dividend was paid.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x: Orbital Fasteners S.A. makes titanium bolts certified for satellites. On a single Monday: (1) the purchasing team ordered 2 tonnes of titanium bar; (2) the CNC lines produced 40,000 bolts; (3) the sales engineer presented the company at a space-industry fair; (4) the finance department negotiated a bank loan to buy a new thread-rolling machine; (5) it collected an invoice from a satellite integrator and paid the titanium supplier; (6) HR interviewed two quality inspectors; (7) the plant manager set the production targets for the next quarter and checked last month's scrap rate against the plan; (8) the IT team upgraded the traceability database.

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x: Real functions follow the product (supply, production, marketing, support); financial functions follow the money (financing, investing, paying and collecting); management functions are planning, organization and control [Slide 13].

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x:
- Real: 1 (supply), 2 (production), 3 (marketing), 6 and 8 (support: HR, information systems).
- Financial: 4 (financing and investing), 5 (collecting revenues and paying for inputs).
- Management: 7 (planning and control).

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x:
| Activity | Function | Group [Slide 13] |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Ordering titanium | Supply (acquisition of inputs) | Real |
| 2. Producing bolts | Production | Real |
| 3. Trade fair | Marketing | Real |
| 4. Bank loan for a machine | Financing and investing | Financial |
| 5. Collecting and paying | Receiving revenues and paying for inputs | Financial |
| 6. Hiring inspectors | Support (Human Resources) | Real |
| 7. Targets and scrap check | Planning and control | Management |
| 8. Traceability database | Support (Information Systems) | Real |

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x: The financial functions run alongside the real cycle [Slide 13]; recall the role of engineers in business management [Slide 15].

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x:
- The financial cycle mirrors the real one: funds raised → inputs paid → revenues collected → capital and interest returned.
- Engineers: project planning, time management, problem solving, attention to detail, data processing, technical knowledge.

chunks.t: Orbital Fasteners: sorting a day of activity into the functional areas
chunks.x:
The **financial cycle runs alongside the real cycle** [Slide 13]: the company raises funds (the loan of activity 4), uses them to pay for inputs (the titanium of activity 1, paid in activity 5), turns the inputs into bolts and sells them, collects the revenue (activity 5) and finally returns capital and interest to those who lent the money. Without the financial functions the real cycle stops; without the real cycle there is no revenue to repay the funds.

Engineers bring **project planning, time management and problem solving, attention to detail, experience in data processing, computer skills and technical knowledge** [Slide 15]: exactly what activity 7 (targets and scrap control) and activity 8 (traceability data) require.

chunks.t: Atlas Line Maintenance: the four stages of the management process in a ramp-up
chunks.x: Atlas Line Maintenance S.L. has won a contract to perform the overnight checks of a low-cost airline at a new base. The station manager, Marta, has six months to be ready. She sets the goal of "zero technical delays in the first summer" and a plan to hire and certify 25 mechanics. She draws the shift structure and decides who is responsible for each aircraft type and which tools each shift needs. During the first weeks she holds daily briefings, encourages the team and mediates a conflict between the night and day shifts over handovers. Every Friday she compares the delays and the hours per check with the targets and adjusts the shifts.

chunks.t: Atlas Line Maintenance: the four stages of the management process in a ramp-up
chunks.x:
- Planning: the zero-delay goal and the hiring and certification plan.
- Organizing: shift structure, responsibilities, tools.
- Leading: daily briefings, motivation, resolving the shift conflict.
- Controlling: weekly comparison of delays and hours with the targets.

chunks.t: Atlas Line Maintenance: the four stages of the management process in a ramp-up
chunks.x:
| Stage [Slide 14] | Content | At Atlas |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Planning** | Defining goals, establishing strategy, developing subplans | "Zero technical delays"; plan to hire and certify 25 mechanics |
| **Organizing** | What must be done, how, and by whom | Shift structure, responsibilities per aircraft type, tools per shift |
| **Leading** | Directing and motivating, resolving conflicts | Daily briefings, encouragement, mediation between shifts |
| **Controlling** | Monitoring that activities go as planned | Friday comparison of delays and hours per check with the targets |

chunks.t: Atlas Line Maintenance: the four stages of the management process in a ramp-up
chunks.x:
- Control results feed the next round of planning: the process is cyclical.
- A deviation triggers corrective action: reorganizing the shifts or revising the plan, then leading the change.

chunks.t: Atlas Line Maintenance: the four stages of the management process in a ramp-up
chunks.x:
The management process is a **cycle** around the organization's purpose [Slide 14]. Control is not the end: when the Friday review shows a deviation (for example, more hours per check than planned), Marta corrects it by **reorganizing** the shifts or by **revising the plan** (more mechanics, new targets), and she must then **lead** the team through the change. The new results are controlled the following week, so the four stages keep repeating while the base operates.

chunks.t: An eVTOL founder: the four views of the entrepreneur and her rights
chunks.x: Lucía, an aerospace engineer, noticed in 2023 that city hospitals needed faster transfers of organs than road ambulances could offer, and that nobody was serving that need. She designed an electric vertical-take-off aircraft with a new battery-cooling system, mortgaged her flat to fund the first prototype, and brought together a team of engineers, a supplier of carbon structures and a hangar owner. Today she signs every contract of the company, decides who works on each project, keeps whatever profit is left once everyone has been paid, and has been offered a large sum by an airline for her stake.

chunks.t: An eVTOL founder: the four views of the entrepreneur and her rights
chunks.x:
- On alert (Kirzner): she detected an unserved need.
- Innovator (Schumpeter): a new aircraft and battery-cooling system.
- Risk taker (Knight): she mortgaged her flat.
- Coordinator: she brought together engineers, supplier and hangar owner.

chunks.t: An eVTOL founder: the four views of the entrepreneur and her rights
chunks.x:
| View [Slide 17] | Evidence in the case |
| :--- | :--- |
| **"On alert"** (Kirzner, 1973) | She detected a new business opportunity, a need nobody was serving |
| **Innovator** (Schumpeter, 1950) | She introduced a new product with a new battery-cooling technology |
| **Risk taker** (Knight, 1921) | She risked her own flat to finance the prototype |
| **Coordinator** | She brought land (hangar), labour (engineers) and capital (supplier, funds) together |

Together these are the functions of the entrepreneur: coordinate and control production, ensure payment of the factors, take risky decisions, innovate, and detect opportunities [Slide 17].

chunks.t: An eVTOL founder: the four views of the entrepreneur and her rights
chunks.x:
- Right to the residual income (the profit left after paying the factors).
- Right to control and reassign the other factors (who works on each project).
- Being the central party in all contracts.
- Right to sell these rights (the airline's offer).

chunks.t: An eVTOL founder: the four views of the entrepreneur and her rights
chunks.x:
A firm is teamwork, and team production needs someone who controls it; the incentive to take that role comes from four **rights** [Slide 18]. Lucía holds all of them: she receives the **residual income** (the profit left once every factor is paid); she **controls and reassigns** the other factors (she decides who works on each project); she is the **central party in all the contracts** with the inputs (she signs them); and she can **sell these rights** (the airline's offer for her stake). The person who holds all these rights is, by definition, the entrepreneur.

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x: Ana, Bruno and Carla want to open a shop that repairs composite parts of light aircraft. Ana would invest 60,000 m.u. of savings; Bruno and Carla only their work. A single faulty repair could lead to claims far larger than everything they own, so they worry about losing their homes. They want to start quickly and cheaply, but in five years they hope to open three more shops with outside investors, and they want the business to continue if one of them leaves.

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x:
- Sole proprietorship: one owner only, unlimited liability: ruled out.
- Partnership: easy to start, pooled talents; unlimited and joint liability, relative impermanence.
- Corporation: limited liability, permanence, easy transfer of shares, greater financial capability; complex and costly, double taxation.

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x:
| Feature | Sole proprietorship | Partnership | Corporation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Owners | One person | Two or more co-owners | Shareholders |
| Liability | Unlimited | **Unlimited and joint** | **Limited** |
| Starting | Simple | Few restrictions | Complex and costly |
| Permanence | Impermanent | Relatively impermanent | Permanent |
| Funds | Hard to raise | Pooled funds and talents | Greater financial capability |
| Taxation | No separate tax | No separate tax | Special and double taxation |

A sole proprietorship belongs to **one** person [Slide 21], so it does not fit three owners. A partnership is easy to set up through a partnership agreement and pools Ana's money with Bruno's and Carla's skills [Slide 22], but each partner answers for the firm's debts with all their personal wealth, jointly [Slide 23]. A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners have **limited** liability [Slide 24].

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x: Weigh their biggest fear (claims) and their plans (outside investors, continuity) against the cost of forming the company.

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x:
- Recommend a corporation: limited liability protects their homes; permanence; easy entry of investors through shares.
- Accept its drawbacks: cost of formation, regulation and disclosure, double taxation.

chunks.t: Three engineers choosing a legal form for a composite-repair shop
chunks.x:
The **corporation** fits best. Limited liability addresses their main fear: a large claim would affect the company's assets, not their homes. It is **permanent**, so the business continues if one partner leaves, and ownership is **easily transferred through shares**, which is how the outside investors of the expansion would enter; it also has greater financial capability [Slide 24]. The price is a more complex and costly formation, government regulation and disclosure requirements, and double taxation; the engineers should accept these costs in exchange for protection and growth. The course also lists forms of partnership that limit liability: the limited liability partnership (LLP) [Slide 20] and the limited partnership, where some partners answer only up to what they invested [Slide 29]. An LLP would also meet the fear of claims, but the corporation fits better with the plans for outside investors and continuity.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Meseta Aerostructures: a CEO, dispersed shareholders and the agency problem
chunks.x: Meseta Aerostructures S.A. is listed on the stock exchange; no shareholder owns more than 2% of its shares. Its CEO, a professional manager, is paid a fixed salary that grows with the number of employees under her. In three years she has bought two loss-making companies, moved headquarters to an expensive tower and ordered a corporate jet, while the share price has fallen by 30%. The annual report gives little detail on these decisions, and most small shareholders do not attend the general meeting.

chunks.t: Meseta Aerostructures: a CEO, dispersed shareholders and the agency problem
chunks.x:
- Ownership (shareholders) is separated from control (the professional CEO).
- The CEO pursues her own benefit (size, prestige) instead of the shareholders' (value).
- Different access to information and different objectives; dispersed shareholders lack information and incentives to monitor.

chunks.t: Meseta Aerostructures: a CEO, dispersed shareholders and the agency problem
chunks.x: In large corporations the company is run by **managers**, professional employees, while it is owned by the **shareholders**: ownership is separated from control [Slide 25]. At Meseta, the CEO's pay rises with the number of employees, so her objective is **size and prestige** (acquisitions, tower, jet), not the value of the shares. Shareholders and managers have **different objectives** and **different access to information** (the report gives little detail), and with stakes below 2% no shareholder has enough information or **incentive** to assess her performance. The result is a conflict of interest between ownership and control: the **agency problem**.

chunks.t: Meseta Aerostructures: a CEO, dispersed shareholders and the agency problem
chunks.x:
- Select a Board of Directors that supervises the CEO.
- Contracts linked to goals (pay tied to profit or share value instead of headcount); incentive compensation.
- Audits and indicators.
- External discipline: the market of enterprises (takeover risk) and the labour market for managers.

chunks.t: Meseta Aerostructures: a CEO, dispersed shareholders and the agency problem
chunks.x:
Shareholders must be able to control how the manager acts [Topic 1, Slide 26]:
1. **Select the Board of Directors** so that it actually supervises the CEO and approves large acquisitions.
2. **Contracts linked to goals:** replace pay tied to headcount with incentive compensation tied to profit or share value [Topic 2, Slide 4].
3. **Request audits** of the acquisitions and expenses, and publish **indicators** that let shareholders judge performance.
4. Outside the firm, the **market of enterprises** (a falling share price invites a takeover that would replace the CEO) and the **labour market** for managers (her reputation) also discipline her [Topic 2, Slide 4].

Increasingly, shareholders with large blocks of shares take the decisions [Slide 26]; a group of institutional investors could build such a block at Meseta.

chunks.t: A drone-spraying cooperative and a launcher joint venture
chunks.x:
Two situations in the same region:

**Case 1.** Forty vineyard owners cannot each afford a crop-spraying drone. They create an organization that buys three drones and hires two pilots; any vineyard owner of the area may join, each member has one vote in the assembly regardless of size, and at the end of the year what is left after paying the expenses is returned to each member in proportion to the hectares sprayed.

**Case 2.** A European launcher manufacturer and a Japanese engine company set up a company owned 50/50 for the sole purpose of developing a reusable upper stage over eight years. When the stage is certified, the company will be dissolved.

chunks.t: A drone-spraying cooperative and a launcher joint venture
chunks.x:
- Case 1: cooperative association (open membership, democratic control, benefits in proportion to participation, user-members are owners); closest type: a buying co-op.
- Case 2: joint venture: a special partnership for a specific task or project, common in international business.

chunks.t: A drone-spraying cooperative and a launcher joint venture
chunks.x:
**Case 1 is a cooperative association** [Slides 27-28]: an incorporated organization whose **user-members are also its owners** and get back the revenue left after expenses. It follows the cooperative principles: **open membership** (any vineyard owner may join), **democratic control** (one member, one vote), and **benefits distributed in proportion to each member's participation** (hectares sprayed). Of the course's common types, the closest is a **buying co-op**, which helps members buy at lower prices (here, a spraying service); it is not an agricultural co-op in the course's sense, which helps member farmers **market** their products [Slide 28].

**Case 2 is a joint venture** [Slide 29]: a special type of partnership set up by firms to **accomplish a specific task or project**, the reusable upper stage, and dissolved once the task is done. It is very common in **international business**, as here.

chunks.t: A drone-spraying cooperative and a launcher joint venture
chunks.x:
- Co-op: access to expensive equipment and lower costs, with democratic control and fair sharing.
- Joint venture: sharing a large, risky project and combining complementary know-how across countries without merging the parent companies.

chunks.t: A drone-spraying cooperative and a launcher joint venture
chunks.x:
The **cooperative** gives small vineyard owners access to equipment that none could buy alone, at cost, while keeping control democratic and sharing the surplus fairly. The **joint venture** lets two firms from different countries **share the cost and risk** of a long, uncertain project and **combine complementary know-how** (launcher and engines) without merging the whole companies; each parent keeps its independence in the rest of its business. These advantages are reasoning applied to the case; the deck defines the forms but does not list their advantages.

chunks.t: Classifying three aerospace enterprises, and why firms exist at all
Classifying three aerospace enterprises, and why firms exist at all
chunks.x:
- TitanMine: primary, small, one market and national, private.
- AeroNational: secondary, big, multi-market and multinational, state-owned; corporation.
- Wingtip: tertiary, small, multi-market and national, private, sole proprietorship.

chunks.t: Classifying three aerospace enterprises, and why firms exist at all
chunks.x:
| Criterion [Slide 19] | TitanMine | AeroNational | Wingtip Consulting |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sector | Primary (extraction) | Secondary (manufacturing) | Tertiary (services) |
| Size | Small | Big | Small |
| Scope | One market, national | Multi-market, multinational | Multi-market, national |
| Ownership of the factors | Private | State-owned | Private |
| Form of ownership | Company (likely a corporation) | Corporation | Sole proprietorship |

The deck gives the criteria and their classes but no thresholds; reading 35 employees as small and 9,000 as big is the usual interpretation (extension).

chunks.t: Classifying three aerospace enterprises, and why firms exist at all
chunks.x:
- Wants are met through specialization (division of labour), which requires coordination.
- Coordination can be done by the market or by the enterprise; the enterprise appears where there is a dissatisfied need that it coordinates better.

chunks.t: Classifying three aerospace enterprises, and why firms exist at all
chunks.x:
Economics studies how scarce resources are used to satisfy unlimited wants; those wants are met through **specialization**, the division of labour, and specialization requires **coordination** [Slide 12]. Coordination can be carried out either by the **market**, as the classmate suggests, or by the **enterprise**. Building a transport aircraft requires thousands of specialists working together on one product: coordinating them through separate market contracts would be impractical, so an enterprise appears to coordinate them (reasoning applied to the case, beyond the slides). In the course's words, an enterprise appears because there is a **dissatisfied need** [Slide 12]. Wingtip shows that, for simple services, one person selling directly to the market can also work.

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x: A private company operates Costa Airport. A new board member argues: "Our only objective is to maximize this year's profit: let's double parking fees, cut the night shift of air-traffic support staff and postpone the runway resurfacing." The finance director replies that the board should instead aim to "maximize the value of the company", and the operations director warns that the airline customers, the unions, the city council and the regional government will all react to such measures.

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x:
- Profit is hard to define and quantify (this year vs future years).
- It ignores the risk of achieving the profits (postponed resurfacing, safety, reaction of airlines).
- The very idea of "maximizing" is questionable.
- It gives an excessive role to the entrepreneur, whereas ownership and control are separated.

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x:
The proposal follows the classical objective, **profit maximization**, which has four limitations [Slide 3]:
1. **Profit is difficult to define and to quantify:** cutting maintenance raises this year's profit but lowers future profits (a degraded runway, a closure for emergency works).
2. **It ignores risk:** the cuts raise the risk of incidents and of losing airlines, which a single profit figure does not show.
3. **The concept of maximization itself is questionable** [Slide 3]; in practice managers aim at a minimum level of profit that satisfies the shareholders [Slide 4].
4. **It gives an excessive role to the entrepreneur:** in a company like this, ownership and control are separated, and the board, managers and shareholders have different goals.

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x: Organizational theory: objectives are the outcome of a negotiation among stakeholders, limited by survival and unequal power [Slides 5-6]. Recall the unified vision of survival, profit and growth [Slide 7].

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x:
- Objectives result from negotiation among stakeholders (shareholders, customers, employees, State, society...).
- Constraints: the firm must survive; groups have different bargaining power.
- The resulting objective: maximize the value of the enterprise (create value), linking survival, profit and growth.

chunks.t: Costa Airport: profit maximization or value creation?
chunks.x:
According to **organizational theory**, the objectives of the firm are the **outcome of a negotiation among its stakeholders**: here the shareholders, the airlines (customers), the employees and unions, the city council and regional government (the State), suppliers, banks and society [Slides 5-6]. The negotiation is limited because the firm must **survive** and because **not all groups have the same power**. The objective that satisfies the most powerful group while respecting the others and the firm's survival is to **maximize the value of the enterprise**, to create value [Slide 6]. In the unified vision, value comes from a cycle in which sales generate profits, retained profits finance investments (such as the resurfacing) and these renew the products and markets [Slide 7]; sacrificing the investment for one year's profit breaks that cycle.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x: TurboCast S.A., a maker of turbine blades, plans to close its oldest plant, in a town of 8,000 inhabitants where it employs 600 people, and move production to a new automated plant. The shareholders support the plan; the main bank, which financed the new plant, wants it to happen fast. The unions call a strike. The regional government offers a subsidy if the plant stays open two more years. The engine manufacturer that buys 70% of the blades demands that deliveries are not interrupted. Local suppliers and environmental groups also make their voices heard.

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x: Around management stand shareholders, banks and financial agents, customers, suppliers, the State, employees and unions, and society [Slide 5].

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x:
- Shareholders: higher profit and value through automation.
- Bank: repayment of the loan for the new plant.
- Employees and unions: keep their jobs.
- State (regional government): employment in the region.
- Customer (engine maker): uninterrupted deliveries.
- Suppliers and society: local business, environment.

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x:
| Stakeholder [Slide 5] | In the case | What it wants |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Shareholders | Owners of TurboCast | Lower costs and higher value through automation |
| Banks and financial agents | Lender of the new plant | Repayment; a fast transition that makes the plant profitable |
| Employees and unions | 600 workers | To keep their jobs and conditions |
| The State | Regional government | Employment and activity in the region |
| Customers | Engine manufacturer | Uninterrupted, on-time deliveries |
| Suppliers | Local suppliers | To keep their contracts |
| Society | Town, environmental groups | Local activity, responsible behaviour (CSR) |

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x:
- The decision is a negotiated outcome, not one group's wish.
- It satisfies the group with the most bargaining power (here the engine maker, which buys 70%, together with shareholders and bank) while taking the others into account.
- Constraint of survival: TurboCast must stay competitive.
- A likely compromise: a phased closure (subsidy, two years), guaranteed deliveries, relocation or retraining.

chunks.t: Closing an engine-parts plant: mapping the stakeholders and their power
chunks.x:
Organizational theory sees the objective as the **outcome of a negotiation among stakeholders**, limited by two facts: the firm must **survive**, and **not all groups have the same power** [Slide 6]. Here the engine manufacturer has very high bargaining power (70% of sales), as do the shareholders and the bank; the unions and the government have less power but can impose costs (strikes, subsidies withdrawn). The likely outcome is a **compromise**: the move to the automated plant goes ahead, because survival requires competitive costs, but it is **phased** over two years with the regional subsidy, deliveries are protected with stock built in advance, and part of the staff is relocated or retrained. That decision satisfies the most powerful groups while taking the others into account, which is what maximizing the value of the enterprise means in practice.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x: Altair Launch S.L. is developing a rocket for satellites under 200 kg. In its business plan it lists: interest rates have doubled in two years and venture capital is scarcer; the European Union has created a fund to secure independent access to space, and a new national space law sets licensing rules; additive manufacturing has made engine parts much cheaper, while reusable rockets are becoming a key technology; the country trains many aerospace engineers, but public opinion is increasingly worried about space debris and the noise of the launch site.

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x: Economic, political-legal, socio-cultural and technological factors [Slide 11]. (Many textbooks use PESTEL, which separates environmental and legal factors; the course uses four groups.)

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x:
- Economic: interest rates, scarce venture capital.
- Political-legal: EU fund, national space law and licensing.
- Socio-cultural: supply of trained engineers (education), public concern about debris and noise (value system).
- Technological: additive manufacturing (key), reusability (incipient/key).

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x:
| Group [Slide 11] | Element of the case | Effect on Altair |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Economic** | Higher interest rates, less venture capital | Financing becomes harder and costlier |
| **Political-legal** | EU fund for independent access to space; national space law and licences | Opportunity (public demand and funding) and a regulatory requirement |
| **Socio-cultural** | Many trained engineers (level of education); concern about debris and noise (value system) | Easier hiring; pressure on the launch site and on debris mitigation |
| **Technological** | Additive manufacturing; reusable rockets | Cheaper engines; a key technology that may become a must |

The course's four groups have no separate environmental factor: the table places the public's concern under the socio-cultural value system (public opinion), while the outside-in view of [Slide 13] also lists the natural environment among the forces around the industry. The PESTEL framework of other books would treat debris and noise as a separate environmental factor (extension).

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x:
- Generic environment: factors that affect every firm in the country/economy.
- Specific environment: the firm's own industry (rivalry, entry and exit barriers, substitutes, customers, suppliers), analysed with Porter's five forces.
- The analysis moves from the outside in.

chunks.t: A small-launcher start-up reads its generic environment
chunks.x:
The **generic environment** affects all firms, whatever their industry: the interest rates or the space law hit every company in the country [Slide 11]. The **specific environment** is the environment of the firm's **own industry**: the rivalry among launch providers, entry and exit barriers, substitutes (for example rideshare launches on large rockets), and the relationships with customers and suppliers [Slide 12]. The analysis moves **from the outside in**, from the economy, technology and politics to the industry at the centre [Slide 13]. Altair needs both: the generic factors explain the conditions it cannot change, and the specific ones explain whether it can earn money against its direct competitors.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x: Three airlines fly between the islands of an archipelago with similar turboprops and similar fares; none is clearly larger. Two manufacturers in the world build turboprops of that size, and a single company supplies the jet fuel at the airports. Most passengers are price-sensitive residents who compare fares online, plus the regional government, which buys tickets for public employees. A fast-ferry company has just started services between the two main islands. To start a new airline one needs aircraft, an operating certificate and slots at airports that are almost full.

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x: Rivalry, supplier power, buyer power, threat of entry, threat of substitutes, each with its determinants [Slides 14-15].

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x:
- Rivalry: high (three similar firms, little differentiation, no leader).
- Suppliers: high (two aircraft makers, one fuel supplier).
- Buyers: high (price-sensitive residents; the government as a large buyer).
- New entrants: low-medium (capital, certificate, full slots: legal and access barriers).
- Substitutes: medium-high (fast ferry on the main route).

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x:
| Force [Slides 14-15] | Rating | Determinants in the case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rivalry among existing firms** | High | Three firms of similar size (low concentration, no leader), similar product and fares (little differentiation) |
| **Bargaining power of suppliers** | High | Only two turboprop manufacturers and a single fuel supplier: high relative bargaining power |
| **Bargaining power of buyers** | High | Residents are price-sensitive and compare online; the government buys in volume |
| **Threat of new entrants** | Low to medium | Capital requirements (aircraft), legal and regulatory barriers (operating certificate), access to "distribution" (airport slots almost full) |
| **Threat of substitutes** | Medium to high | The fast ferry: buyers' propensity to substitute depends on its relative price and travel time |

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x: The stronger the forces, the lower the profitability the industry allows. Connect your answer with the sources of competitive advantage [Slide 20].

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x:
- Low attractiveness: four of five forces are strong.
- A response: cost advantage (fleet standardization, high capacity utilization) or differentiation (schedule, connections, service) that weakens buyer power; possibly cooperation or consolidation to reduce rivalry.

chunks.t: Island regional airlines under Porter's five forces
chunks.x:
With strong rivalry, strong suppliers, strong buyers and a growing substitute, the industry is **unattractive**: the profit available is squeezed from every side, and only the entry barriers protect it. An airline can respond by building a **cost advantage** (a single aircraft type [Slide 21], high capacity utilization [Slide 22]) to survive the price war, or a **differentiation advantage** (frequent schedules, connections with long-haul flights, loyalty schemes for residents) that reduces buyers' price sensitivity [Slides 23-24].
