chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x: ComfortAuto S.A., a large maker of car seats, wants to enter the market of passenger seats for commercial aircraft. Three established firms supply almost all airlines. Each new seat model must pass crash and flammability certification that takes two years. Airlines buy seats through long contracts linked to aircraft orders, and the established firms have decades of reputation for reliability. They produce in large volumes in plants built for this purpose, and they own patents on lightweight seat frames. ComfortAuto, however, has strong engineering, low-cost purchasing of foam and fabrics, and spare plant capacity.

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x: Capital requirements, economies of scale, absolute cost advantage, product differentiation, access to distribution channels, legal and regulatory barriers [Slide 15].

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x:
- Legal and regulatory: two-year certification; patents.
- Product differentiation: reputation for reliability.
- Access to distribution channels: long contracts linked to aircraft orders.
- Economies of scale: incumbents' volumes in dedicated plants.
- Capital requirements and absolute cost advantages (patents, experience).

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x:
| Determinant [Slide 15] | In the case |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Legal and regulatory barriers** | Two years of crash and flammability certification per model; patents on lightweight frames |
| **Product differentiation** | The incumbents' decades of reputation for reliability make airlines reluctant to switch |
| **Access to distribution channels** | Seats are sold through long contracts tied to aircraft orders, already held by the incumbents |
| **Economies of scale** | Incumbents produce large volumes in dedicated plants, so their unit cost is lower |
| **Absolute cost advantage** | Patents and accumulated experience (economies of learning) |
| **Capital requirements** | Certification programmes and adapting a plant require large investment before any sale |

These barriers make the threat of entry low and protect the profitability of the three incumbents.

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x: A diversification decision asks two questions: how attractive is the sector, and can the firm achieve a competitive advantage in it [Slide 25]?

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x:
- Attractive sector: high barriers keep profitability high for those inside.
- Competitive advantage: ComfortAuto has transferable strengths (engineering, cheap inputs, spare capacity) but lacks certification, reputation and contracts.
- Related diversification: a gradual entry (a niche, a partnership or acquiring a small certified firm) is more realistic.

chunks.t: Can a car-seat maker enter the aircraft-seat market? Barriers to entry
chunks.x:
The diversification answers the two questions of [Slide 25] differently. **Attractiveness:** the same barriers that block ComfortAuto keep the industry profitable for those inside, so the sector is attractive. **Competitive advantage:** ComfortAuto brings real strengths (seat engineering, low-cost inputs, spare capacity), which makes this a **related diversification**, but it lacks certification, reputation and access to contracts. Entering head-on would be slow and risky; a more realistic path is to start in a niche (crew seats, business-jet seats), partner with an incumbent, or acquire a small certified firm.

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x: At its annual meeting, the Nordic MRO Group took these decisions: (1) to open a maintenance base in Morocco to serve African airlines; (2) to buy the company that overhauls the landing gear it used to outsource; (3) to compete in its engine-overhaul business by guaranteeing the shortest turnaround time in Europe, even at higher prices; (4) to schedule a second shift in the paint hangar during the summer; (5) to change the supplier of cleaning products next month.

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x: Corporate strategy decides **where** the firm competes (its scope: geographical, vertical, product); business strategy decides **how** it competes (cost or differentiation) [Slides 9, 17-19].

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x:
- 1: corporate strategy, geographical scope.
- 2: corporate strategy, vertical scope (backward integration).
- 3: business strategy, differentiation advantage (turnaround time, price premium).

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x:
| Decision | Type [Slides 9, 18] | Detail |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Base in Morocco | **Corporate strategy** | **Geographical scope** (internationalization), part of the question "which businesses should we be in?" |
| 2. Buying the landing-gear overhauler | **Corporate strategy** | **Vertical scope** (backward vertical integration) |
| 3. Shortest turnaround at higher prices | **Business (competitive) strategy** | **Differentiation**: a valued, unique feature that earns a price premium [Slides 20, 23] |

Corporate strategy answers "which businesses should we be in?" and business strategy "how should we compete?" [Slide 17].

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x:
- 4: tactic decision (one area; it implements the strategy).
- 5: operative decision (routine).
- The deck only names the three levels; their characterisation is the usual reading (extension).
- Success: long-term, simple and agreed objectives; deep understanding of the competitive environment; objective appraisal of resources; effective implementation.

chunks.t: Nordic MRO Group: corporate strategy, business strategy and levels of decision
chunks.x:
Decisions 1–3 are **strategic**: long-term, affecting the whole firm. Decision 4 (a summer shift in one hangar) is **tactic**: it concerns one area over a season and implements the strategy. Decision 5 (a cleaning supplier next month) is **operative**: routine and short term. The deck names the three levels [Slide 8]; this characterisation of each one is the usual reading (extension).

A strategy succeeds through **effective implementation** resting on **long-term, simple and agreed objectives**, a **deep understanding of the competitive environment** and an **objective appraisal of resources** [Slide 10]. Nordic's differentiation on turnaround time, for instance, only works if it has the hangar capacity and staff (resources) to deliver it.

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x: LowOrbit S.A. sells the "bus" (platform) of small Earth-observation satellites at 40% below its rivals. It builds one standard design with interchangeable modules instead of custom platforms, and has designed every part to be machined in a single setup. Its line now produces 120 buses a year, and the hours per bus have fallen by half since the first 20 units as the teams repeated the same tasks. It bought a solar-cell supplier located next to the plant, keeps the factory running in three shifts, and its managers are paid for removing waste in every process.

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x: Economies of learning, economies of scale, production techniques, product design, input costs, capacity utilization, residual efficiency [Slides 21-22].

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x:
- Product design: one standard design, interchangeable modules, design for manufacture.
- Economies of scale: 120 buses a year.
- Economies of learning: hours per bus halved with repetition.
- Input costs: ownership of a low-cost input (solar cells), location.
- Capacity utilization: three shifts.
- Residual efficiency: managers paid to remove waste (motivation, culture).

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x:
| Driver [Slides 21-22] | Evidence at LowOrbit |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Product design** | Standardization of designs and components; parts designed for manufacture (single setup) |
| **Economies of scale** | 120 buses a year: specialization and division of labour |
| **Economies of learning** | Hours per bus halved as routines improved |
| **Input costs** | Ownership of a low-cost input (the solar-cell supplier) and a location advantage |
| **Capacity utilization** | Three shifts spread the fixed costs over more units |
| **Residual efficiency** | Managerial efficiency, motivation and culture of eliminating waste |

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x:
- Cost advantage: offering a similar product at a lower cost than rivals.
- Risk: standardization limits customization; customers who value unique features may prefer differentiated rivals; rivals may copy the cost drivers.

chunks.t: LowOrbit: the drivers behind a cost-leadership strategy in satellite buses
chunks.x:
A **cost advantage** means offering a **similar product at a lower cost** than competitors, whereas a differentiation advantage obtains a **price premium from a unique product** [Slide 20]. LowOrbit's standard bus is its main cost driver, but it is also its main risk: customers whose missions need a custom platform will go to differentiated rivals, and competitors can copy standardization and scale. To keep the advantage it must keep reducing costs faster than its rivals (learning, scale) while keeping the product "similar enough" in performance to theirs.

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x: Aurum Interiors S.L. designs cabins for private jets and charges about twice what its competitors charge. Its cabins use sound-absorbing panels that make them the quietest in the market and seats 20% lighter than average, and they are delivered with a personalised maintenance plan and a 24-hour technical hotline. Each cabin is signed by a well-known designer, carries a numbered plaque, and owners are invited to an exclusive yearly event. Aurum's account managers accompany each customer from the first sketch to years after delivery.

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x: Tangible differentiation rests on observable characteristics (features, performance, packaging, complementary services); intangible differentiation appeals to image, status, identity and exclusivity [Slide 24].

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x:
- Tangible: quietness (performance), lighter seats (materials/performance), maintenance plan and hotline (complementary services).
- Intangible: designer's signature, numbered plaque, exclusive event (status, exclusivity).
- The account managers: the whole supplier–customer relationship.

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x:
| Source | Type [Slide 24] | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Quietest cabins (sound-absorbing panels) | Tangible | Performance, observable and measurable |
| Seats 20% lighter | Tangible | Materials and performance |
| Maintenance plan and 24-hour hotline | Tangible | Complementary services |
| Designer's signature, numbered plaque | Intangible | Image, status, desire for exclusivity |
| Exclusive yearly event | Intangible | Identity and status of belonging to a select group |
| Account managers from sketch to after-sales | Whole relationship | Total customer responsiveness [Slide 24] |

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x:
- Differentiation creates value for the customer, which earns a price premium [Slide 20].
- The premium must exceed the extra cost of differentiating.
- Aurum must protect what is valuable and hard to copy: reputation, design, relationship.

chunks.t: Aurum Interiors: tangible and intangible differentiation in business jets
chunks.x:
Differentiation means **providing something unique that the buyer values** beyond a low price [Slide 23]; because the customer values it, they accept a **price premium** [Slide 20]. Aurum's quiet, light cabins and its exclusive image create that value, so jet owners pay double. The strategy works only while the premium exceeds the extra cost of the panels, designers and services, and while the uniqueness lasts. The tangible features can eventually be copied; the intangible ones (brand, designer, relationship with owners) are harder to imitate and are what Aurum must protect.

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x: Vega Avionics S.A. makes flight-control electronics. Its sales follow the aircraft-order cycle: in good years profits soar, in crises they collapse. The board studies three moves: (A) launching a line of electronic monitors for hospital intensive-care units, using its expertise in certified, fault-tolerant electronics; (B) opening a sales office in India to sell its current avionics to Indian aircraft makers; (C) buying a chain of hotels near airports because "it is profitable and has nothing to do with aircraft cycles".

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x: Reasons: growth, risk, profit [Slide 25]. Types: related vs unrelated; forms: vertical, horizontal, geographical [Slide 26].

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x:
- Reasons: risk (volatile earnings tied to the aircraft cycle), growth, profit.
- A: horizontal diversification, related (shared technology).
- B: geographical diversification of existing products, related.
- C: horizontal diversification, unrelated.

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x:
Firms diversify for three reasons [Slide 25]: **growth**, **risk** (diversification reduces the volatility of earnings) and **profit**. Vega's main motive is **risk**: its earnings depend on one cycle, and businesses that do not follow it would stabilise them; growth and profit are secondary motives.

| Move | Form [Slide 26] | Related or unrelated |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A. Hospital monitors | Horizontal diversification (new industry) | **Related**: it expands Vega's existing line of certified electronics into a new market [Slide 26] |
| B. Sales office in India | Geographical diversification (new market) | **Related**: same products, new market |
| C. Airport hotels | Horizontal diversification (new industry) | **Unrelated**: it adds a new, unrelated product line [Slide 26] |

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x:
- The hotel sector may be attractive, but Vega has no source of competitive advantage there.
- Unrelated diversification reduces risk; whether it adds profitability depends on achieving an advantage in the new sector.

chunks.t: Vega Avionics: reasons for and types of diversification
chunks.x:
A diversification decision asks **how attractive the sector is** and **whether the firm can achieve a competitive advantage in it** [Slide 25]. Hotels near airports may be profitable, but Vega brings nothing that would give it an advantage over hotel chains: no shared technology, customers or skills. The move would lower the volatility of earnings, but shareholders could achieve that themselves by investing in hotel companies (an argument beyond the slides). Move A, related to Vega's know-how, answers both questions far better.

chunks.t: A launcher maker buys its engine supplier: vertical integration
chunks.x: Helios Launch S.A. builds medium rockets. Its engines come from a single independent supplier that has raised prices twice in two years and delayed deliveries, and the two firms argue about who must pay for each design change. Helios is negotiating to buy the supplier. A director objects: engine technology is changing fast, the supplier also sells engines to other launch companies, and Helios has no experience in managing a factory of that size. Another director proposes, instead, to also buy the satellite-integration company that prepares customers' payloads before launch.

chunks.t: A launcher maker buys its engine supplier: vertical integration
chunks.x:
- Buying the engine supplier: backward vertical integration; buying payload integration: forward vertical integration.
- Advantages: control of inputs, reduction of transaction costs (disputes over design changes), independence, better competitive position, reduction of information asymmetries.

chunks.t: A launcher maker buys its engine supplier: vertical integration
A launcher maker buys its engine supplier: vertical integration
chunks.x:
- Decreased flexibility: tied to its own engine technology when it changes fast.
- Loss of specialization advantages: the supplier's scale from selling to other launchers may be lost.
- Increased administrative costs and risk: managing a large new factory without experience.

chunks.t: A launcher maker buys its engine supplier: vertical integration
chunks.x:
The director's points match the **disadvantages** of vertical integration [Slide 27]. When engine technology changes fast, owning the factory means **decreased flexibility**: Helios cannot simply switch to a better engine on the market. If rival launch companies stop buying from a supplier owned by a competitor, the factory loses volume and the **advantages of specialization**. Running a large factory without experience brings **increased administrative costs** and **increased risk**. A balanced conclusion: integration is worth it if engines are critical and the supplier abuses its power, but Helios should first consider alternatives such as a long-term contract or a second supplier.

chunks.t: SkyEye Drones: mapping activities onto Porter's value chain
chunks.x: Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service [Slide 30]. Support: procurement, human resource management, technological development, infrastructure [Slide 31].

chunks.x:
- Primary: 1 inbound logistics, 2 operations, 3 outbound logistics, 4 marketing and sales, 5 service.
- Support: 6 procurement, 7 HRM, 8 technological development, 9 infrastructure.

chunks.x:
| Activity | Value-chain activity | Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Receiving and storing components | Inbound logistics | Primary [Slide 30] |
| 2. Assembling and testing | Operations | Primary |
| 3. Packing and shipping | Outbound logistics | Primary |

chunks.t: SkyEye Drones: mapping activities onto Porter's value chain
chunks.x: The chain arranges resources into activities customers are willing to pay for; the management of the activities and of their linkages gives the competitive advantage [Slides 28-29].

chunks.t: SkyEye Drones: mapping activities onto Porter's value chain
chunks.x:
- The activities together produce the margin [Slide 29], read (extension) as what customers pay minus the cost of all activities.
- Competitive advantage comes from managing the activities and their linkages (e.g. software development linked to after-sales updates).

chunks.t: SkyEye Drones: mapping activities onto Porter's value chain
chunks.x:
The value chain (Porter, 1985) shows that a firm is not a random collection of resources but a set of **activities** that produce goods customers are willing to pay for; together they produce the **margin** shown at the end of the chain [Slide 29], usually read (extension) as the difference between what customers pay and the cost of all the activities. The **management of the activities and of their linkages** is what gives the competitive advantage: for SkyEye, the link between technological development (activity 8) and service (activity 5) allows software updates that keep old drones competitive, a reason for customers to pay more.

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x: The finance manager of Rotorline S.A., a helicopter-tour operator, has two items on her desk this week. First, whether to buy a fourth helicopter now or wait until next spring, and whether to replace the old hangar. Second, how to pay for whatever is bought: a bank has offered a five-year loan, the shareholders could put in more money, or the company could keep this year's profit instead of paying dividends. She knows that the helicopter would earn about 9% per year and that the money to buy it would cost, on average, about 7%.

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x: What to invest in and when? How to obtain the money to invest? [Slide 3]. Economic and financial structure [Slides 4-5].

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x:
- Investing decisions (helicopter, hangar, timing) → economic structure → assets (what is owned).
- Financing decisions (loan, new equity, retained profit) → financial structure → equity and liabilities (what is owed).

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x:
The finance manager faces the two decisions of the finance area [Slide 3]:
- **Investing decisions** — *what to invest in and when?*: the fourth helicopter (now or in spring) and the new hangar. They define the **economic structure**, the use of the financial resources in goods and rights: the **assets**, what the company owns [Slides 4-5].
- **Financing decisions** — *how to obtain the money?*: bank loan, new equity from shareholders, or retained profit. They define the **financial structure**, the sources of financing: **equity and liabilities**, what the company owes [Slides 4-5, 6].

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x:
- Assets generate profitability; financing has a cost.
- Objective: maximize value, which requires profitability > cost.
- 9% > 7%: the helicopter creates value.

chunks.t: Rotorline: investing and financing decisions, economic and financial structure
chunks.x:
The **assets** produce **profitability**, while **equity and liabilities** have a **cost**; the objective of the company is to **maximize value**, which requires that **profitability exceed cost** [Slide 5]. The new helicopter would earn about 9% per year while the funds to buy it cost about 7%, so it creates value: each year it returns 2 points more than it costs. If the cheapest financing available cost more than 9%, the same helicopter would destroy value, which is why the investing and financing decisions must be taken together.

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank · Business Management MOC

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x: Nacelle Works S.A. manufactures engine nacelles. Its CFO lists how the company was financed last year: (1) profits of previous years kept in the company; (2) a capital increase subscribed by a venture fund; (3) bonds maturing in 2032; (4) a seven-year bank loan for a new autoclave; (5) a contract to use a robotic drilling cell for five years with an option to buy it at the end; (6) suppliers of aluminium who are paid at 90 days; (7) customer invoices sold to a specialised company that collects them and bears the risk if the customer does not pay.

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x: Nature: equity or liabilities [Slide 21]; origin: company resources or external resources [Slide 22]; term: long or short [Slides 29-35].

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x:
- Equity, company resources: (1) self-financing (internal); (2) equity capital (external equity).
- Liabilities, external, long term: (3) bonds, (4) long-term loan, (5) leasing.
- Liabilities, external, short term: (6) accounts payable (trade credit), (7) factoring.

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x:
| Source | Instrument | Nature [Slide 21] | Origin [Slide 22] | Term |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Self-financing (retained earnings) | Equity | Company resources (internal equity) | Permanent |
| 2 | Equity capital, rights issue | Equity | Company resources (external equity) | Permanent |
| 3 | Bonds | Liabilities | External | Long term [Slide 29] |
| 4 | Long-term bank loan | Liabilities | External | Long term [Slide 31] |
| 5 | Leasing (use with purchase option) | Liabilities | External | Long term [Slide 33] |
| 6 | Accounts payable (trade credit) | Liabilities | External | Short term [Slide 35] |
| 7 | Factoring | Liabilities | External | Short term [Slide 35] |

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x:
- Bond: a loan in the form of a security; the issuer owes the holders principal and coupon at maturity.
- Loan: an amount received and paid back at a certain time, with debt interest.
- Factoring: the credit is sold and the factor assumes the insolvency risk.
- Trade discount: the bank advances the amount of a bill before maturity after deducting expenses; the risk stays with the company.

chunks.t: Nacelle Works: placing seven sources of financing on the map
chunks.x:
A **bond** is a **debt security**: a loan in the form of a security, in which the issuer is the borrower and the bondholder the lender; the issuer must repay the principal and pay the coupon at maturity [Slide 29]. With a **long-term loan**, the company receives an amount that must be paid back at a certain time and pays **debt interest** for it [Slide 31].

With **factoring**, the company **sells** its credit to a factoring company, which collects it and **assumes the risk of insolvency** [Slide 35]. With a **trade discount**, the bank only **advances** the amount of a bill before it falls due, after deducting interest and commission [Slide 35]; if the customer does not pay, the company usually has to return the money (discount with recourse, extension).

chunks.t: Talon Avionics: pay a dividend or keep the profit?
chunks.x: Talon Avionics S.A. earned a profit of 800,000 m.u. in 2025. Its retired founding shareholders, who live on the dividends, ask the board to distribute 600,000 m.u. The CEO wants to distribute only 160,000 m.u. and keep the rest to develop a new radar altimeter next year; otherwise she would have to ask a bank for a loan or issue new shares, which the founders dislike because they would lose part of their control.

chunks.t: Talon Avionics: pay a dividend or keep the profit?
Talon Avionics: pay a dividend or keep the profit?
chunks.x: Think about repayment, explicit vs implicit cost, control, and the fact that paying dividends is not compulsory [Slides 23-26, 37].

chunks.t: Talon Avionics: pay a dividend or keep the profit?
chunks.x:
- Self-financing: internal equity generated by the activity; no repayment, no explicit cost, no new owners; but it has an opportunity cost for shareholders and depends on profits.
- Loan: explicit cost (interest), must be repaid, increases leverage and risk.
- Rights issue: no repayment, but new shareholders dilute control.
- Dividends are not compulsory; a balanced pay-out may be agreed.

chunks.t: Talon Avionics: pay a dividend or keep the profit?
chunks.x:
**Self-financing** (retained earnings) is internal equity generated by the company's normal activity [Slide 23]. It does not have to be repaid, carries no **explicit** cost and brings in no new owners, so the founders keep their control; its cost is **implicit**: the shareholders give up dividends today (an opportunity cost, [Slide 37]).

The alternatives have other drawbacks: a **bank loan** carries an explicit cost (interest), must be repaid, and raises leverage and risk [Slides 31, 36]; a **rights issue** need not be repaid but brings in new shareholders who share future dividends [Slides 25-26] and voting power (extension).

**Recommendation:** since paying dividends is not compulsory [Slide 26] and the founders want to keep control, the CEO's high self-financing is the way to fund the project that needs no repayment, carries no explicit cost and keeps control in their hands. A compromise (for example a 30–40% pay-out) can still meet part of the founders' income needs if the project does not require all 640,000 m.u. (a suggestion beyond the course).

chunks.t: A flight school's simulator: leasing, a long-term loan or a credit line?
chunks.x: Cumulus Flight School S.L. needs a full-flight simulator that will be used for about eight years. A bank offers three options: (A) a long-term loan for the full price, repaid over eight years with interest; (B) a leasing contract: the school uses the simulator in exchange for monthly payments for eight years and can buy it at the end for a small amount; (C) a credit line with a limit equal to the price, renewable every year, on which interest is paid only on the amount drawn. Separately, the school expects short cash gaps every winter, when fewer students enrol.

chunks.t: A flight school's simulator: leasing, a long-term loan or a credit line?
chunks.x:
- Loan: an amount received and repaid at a certain time, paying debt interest.
- Leasing: use of a fixed asset for periodic payments; the lessee has the right to buy at the end; finance or operating leasing.
- Credit line: the bank makes a maximum available; interest only on the amount borrowed; higher rates.

chunks.t: A flight school's simulator: leasing, a long-term loan or a credit line?
chunks.x:
- **(A) Long-term loan:** the school receives an amount that must be paid back at a certain time and pays for the service through the **debt interest** [Slide 31].
- **(B) Leasing:** the school obtains the **use of a fixed asset** in exchange for contractual, periodic payments; as lessee, it has the **right to buy** the asset at the end of the period. It can be **finance** or **operating** leasing [Slide 33].
- **(C) Bank credit (credit line):** the bank makes a **maximum amount** available; the school borrows what it needs up to that limit and pays interest **only on the amount borrowed**; interest rates are higher. Renewed yearly, it is short-term bank financing [Slides 31, 35].

chunks.t: A flight school's simulator: leasing, a long-term loan or a credit line?
chunks.x:
- Simulator (8-year asset): long-term financing, loan or leasing; leasing also offers flexibility and the purchase option.
- Winter gaps (short, recurring): the credit line, since interest is paid only on the amount drawn.
- Financing a long-lived asset with a yearly-renewable credit line is risky and expensive.

chunks.t: A flight school's simulator: leasing, a long-term loan or a credit line?
chunks.x:
The simulator will be used for eight years, so it should be financed with **long-term** resources: either the **loan** (A) or the **leasing** (B), whose eight-year payments match its useful life. Leasing is attractive for a flight school because it obtains the use of the asset [Slide 33] without a large initial outlay (reasoning applied to the case, beyond the slides) and keeps the **option to buy** it at the end. Financing it with the **credit line** (C) would be a mistake: the line must be renewed every year, so the bank could refuse (reasoning applied to the case, beyond the slides), and its interest rates are higher [Slide 31].

The **winter cash gaps**, instead, are short and recurring, so the **credit line** is the right tool: the school draws only what it needs for a few weeks and pays interest **only on the amount borrowed** [Slide 31].

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x: The owner of Radome Composites S.L., which makes radar domes for aircraft noses, says: "In December we delivered 20 domes to an airline that will pay in February, so they are not sales of this year. We received in November a 30,000 m.u. advance for domes to be delivered next March, so that is income of this year. The electricity of December will be paid in January, so it is a cost of next year. And the five-year bank loan is all a long-term debt, even the instalment due next June."

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x: Revenues are recorded when the sale is made, expenses when goods and services are received, whether paid or not [Slide 8]. Current items are settled within one year [Slides 14-16].

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x:
- December deliveries: revenue of this year; the amount owed is an account receivable (current asset).
- November advance: not revenue yet; a liability (unearned revenue) until delivery in March.
- December electricity: expense of this year; unpaid amount is a current liability.
- Loan: the instalment due next June is a current liability; the rest is long-term.

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x:
| Owner's statement | Correction | Basis |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| December deliveries are not sales of this year | **They are revenue of this year**: the sale was made in December. The amount owed is an **account receivable**, a current asset | Revenues are recorded when the sale is made, paid or not [Slide 8]; current assets [Slide 14] |
| The November advance is income of this year | **It is not revenue yet**: no domes have been delivered. It is a **liability** (unearned revenue) until March | Liabilities include unearned revenues [Slide 13] |
| December electricity is a cost of next year | **It is an expense of this year**: the service was received in December. The unpaid amount is a **current liability** | Expenses are recorded when the services are received [Slide 8] |
| The whole loan is long-term | **The instalment due next June is a current liability**; only the instalments due after one year are long-term | Current liabilities are paid within the coming year [Slide 16] |

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x:
- The income statement reports performance over a period: it must match the revenues and expenses of that period, not cash movements.
- The balance sheet reports the financial position at a point in time: classifying by maturity shows liquidity.

chunks.t: Radome Composites: revenues vs collections and current vs non-current items
chunks.x:
The **income statement** reports the **performance** of the business over a specific period [Slide 7]: it must contain the revenues earned and the expenses incurred in that period, whatever happens to the cash, otherwise the profit of a year would depend on when customers happen to pay. The **balance sheet** reports the **financial position at a particular point in time** [Slide 12]: splitting assets and liabilities into current and non-current shows whether the company can meet the debts due within the year with the resources that become cash within the year.

The newly appointed financial director of **LOGÍSTICA FRIGORÍFICA DEL LEVANTE S.L. (FRIGOLEV)**, a company located in the port area of Castellón and dedicated to the manufacturing of isothermal containers and cold-chain storage equipment for agricultural exporters, is working on the closing of its financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018).

The company was originally incorporated on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) by four partners, with an initial contribution of each of 1.500 m.u. disbursed fully in cash at that time, and no further capital modifications took place until fiscal year 2018. Due to the sudden departure of the previous chief accountant, the financial director only has an incomplete balance of the company as of 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), which is included below with certain missing figures marked as (?), along with the audit notes detailing the operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018) to 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018):

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
**I.** On 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), the company had as depreciable fixed assets only the industrial refrigeration chambers purchased on a certain date during 2016, which have a useful life of 10 years and are amortized linearly with a residual value of 10% of their acquisition cost. In addition, the balance sheet at 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) reflected an industrial plot of land acquired in 2016 and financial shares of other companies acquired as a permanent investment.

**II.** During the year 2018, the company has sold 3.600 units of isothermal containers at a catalog price of 25 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 300 u.). The general payment condition agreed with the customers implies that this will occur 60 days after the sale. However, a very important agricultural cooperative (representing 25% of the physical units sold each month), which has bought an equal amount every month, has been given a discount of 8% on the catalog price of their purchases in exchange for paying strictly in cash in the same month of the sale.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
**III.** At 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) there was a stock (stock in stock) of 400 tons of insulating raw material valued at 2,00 m.u. / ton. On 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), the company purchased 5.000 tons of raw material at a cost of 2,00 m.u. / ton. The payment condition agreed with the suppliers was 40% paid in cash on the date of purchase, 30% payable to 90 days, and the remaining 30% deferred until 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019). At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), after conducting the warehouse count, there remains a final stock (stock in stock) of 900 tons.

**IV.** During the first quarter of 2018, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances from the previous year were paid in full. Regarding the customer debt outstanding from 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), 75% was charged in cash during the first semester of 2018, except 200 m.u. from a customer who requested and was granted a deferral of payment until 15 March 2019 (15/03/2019), and 100 m.u. corresponding to a client declared definitively insolvent on 1 June 2018 (01/06/2018), which must be recorded as an unrecoverable bad debt loss for the period.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
**V.** Fixed personnel expenses have been 2.200 m.u. / month (to which 600 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security) from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018). To respond to seasonal peaks in container assembly, production staff also received variable wages that amounted in 2018 to 3.620 m.u. Fixed and variable wages are paid in the month in which they are produced, whereas Social Security contributions (starting from January 2018) are paid on the 15th day of the following month. General expenses and utilities (electricity, phone, insurance, etc.) amounted to 1.100 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

**VI.** The company carried out a renting contract on 1 March 2018 (01/03/2018) (with a duration of 2 years) with a specialized company for electric warehouse forklifts, for a value of 350 m.u. monthly. The contract establishes a condition of payment to 90 days (payment at the end of each month).

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x: **VII.** On 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), the company made a capital increase by issuing 1.000 new shares of 2,00 m.u. nominal value each, fully disbursed in cash and with an issue premium of 50% over the nominal value. On the same date, 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), it bought two refrigerated delivery vehicles that cost a total of 4.800 m.u., of which it paid 50% in cash, postponing the payment of the remainder in two equal installments: half on 1 October 2018 (01/10/2018) and the other half on 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019). These vehicles will be amortized linearly in 6 years with a total residual value of 480 m.u. Furthermore, on 1 October 2018 (01/10/2018), it bought a software license for cold-chain tracking for a value of 1.600 m.u., payable to 120 days, which is amortized linearly in 4 years with residual value zero.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x: **VIII.** The long-term bank loan appearing on the balance sheet at 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) was granted on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) at an annual interest rate of 6%. Each 31 December, the company must pay the accrued annual interest calculated from the loan value at the beginning of each year, and starting on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) it must also return to the bank an annual principal amount of 500 m.u. until completing the repayment on 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021). Additionally, on 1 July 2018 (01/07/2018), the company obtained a new short-term bank credit of 1.500 m.u. at 8% annual interest, agreeing to return 50% of the principal each semester for the next year. Both the principal installment and the semiannual interest calculated on the amount actually due in that semester will be paid the day after the end of each semester (i.e., on 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) and 1 July 2019 (01/07/2019)).

**Hypotheses** (readings of the statement that the solution depends on):
1. Item IV: 75% of the 1.200 m.u. (900 m.u.) is collected; the remaining 25% (300 m.u.) is exactly the 200 m.u. deferred plus the 100 m.u. written off.

- Raw material consumed −225 (90 fewer units × 2,50); net profit 17.831,25 (−168,75).
- Receivables +3.375; inventory +225; cash 10.302,50 (−3.757,50); total assets 38.112,50.
- Profit and cash are both higher with the discount.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. New sales of the cooperative

$$75 \times 0{,}90 = 67{,}5 \text{ u./month}, \qquad 67{,}5 \times 25 = 1.687{,}5 \text{ m.u./month}, \qquad 12 \times 1.687{,}5 = 20.250 \text{ m.u.}$$

$$\Delta\text{Revenue} = 20.250 - 20.700 = -450 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Revenue} = 87.750 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 2. Raw material (hypothesis 4)

In the base case 4.500 tons were consumed for 3.600 units: $4.500 / 3.600 = 1{,}25$ t/unit $= 2{,}50$ m.u./unit. Selling $12 \times 7{,}5 = 90$ units fewer:

$$\Delta\text{Consumption} = -90 \times 2{,}50 = -225 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{final stock} = 1.800 + 225 = 2.025 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 3. New results

$$\text{Profit before taxes} = 24.000 - 450 + 225 = 23.775, \qquad \text{Tax} = 0{,}25 \times 23.775 = 5.943{,}75$$

$$\text{Net profit} = 23.775 - 5.943{,}75 = 17.831{,}25, \qquad \text{Remaining} = 17.431{,}25$$

$$\text{Reserves} = 0{,}60 \times 17.431{,}25 = 10.458{,}75, \qquad \text{Dividends} = 0{,}40 \times 17.431{,}25 = 6.972{,}50$$

#### Step 4. New cash

The cooperative now pays at 60 days: January to October collected, $10 \times 1.687{,}5 = 16.875$ instead of 20.700 (−3.825). The dividend paid falls by 67,50; the tax is not paid in 2018.

$$\text{Cash} = 14.060 - 3.825 + 67{,}50 = 10.302{,}50 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 5. Changes in the statements

chunks.x:
| Item | Base | Without discount | Change |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 88.200 | 87.750 | −450 |
| Raw material consumed | 9.000 | 8.775 | −225 |
| Net profit | 18.000 | 17.831,25 | −168,75 |
| Inventory | 1.800 | 2.025 | +225 |
| Accounts receivable | 11.450 | 14.825 | +3.375 |
| Cash | 14.060 | 10.302,50 | −3.757,50 |
| **Total assets** | 38.270 | 38.112,50 | −157,50 |
| Reserves | 10.560 | 10.458,75 | −101,25 |
| Unpaid taxes | 6.000 | 5.943,75 | −56,25 |
| **Total liabilities and equity** | 38.270 | 38.112,50 | −157,50 |

**Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the discount** (18.000 against 17.831,25): removing the discount gains $2$ m.u. on each of the 810 units the cooperative still buys ($810 \times 2 = 1.620$ m.u.), but the 90 units it stops buying carried a margin over raw material of $23 - 2{,}50 = 20{,}50$ m.u. each ($90 \times 20{,}50 = 1.845$ m.u.); the net effect before taxes is $1.620 - 1.845 = -225$ m.u. The **cash is also higher with the discount** (14.060 against 10.302,50): the cooperative pays in the same month, while under the general condition November and December stay as receivables. Keeping the discount wins on both counts.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit and tons × m.u./ton give m.u.; m.u./year × months/12 gives m.u.; ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why ROA and ROE are so high:** the company's annual sales (88.200 m.u.) are ten times its 2017 assets; the ratios are measured on the year-end balance, which already includes most of the year's profit.
- **Accrual vs cash:** net profit 18.000 m.u., but cash grew by only 13.120 m.u. because 11.250 m.u. of sales are uncollected, although many expenses (tax, software, raw material, renting) are still unpaid.
- **Typical mistakes:** depreciating the vehicles for 12 months, forgetting the residual values, treating the issue premium as capital, and putting the whole short-term credit or the 200 m.u. deferred receivable outside current items.

chunks.t: AGRODRON: the second year of a drone start-up that closed its first year with a loss
chunks.x:
The company **AGRODRON LEVANTE S.L.** was incorporated on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) by a group of agricultural engineers with a registered paid-in capital of 4.500 m.u., having an objective of providing precision crop-monitoring services by drone and distributing organic fertilizers in the region of Murcia.

**The following information applies to fiscal year 2017:**

To finance the operations of the company, on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) a bank granted the company a loan of 1.500 m.u. at 6% annual interest, with a duration of 5 years, i.e. until 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021). Each 31 December, the company must return to the bank an equal principal amount of 300 m.u. and should also pay the due annual interest (6%) calculated from the loan value at the beginning of each year.

chunks.t: AGRODRON: the second year of a drone start-up that closed its first year with a loss
chunks.x:
During 2017, the company invested in a fleet of agricultural drones worth 2.400 m.u. The useful life of the drones purchased was 8 years (amortized linearly, with no residual value) and at the end of 2017 the company recorded in accumulated depreciation an amount of 75 m.u. for those assets. Also, a further investment of 400 m.u. in mapping software licenses was made on 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) to process aerial images. They use these licenses for 4 years (linear amortization with residual value zero). In addition, the company spent 800 m.u. to purchase a plot of rural land for its flight testing base. Most of 2017 was devoted to obtaining civil aviation permits and only the actual business work was started in the final months of the year. At 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), its balance sheet reflected a loss of 220 m.u., there was no stock (stock in stock) nor pending customer or supplier balances, and the cash in hand and bank account was 1.955 m.u.

**The following information applies to fiscal year 2018:**

chunks.x:

Additionally, the company billed 840 m.u. for the direct sales of organic fertilizers. At the end of 2018, AGRODRON had accounts receivable of 310 m.u. from their customers.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
The external auditor of **TALLERES AERONÁUTICOS DEL HENARES S.A. (TAHSA)**, a company of Alcalá de Henares dedicated to the machining of titanium brackets and fittings for the aircraft structures industry, must issue the audit report on the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019). The auditor has the balance of the company as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), which is included below, and the following operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) to 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019).

**I.** The company has sold during the year 2.400 brackets at a price of 8 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 200 u.). A part of the sales of each month, always the same percentage, is charged in cash in the moment of the sale; the rest is payable to 90 days. Unfortunately the commercial department has lost the contract that fixes this percentage.

**II.** During the first quarter of 2019, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances of the previous year were paid. The customer debt outstanding from the previous year was charged in January, except 160 m.u. from an airline component maker declared in insolvency on 1 March 2019 (01/03/2019), which is definitively lost.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**III.** At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 800 kg of titanium bar valued at 1,50 m.u. / kg. On 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019) the company purchased 3.000 kg at 1,50 m.u. / kg, 50% payable to 60 days and the other 50% deferred until 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020). On 1 August 2019 (01/08/2019) it purchased 2.000 kg more at the same price, payable to 120 days. The count of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) shows 900 kg in the warehouse.

**IV.** Personnel expenses have been 400 m.u. / month (to which 120 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security); salaries are paid in the month in which they are produced and Social Security the month after. General expenses (electricity, insurance, cleaning) amount to 150 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

**V.** The machinery of the balance of 2018 was bought on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with residual value zero. On 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019) the company bought a 5-axis CNC centre that cost 4.800 m.u., paid in full in cash that day. To finance it, the same day a bank granted a loan of 3.600 m.u. at 5% annual interest, to be returned in one single payment on 1 April 2022 (01/04/2022); the interest is paid every 1 April for the year that ends that day. The CNC centre will be amortized linearly in 8 years with a residual value of 480 m.u.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**VI.** The long-term loan of the balance of 2018 bears 4% annual interest. The company returns 300 m.u. of principal every 30 June and every 31 December, paying the same days the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester.

**VII.** On 1 October 2019 (01/10/2019) the shareholders subscribed a capital increase of 500 new shares of 2 m.u. nominal value, without issue premium, disbursing that day only 50%; the rest will be called in 2020. On 15 November 2019 (15/11/2019) the company received in cash a dividend of 80 m.u. from its financial shares in AEROPIEZAS S.A., a permanent investment.

**VIII.** The bank statement at 23:00 hrs on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), before any operation of the closing, shows a balance of 3.024 m.u. The results are declared at 23:59 hrs; the corporation tax of 30% is paid immediately, and 50% of the profit after taxes is paid as dividends before the final balance at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019); the rest goes to reserves.

**Required:**
1. Deduce, justifying it from the bank statement, the percentage of the sales that is charged in cash, and construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of TAHSA for the year 2019.
2. Construct and justify the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), showing all the intermediate calculations.
3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios in 2019.

Indicate what changes would have occurred in the Income Statement, the cash and the balance sheet of 2019 if this policy had been applied from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019). In which case is the profit higher, and in which case is the final cash balance higher? Discuss, reasoned, why.

**Unknown of the problem:** the share $p$ of each month's sales charged in cash. Every other flow of cash can be computed, so the bank statement before the closing (3.024 m.u.) gives one equation in $p$.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x: **Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the present policy**: the discount is a real cost of 384 m.u. (269 m.u. after tax). The **cash is higher with the new policy**: 576 m.u. more are collected in 2019 because more of each sale is charged at once, and the lower profit also means less tax and fewer dividends paid at the closing. The discount buys liquidity at the price of profitability; it is worth it only if the company needs the cash or if the money collected earlier earns more than the discount costs.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit, kg × m.u./kg and m.u./year × months/12 all give m.u.; $p$ and the ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why the bank balance is enough:** all the other flows are fixed by the terms of the contracts, so the cash balance determines the single unknown term, the share of cash sales.
- **Uncalled capital:** the 500 m.u. not disbursed are a debt of the shareholders to the company, not cash; showing them as a deduction keeps equity at the money actually contributed.
- **Typical mistakes:** paying the CNC loan interest in 2019, depreciating the CNC for 12 months, counting the dividend received as revenue from operations, and treating the bad debt as a collection.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x:
**AVIÓNICA DEL EBRO S.L. (AVIEBRO)**, a Zaragoza workshop dedicated to the repair and calibration of avionics equipment for regional airlines and flying schools, must present to the bank that finances it the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020). The financial director has the balance of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), included below, and the following operations of the first semester, from 1 January 2020 (01/01/2020) to 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020):

**I.** The company has invoiced repairs for 1.600 m.u. every month. The payment condition agreed with the customers is payable to 60 days. A regional airline, which represents 40% of the invoicing of every month, surpassed in March the annual volume agreed in its contract, and from 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) it receives a discount of 5% on all its invoices.

**II.** The customer debt outstanding at 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) was charged in January, except 250 m.u. from a flying school that has been granted to pay it on 30 September 2020 (30/09/2020). The suppliers of the previous year were paid in February. As the company closed 2019 with losses, there were no taxes to pay.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x:
**III.** At 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 300 spare parts valued at 2 m.u. / unit. On 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020) the company purchased 400 parts at 2 m.u., 50% paid in cash and 50% payable to 90 days; on 1 May 2020 (01/05/2020) it purchased 300 parts more at the same price, payable to 120 days. At 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020) there remain 250 parts in the warehouse.

**IV.** The technicians cost 600 m.u. / month, paid in the same month, to which 180 m.u. / month of Social Security must be added, paid the month after. The overheads (electricity, telephone, cleaning) are 100 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made. On 1 March 2020 (01/03/2020) the company carried out a renting contract for a test bench of 120 m.u. monthly, paid at the end of each month.

**V.** The patent of the balance (a calibration procedure) is amortized linearly in 5 years with residual value zero; the computer equipment was bought on 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) and is amortized linearly in 3 years with residual value zero.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x:
**VI.** On 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) AVIEBRO bought a small hangar next to the airport: the building is valued at 2.000 m.u. and the land at 1.000 m.u. It paid 20% in cash and the rest with a mortgage loan at 4% annual interest, to be returned in installments of 120 m.u. every 1 October and every 1 April, the first one on 1 October 2020 (01/10/2020); the same days it pays the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester. The building is amortized linearly in 50 years with residual value zero.

**VII.** The long-term loan of the balance bears 5% annual interest, which is paid every 31 December, and it is returned in one single payment on 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022).

**VIII.** The corporation tax is 25%. The taxable base of the semester is the profit before taxes minus the losses from previous years still pending to offset, and the resulting tax will be paid on 20 July 2020 (20/07/2020) (counted in the balance as "taxes to pay"). No dividends are distributed at the half-year.

**BALANCE 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019)**

**Required:**
1. Deduce the exact date on which the patent was acquired, and construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of AVIEBRO for the first semester of 2020, explaining the intermediate calculations.
2. Calculate the cash and construct the balance sheet at 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020).
3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios of the semester, and indicate how the Income Statement and the balance sheet would change if the tax authority did not allow to offset the losses from previous years.
4. Instead of buying the hangar, the company could have rented it from 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) for 50 m.u. monthly, paid at the end of each month. Indicate the changes in the Income Statement, the cash and the balance sheet at 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020). In which case is the profit higher, and in which case is the final cash balance higher? Discuss, reasoned, why.

1. The airline's discount applies to the invoices of April, May and June only.
2. "Payable to 90 days" from 1 February means payment on 1 May; "payable to 120 days" from 1 May means payment at the end of August, outside the semester.
3. The losses from previous years are offset for tax purposes, but they stay in the balance sheet until the annual meeting distributes the profit of the year; the result of the semester is shown separately in equity.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x: **Discussion.** The **profit is higher buying the hangar**: three months of rent (150) cost more than the depreciation of the building (10) and the mortgage interest (24) together, because the land is not depreciated and the mortgage is cheap. The **cash is higher renting**: the company keeps the 600 m.u. of down payment and pays only 150 of rent. Buying gives more profit but ties up cash and adds 2.400 m.u. of debt; renting preserves liquidity, which matters for a workshop that ends the semester with only 538 m.u. in the bank.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** m.u./month × months gives m.u.; rates × m.u. × months/12 give m.u.; ratios dimensionless.
- **Half-year ratios:** ROA and ROE of a semester are not annual returns; annualising them would roughly double them.

**II.** At 31 December 2020 (31/12/2020) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 500 kg of epoxy resin valued at 3 m.u. / kg. On 1 March 2021 (01/03/2021) the company purchased 4.000 kg at 3 m.u. / kg, paying 30% in cash and the remaining 70% in two equal parts, on 1 September 2021 (01/09/2021) and on 1 March 2022 (01/03/2022). chunks.t: CAESA: financing a second autoclave with a semiannual loan or with new shares
chunks.x:
| Ratio | Loan | Capital increase |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| ROA | 12,97% | $3.530 / 27.143{,}20 = 13{,}01\%$ |
| ROE | 19,01% | $2.776 / 21.143{,}20 = 13{,}13\%$ |
| $L/E$ [Slide 36] | 0,97 | $6.000 / 21.143{,}20 = 0{,}28$ |

The assets earn the same income from operations in both cases (about 13% of the assets), while the new loan costs only 5%. Each m.u. borrowed earns more than it costs, and the difference goes to the shareholders: with the loan, equity is 7.300,80 m.u. smaller while the net profit is only 144 m.u. lower, so the ROE rises from 13,13% to 19,01%. (Separately, the profit is shared among 10.000 shares instead of 14.800, which raises the earnings per share, an extension.) This is the positive **financial leverage effect** (the relation ROE vs ROA − cost of debt is an extension). Its price is risk: the loan raises the debt-to-equity ratio from 0,28 to 0,97 and commits the company to 1.800 m.u. of installments plus interest every year, while the new shares never have to be repaid [Slides 25, 36].

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: 🏢 Topic 1: The Firm — Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** a business transforms inputs into the goods and services that people need. Firms and households are tied together by a circular flow of goods, factors and money. Inside the firm, real, financial and management functions are coordinated by an entrepreneur, the person who holds the rights over the residual income. The law offers several forms of ownership, and in large corporations the separation between owners and managers gives rise to the agency problem.

The topic covers six points [Slide 2]: the concept and nature of business, the functional areas of a business, the management process, the role of engineers in business management, the enterprise and the entrepreneur, and the types of companies and their legal forms.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
A **business** is an economic activity that **transforms a set of inputs**, the factors of production, **into outputs**: goods and services aimed at satisfying customers' needs and wants.

| Inputs (factors of production) | Outputs |
| :--- | :--- |
| Land (natural resources) | Goods |
| Labour | Services |
| Capital | |
| Entrepreneurship | |

Making bread is a simple case. Salt, baking powder, flour, sugar and water are the inputs and bread is the output, but the ingredients do not become bread by themselves: something has to transform them, and that transformation is precisely the business activity.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
The **circular flow of income** is a simple economic model of the reciprocal circulation of income between producers and consumers. The markets of goods and services and the markets of factors interact continuously and create a **double flow, real and monetary**; through it, the economy of a country decides **what to produce, how, and for whom** [Slide 5].

Two economic agents take part [Slide 6]:
- **Households** play a double role [Slide 7]: they **own the factors of production** (land, labour, capital, technology and know-how) and they are the **fundamental units of consumption**.
- **Firms** use the factors supplied by households to produce the goods and services that households demand [Slide 8].

The exchange between them takes place in two markets:
- In the **factor markets**, such as the labour market and the stock-exchange market, households deliver inputs to firms and receive incomes in return: **wages, rents and dividends** [Slide 9].
- In the **market of goods and services**, firms sell what they produce to households and collect the money that households spend [Slide 10].

Every exchange therefore has two sides [Slide 11]. **Real flows** are the goods, services and factors themselves; **financial flows** are their monetary compensation, which runs in the opposite direction. What the firm keeps after paying for the factors is its **profit**.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: 3. The nature of business: market and enterprise [Slide 12]
chunks.x: **Economics** studies how people and societies choose to use **scarce resources** (the factors of production) to satisfy **unlimited wants**. These wants are met through **specialization**, that is, the division of labour. Specialization in turn requires **coordination**, and coordination can be carried out in two ways: by the **market** or by the **enterprise**. An enterprise appears because there is a **dissatisfied need**.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
The functions of a business fall into three groups:
- **Real functions** turn inputs into outputs through the real activity: functions related to **supply** (acquisition of inputs), to **production** and to **marketing**, plus **support** functions such as Human Resources or Information Systems.
- **Financial functions** run alongside the real cycle. The firm raises funds (searches for financial resources), pays for the acquisition of inputs, receives revenues from sales, and returns capital and interests to those who provided the funds. They include the functions related to **financing** and to **investing**.
- **Management functions**: **planning**, **organization** and **control**.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
Managing consists of four activities, as formulated by Henri Fayol (1841-1925), which are repeated as a cycle around one common aim, **achieving the organization's stated purpose**:

| Stage | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Planning** | Defining goals, establishing strategy and developing subplans to coordinate activities |
| **Organizing** | Determining what needs to be done, how it will be done and who is to do it |
| **Leading** | Directing and motivating all involved parties and resolving conflicts |
| **Controlling** | Monitoring activities to ensure that they are accomplished as planned |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: 6. The role of engineers in business management [Slide 15]

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
An **entrepreneur** is a risk taker who starts and operates a business in the hope of making a profit. **Entrepreneurship** is the process of bringing land, labour and capital together and taking the risk involved in producing a good or service in the hope of making a profit [Slide 16].

There is no conclusive agreement on who the entrepreneur is or on his or her role in the enterprise. The duties are especially unclear in big companies, where owners, management directors and moneylenders each seem to share some of the characteristics attributed to a single person, the entrepreneur [Slide 16].

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
| The entrepreneur as... | Author |
| :--- | :--- |
| Coordinator | |
| Risk taker | Knight, 1921 |
| Innovator | Schumpeter, 1950 |
| "On alert" | Kirzner, 1973 |

Putting the four views together, the **functions of the entrepreneur** are to coordinate and control the productive process, ensure the payment of the factors of production, take risky decisions, innovate, and detect new business opportunities.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: 7.3 The entrepreneur as the holder of rights [Slide 18]

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
| Criterion | Classes |
| :--- | :--- |
| Economic: sector | Primary, secondary, tertiary |
| Economic: size | Big, medium, small |
| Economic: scope of the business | One market or multi-market; national or multinational |
| Legal: ownership of the factors of production | Private companies; state-owned companies |
| Legal: main forms of business ownership | Sole proprietorship; partnership; corporation |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x: The forms of ownership are the **sole proprietorship**, the **partnership** (general partnership or limited liability partnership, LLP), the **corporation**, and **other forms** such as cooperative associations, joint ventures and mutual companies.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
A **sole proprietorship** is a business owned by **one person**, who assumes all the risk, takes the decisions and looks for business opportunities, and therefore **owns all the rights**.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| Simple to start | Unlimited financial liability |
| The proprietor owns all the profits | Hard to raise funds for expansion |
| Personal satisfaction (being your own boss) | Often no one to share management responsibilities (one person's talents and skills) |
| Sole decision maker | Impermanence |
| No tax on the business as distinct from the owner | |
| Easy to dissolve | |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
A **partnership** is an association of **two or more persons** who carry on a business for profit as **co-owners**. It is formed through a **partnership agreement**, a written contract between the owners that identifies the business and sets out the partners' rights and duties: name, location, type of business, sharing of profits, dissolution of the partnership, and so on [Slide 22].

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| Few restrictions on starting | Unlimited and joint financial liability |
| Pooling of funds, talents and borrowing power | Potential for personal disagreements |
| More chance to specialize than in a sole proprietorship | Relative impermanence |
| No tax on the business as distinct from the owners | Frozen investment |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
A **corporation** is a legally chartered organization that is a **separate legal entity** from its owners and has most of the rights of a person.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| Separate legal entity (the shareholders are the owners) | Special and double taxation |
| Limited financial liability of the owners | Complex and costly to form and to dissolve |
| Permanence (it can exist forever) | Government regulation and public disclosure requirements |
| Easy transfer of ownership (shares) | |
| Greater financial capability | |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: The three main forms side by side
chunks.x:
| Feature | Sole proprietorship | Partnership | Corporation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Owners | One person | Two or more co-owners | Shareholders |
| Liability | Unlimited | Unlimited and joint | Limited |
| Taxation | No tax on the business as distinct from the owner | No tax on the business as distinct from the owners | Special and double taxation |
| Permanence | Impermanent | Relatively impermanent | Permanent |
| Funds | Hard to raise | Pooled | Greater financial capability |
| Starting and ending | Simple to start, easy to dissolve | Few restrictions on starting | Complex and costly |

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.h: 13. Separation of ownership and control: the agency problem [Slides 25-26]

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
A **cooperative association** is an incorporated organization whose **user-members**, who are also its owners, get back any revenue left after expenses are paid [Slide 27]. It follows five principles:
1. Membership is open.
2. It is owned and democratically controlled by its members.
3. Economic benefits are distributed in proportion to each member's level of participation in the cooperative.
4. It is based on the values of self-help, self-responsibility, democracy and equality.
5. Its members believe in the ethical values of honesty, openness, social responsibility and caring for others.

Common types of cooperative [Slide 28]:
- **Employee credit unions** accept savings deposits from members, who own shares in the co-op, and lend to members: savers receive interest and borrowers pay it.
- **Agricultural co-ops** help member farmers market their products.
- **Buying co-ops** help members buy products at lower prices.
- **Consumer co-ops** run customer-owned retail facilities: consumers form a buying pool to obtain quantity discounts and to replace wholesalers and retailers.

chunks.t: Topic 1 - The Firm - Types and Objectives
chunks.x:
- In a **limited partnership**, one or more of the partners, but not all of them, are liable for the firm's debts only up to the amount they have invested in it.
- A **joint venture** is a special type of partnership set up by individuals or firms to accomplish a specific task or project. It is very important and common in international business.
