chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.h: 📈 Topic 2: Value Creation — Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** the objective of the firm moves from the classical maximization of profit to the creation of value, agreed among its stakeholders. To reach it, the firm defines a strategy: it studies the generic and the specific environment (Porter's five forces), decides where to compete (corporate strategy: product, geographical and vertical scope) and how to compete (business strategy: cost or differentiation advantage), and analyses its own activities through Porter's value chain.

The topic is organised in three parts [Slide 2]: business objectives (the traditional concept of profit maximization, and the new objectives that arise from the role of stakeholders), business strategies and their types, and the generic and specific environment.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x: To avoid the conflict of interests between managers and shareholders, their objectives must be **aligned**. Four mechanisms do so: **incentive compensation**, the **market of enterprises**, the **labour market** and the **markets of the factors of production**. In the end, managers try to maximize their own interests, always subject to achieving a **minimum level of profit** that satisfies the shareholders.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
Many groups have a stake in the objectives of the firm. Around **management** stand the **shareholders**, **banks and other financial agents**, **customers**, **suppliers**, the **State**, **employees and labour unions**, and **society** (corporate social responsibility) [Slide 5].

According to **organizational theory**, the objectives of the business are the **outcome of a negotiation** among these stakeholders, limited by two facts: the firm must **survive**, and **not all groups have the same decision-making power**. The business objective is therefore the one that satisfies the group with the highest bargaining power, while taking into account the objectives of the other groups and the survival of the enterprise. That objective is to **maximize the value of the enterprise: to create value** [Slide 6].

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.h: 4. A unified vision: survival, profit and growth [Slide 7]
chunks.x: The three goals form a single cycle. Current and new **products and markets** generate **sales**, and sales generate **profits**. Part of the profits is **retained** for future investments and adds directly to **total equity**; the rest is paid as **dividends**, which support the **capital market valuation of the company** and thus the **equity attributable to investors**, which also feeds total equity. Total equity finances new **investments**, and these renew the products and markets, closing the cycle.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x: To achieve its objective, the firm defines a **strategy**: "a plan, method or series of actions designed to achieve a specific goal or effect" (Wordsmyth Dictionary). The strategy unfolds into three levels of decision: **strategic**, **tactic** and **operative** decisions.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
Strategic decisions belong to two families:
- **Corporate strategy**, which fixes the **scope** of the firm: product scope (diversification), geographical scope (internationalization) and vertical scope (vertical integration).
- **Competitive or business strategy**, which chooses between a **cost-leadership** strategy and a **differentiation** strategy.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x: A strategy succeeds through **effective implementation** resting on three pillars: **long-term, simple and agreed objectives**; a **deep understanding of the competitive environment**; and an **objective appraisal of resources**.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.h: 8. The business environment: generic and specific [Slides 11-12]
chunks.x:
The environment of the firm has two layers.

The **generic environment** affects every firm and is described by four groups of factors [Slide 11]:

| Factors | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Economic** | Macroeconomic variables; business cycle period; type of economic policy; country resources |
| **Political-legal** | Monetary and fiscal policies; labour market regulation; industry regulation |
| **Socio-cultural** | Value system; level of education; class structure; income distribution; population distribution; etc. |
| **Technological** | Basic, key and incipient technologies |

The **specific environment** is the environment of the firm's own industry [Slide 12]. It includes the **rivalry within the industry**, which depends on concentration, the industry rate of growth and product differentiation; the **barriers to entry** and **to exit**; **substitutes**; and the **relationships with customers** and **with suppliers**.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.h: 9. From environmental analysis to industry analysis [Slide 13]
chunks.x: The analysis moves from the outside in. At the centre is the **industry environment**, formed by suppliers, competitors and customers. Around it act the national and international economy, technology, government and politics, the natural environment, the demographic structure and the social structure.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
The industry is analysed with **Porter's five competitive forces** (Porter, 1982). At the centre is the **rivalry among existing firms**; around it act the **bargaining power of suppliers**, the **bargaining power of buyers**, the **threat of new entrants** and the **threat of substitutes** [Slide 14]. Each force depends on a set of determinants [Slide 15]:

| Force | Determinants |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Supplier power** | Suppliers' price sensitivity; relative bargaining power |
| **Buyer power** | Buyers' price sensitivity; relative bargaining power |
| **Threat of entry** | Capital requirements; economies of scale; absolute cost advantage; product differentiation; access to distribution channels; legal and regulatory barriers |
| **Substitute competition** | Buyers' propensity to substitute; relative prices and performance of substitutes |
| **Industry rivalry** | Concentration; diversity of competitors; product differentiation; excess capacity and exit barriers; cost conditions |

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x: Strategic management follows five steps: the **mission statement**, the **performance objectives**, the **development of strategies**, the **implementation** of the strategy, and the **evaluation of performance**.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
The aim is to earn a **rate of profit above the competitive level**; in other words, to answer the question "how do we make money?". Two sources contribute to it [Slide 17]:
- **industry attractiveness**, which raises the question "which businesses should we be in?" and is the domain of **corporate strategy**;
- **competitive advantage**, which raises the question "how should we compete?" and is the domain of **business strategy**.

**Business strategy** is concerned with **how** a firm competes within a particular market. **Corporate strategy** is concerned with **where** a firm competes, that is, with the **scope** of its activities, which has three dimensions: **geographical**, **vertical** and **product** scope [Slide 18].

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
Each dimension of scope can be pictured as a choice between one firm and several (Grant, 2002):
- **Vertical scope**: three independent companies (one producing steel, one rolling it into sheet, one making steel cans), or all three stages of production inside a single company?
- **Geographical scope**: three independent companies producing cans in the US, the UK and Italy, or a single multinational owning and operating the can-making plants in all three countries?
- **Product scope**: should metal cans, plastic packaging and domestic appliances be made by three separate companies, or are there efficiencies to be gained by merging them into one?

In the integrated firm the vertical units (V), product units (P) and country units (G) are linked by an **administrative interface**; under specialization each unit is a **separate firm** linked to the others by **market interfaces**.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.h: 14. Business strategy: sources of competitive advantage [Slide 20]
chunks.x: Competitive advantage comes from two sources: a **cost advantage**, offering a similar product at a lower cost, or a **differentiation advantage**, obtaining a price premium from a unique product.

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
| Driver | How it reduces costs |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Economies of learning** | Improved organizational routines |
| **Economies of scale** | Specialization and division of labour |
| **Production techniques** | Process innovation; reengineering of business processes |
| **Product design** | Standardization of designs and components; design for manufacture |
| **Input costs** | Location advantages; ownership of low-cost inputs; non-union labour; bargaining power |
| **Capacity utilization** | Ratio of fixed to variable costs; speed of capacity adjustment |
| **Residual efficiency** | Organizational slack; motivation and culture; managerial efficiency |

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
**Differentiation** concerns how a firm distinguishes its offerings from those of its competitors, that is, how the firm competes. In Porter's words, it means "providing something unique that is valuable to the buyer beyond simply offering a low price". The key is to **create value for the customer** [Slide 23].

Differentiation can be [Slide 24]:
- **tangible**, based on observable characteristics of the product: size, colour, materials, etc.; performance; packaging; complementary services;
- **intangible**, based on unobservable and subjective characteristics that appeal to the customer's image, status, identity and desire for exclusivity.

Differentiation is not only about the product: it embraces the **whole relationship between supplier and customer** (total customer responsiveness).

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
- **Related diversification**: the business expands its existing product lines or markets.
- **Unrelated diversification**: the business adds new, unrelated product lines or markets.

Diversification takes three forms: **vertical integration** (along the firm's own value chain), **horizontal diversification** (moving into a new industry) and **geographical diversification** (opening new markets).

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
Vertical integration can be **forward** or **backward**.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| Control of inputs and outputs | Increased risk (outsourcing) |
| Reduction of transaction costs | Decreased flexibility |
| Independence | Loss of specialization advantages |
| Better competitive position | Increased administrative costs |
| Reduction of information asymmetries | |

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
The term **value chain** was introduced by Michael Porter (1985). An organization is more than a random collection of resources: it arranges its resources into systems and activities that produce goods customers are willing to pay for, and the **management of these activities and of their linkages** is what gives it a competitive advantage [Slide 28].

The chain has two layers: **support activities** that span the whole firm, and **primary activities** that follow the product from inputs to after-sales. Together they produce the **margin** [Slide 29].

**Primary activities** [Slide 30]:

| Activity | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Inbound logistics** | Relationships with suppliers and all the activities required to receive, store and disseminate inputs |
| **Operations** | All the activities required to transform inputs into outputs (products and services) |
| **Outbound logistics** | All the activities required to collect, store and distribute the output |
| **Marketing and sales** | Informing buyers about products and services, inducing them to purchase, and facilitating the purchase |
| **Service** | All the activities required to keep the product or service working effectively for the buyer after it is sold and delivered |

**Secondary (support) activities** [Slide 31]:

chunks.t: Topic 2 - Value Creation - Environment and Competitive Advantage
chunks.x:
| Activity | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Procurement** | The acquisition of inputs, or resources, for the firm |
| **Human resource management** | Recruiting, hiring, training, developing, compensating and, if necessary, dismissing or laying off personnel |
| **Technological development** | The equipment, hardware, software, procedures and technical knowledge used to transform inputs into outputs |
| **Infrastructure** | Serves the company's needs and ties its parts together: accounting, legal, finance, planning, public affairs, government relations, quality assurance and general management |

Reference: Porter, M. E., *Competitive Advantage*, The Free Press, New York, 1985, Ch. 1, pp. 11-15.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 💰 Topic 3: Financial Management (I) — Financial Statements and Financial Structure
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** a firm has two sides. Its assets (the economic structure, what it owns) generate profitability; its equity and liabilities (the financial structure, what it owes) carry a cost. Value is created when profitability exceeds cost. Two statements describe the firm: the income statement, which measures performance over a period (revenues − expenses = net income), and the balance sheet, which shows the position at one moment (assets = liabilities + equity). The financial structure combines self-financing, external equity and long- and short-term debt; it is measured with the debt-to-equity ratio and priced with the weighted average cost of capital.

The topic has three parts [Slide 2]: an introduction to the economic and the financial structure; the financial statements, namely the income statement and the balance sheet; and the financial structure of the company.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 1. The finance area and its two decisions [Slide 3]
chunks.x: The **finance area** of a company is in charge of the **collection and management of the funds (capital)** the company uses. The finance manager faces two types of decision: what to invest in and when (**investing decisions**), and how to obtain the money to invest (**financing decisions**).

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
The **economic structure** is defined by the **investments** the company carries out. It represents the use of the financial resources in the form of goods (assets) and rights: the **assets**, or what is owned.

The **financial structure** is defined by the **sources of financing**. It includes all the financial resources used to carry out the investments (debt and liabilities): the **liabilities**, or what is owed [Slide 4].

The assets produce **profitability**, while equity and liabilities have a **cost**. The objective of the company is to **maximize value**, which requires **profitability > cost** [Slide 5].

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 3. What the company's decisions focus on [Slide 6]
chunks.x:
**Financing decisions** concern the choice between **equity and debt**. The financial resources available can be **internal equity** (self-financing, i.e. retained earnings), **external equity** or **debt**. Financing decisions involve decisions on the **capital structure** and on **dividends**.

**Investing decisions** consist in allocating capital to the investment projects from which future profits are expected. Companies invest in the projects that **create value** for them, those in which **profits > costs**.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
The **income statement** is the first statement prepared. It reports the **performance** of the business **over a specific period**, and in its simplest form [Slide 7]:

$$\text{Revenues} - \text{Expenses} = \text{Net income}$$

**Revenues** are earned from the sale of goods or services and are recorded **when the sale is made**, whether or not the payment has been received; examples are sales, service revenue and interest revenue. **Expenses** are incurred **when the business receives goods and services**, whether or not it has paid for them; examples are salaries, utility and interest expense [Slide 8].

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
| Line | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Sales revenue | |
| − Cost of goods sold | |
| **= Gross profit** | |
| − Operating expenses | |
| **= Income from operations** | |
| ± Non-operating items | |
| **= Income before taxes** | |
| − Income taxes | |
| **= Net income** | |

The lines are defined as follows:
- The **cost of goods sold** is the expense the business incurred to buy or make a product for resale. If a bookshop buys a book for 25 USD and sells it for 32 USD, the cost of goods sold is 25 USD [Slide 10].
- **Operating expenses** are the usual expenses of running the business, such as salaries, utilities and depreciation [Slide 10].
- **Non-operating items** are the revenues, expenses, gains and losses that do not relate to the company's primary operations, such as interest expense and gains and losses on the sale of equipment and investments [Slide 11].
- **Income taxes** are the income before taxes multiplied by the tax rate [Slide 11]. With an income before taxes of 50,000 USD and a rate of 30%:

$$\text{Income taxes} = 50{,}000 \times 0.30 = 15{,}000 \text{ USD}$$

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
The **balance sheet** reports the **financial position** of an accounting entity **at a particular point in time** [Slide 12]:

$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}$$

- **Assets** are the economic resources owned by the company: cash, accounts receivable, supplies, buildings, equipment.
- **Liabilities** are the company's debts or obligations: accounts payable, unearned revenues, bonds payable.
- **Equity** is the residual balance, $\text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities} = \text{Equity}$. In a corporation it is called **stockholders' equity**, because it represents the financing provided by the stockholders together with the earnings not paid out as dividends (**retained earnings**) [Slide 13].

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 7. Classes of assets, liabilities and equity [Slides 14-17]
chunks.x:
**Assets** are split into **current** and **non-current** [Slides 14-15]:

$$\text{Current assets} + \text{Non-current assets} = \text{Total assets}$$

- **Current assets** will be used or turned into cash **within one year**: cash, accounts receivable, inventory, short-term investments, supplies and prepaids.
- **Non-current assets** are all the others: long-term investments, land, buildings, equipment and patents.

**Liabilities** are split into **current** and **long-term** [Slide 16]:

$$\text{Current liabilities} + \text{Long-term liabilities} = \text{Total liabilities}$$

- **Current liabilities** will be paid in cash (or other services) or satisfied **within the coming year**.
- **Long-term liabilities** will not be paid or satisfied within the year.

**Stockholders' equity** is split into **contributed capital** and **retained earnings** [Slide 17]:

$$\text{Contributed capital} + \text{Retained earnings} = \text{Total stockholders' equity}$$

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x: $$\text{Current assets} + \text{Non-current assets} = \text{Current liabilities} + \text{Long-term liabilities} + \text{Stockholders' equity}$$

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 9. Worked example: from a list of accounts to the two statements [Slide 19]
chunks.x:
A company has the following accounts (tax rate 30%).

**Step 1. Classify each account.**

| Account | Amount | Class | Position |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| Cash | 5,000 | Asset | Current asset |
| Accounts receivable | 10,000 | Asset | Current asset |
| Inventories | 45,000 | Asset | Current asset |
| Supplies | 4,000 | Asset | Current asset |
| Buildings | 65,000 | Asset | Non-current asset |
| Accounts payable | 12,000 | Liability | Current liability |
| Bonds payable | 40,000 | Liability | Long-term liability [Slide 29] |
| Common stock | 45,000 | Equity | Contributed capital |
| Additional paid-in capital | 20,000 | Equity | Contributed capital |
| Retained earnings (beginning balance) | 5,000 | Equity | Retained earnings |
| Sales | 100,000 | Revenue | Sales revenue |
| Cost of goods sold | 58,000 | Expense | Cost of goods sold |
| Utility expense | 8,000 | Expense | Operating expense |
| Supplies expense | 3,000 | Expense | Operating expense |
| Salaries expense | 16,000 | Expense | Operating expense |
| Interest expense | 5,000 | Expense | Non-operating item |

**Supplies** (an asset still held) and **supplies expense** (the part consumed in the period) are different accounts.

**Step 2. Income statement.**

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 9. Worked example: from a list of accounts to the two statements [Slide 19]
chunks.x:
| Line | Computation | Amount |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Sales revenue | | 100,000 |
| − Cost of goods sold | | 58,000 |
| **= Gross profit** | $100{,}000 - 58{,}000$ | **42,000** |
| − Operating expenses | $8{,}000 + 3{,}000 + 16{,}000$ | 27,000 |
| **= Income from operations** | $42{,}000 - 27{,}000$ | **15,000** |
| − Interest expense | | 5,000 |
| **= Income before taxes** | $15{,}000 - 5{,}000$ | **10,000** |
| − Income taxes (30%) | $0.30 \times 10{,}000$ | 3,000 |
| **= Net income** | $10{,}000 - 3{,}000$ | **7,000** |

**Step 3. Retained earnings at the end.** With no dividends, $5{,}000 + 7{,}000 = 12{,}000$.

**Step 4. Balance sheet.**

| Assets | Amount | Liabilities and stockholders' equity | Amount |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Cash | 5,000 | Accounts payable | 12,000 |
| Accounts receivable | 10,000 | **Current liabilities** | **12,000** |
| Inventories | 45,000 | Bonds payable | 40,000 |
| Supplies | 4,000 | **Long-term liabilities** | **40,000** |
| **Current assets** | **64,000** | Common stock | 45,000 |
| Buildings | 65,000 | Additional paid-in capital | 20,000 |
| **Non-current assets** | **65,000** | Retained earnings | 12,000 |
| | | **Stockholders' equity** | **77,000** |
| **Total assets** | **129,000** | **Total liabilities and equity** | **129,000** |

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 9. Worked example: from a list of accounts to the two statements [Slide 19]
chunks.x: **Check:** $129{,}000 = 12{,}000 + 40{,}000 + 77{,}000$. The balance closes with no tax liability, so the cash of 5,000 is the cash after the 3,000 of taxes have been paid.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 10. Financing decisions and the capital structure [Slide 20]
chunks.x: Financing decisions analyse the different financial alternatives. **Business financing** is the collection of the financial resources needed to carry out the company's activity, and the combination of all the possible financial sources is the **capital structure** or **financial structure**.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.h: 11. The map of the financial structure [Slides 21-22]
chunks.x:
The sources of financing can be classified by their **nature**, equity or liabilities [Slide 21], or by their **origin**, the company's own resources or external resources [Slide 22]. Both classifications draw the line in the same place:

| Nature | Origin | Instruments |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Equity** | **Company resources** | Internal equity: self-financing |
| | | External equity: equity capital and shares |
| **Liabilities** | **External resources** | Long term: bonds, long-term loans and bank credits, leasing |
| | | Short term: accounts payable, trade discount, short-term loans and bank credits, factoring |

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
The **retained earnings**, the resources the company generates in its normal activity, constitute its **self-financing**. Profits can either be **retained** in the company (self-financing) or **distributed** (dividends). Two ratios describe the split:

$$\text{Pay-out} = \frac{\text{Dividends}}{\text{Profits}}, \qquad \text{Self-financing (\%)} = \frac{\text{Retained earnings}}{\text{Profits}}$$

With profits of 100,000 €, dividends of 75,000 € and retained earnings of 25,000 €, the pay-out is $75{,}000 / 100{,}000 = 75\%$ and the self-financing ratio is $25{,}000 / 100{,}000 = 25\%$ [Slide 23].

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
When a business is created, its owners put in funds to finance the assets. **Equity capital** is the money raised from the owners at the start of the business (**initial capital**) and through later **rights issues** (issues of new shares), used to finance the company's investments. It is **not repaid** to the investor at any maturity date, and a share can be turned into cash **only by selling or transferring it** [Slide 25].

A **share** is one of a finite number of equal portions of the capital of a company. It entitles its owner to a proportion of the distributed, non-reinvested profits (**dividends**) and to a portion of the value of the company in case of liquidation. Shares are equity securities and have several values: **nominal, accounting (book), intrinsic and market** value. New shares are issued through a **rights issue** (capital increase), and paying dividends is **not compulsory** [Slide 26].

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x: A **bond** is a **debt security**: the issuer owes the holders a debt and must repay the **principal** and pay **interest (the coupon)** at a later date, the **maturity**. It is a loan in the form of a security, in which the issuer is the borrower, the bondholder is the lender and the coupon is the interest. Bonds allow the issuer to finance **long-term investments** with external funds.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x: With a **long-term loan**, the company receives an amount of money that must be paid back at a certain time, and pays for this service through the **debt interest**. With a **bank credit**, the financial institution makes a **maximum amount** available to the customer, who can borrow any amount up to that limit and pays interest **only on the amount borrowed**; interest rates are higher.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x: **Leasing** lets a firm obtain the **use of a fixed asset** in exchange for a series of contractual, periodic payments. The **lessee**, who receives the asset or the services under the lease contract, has the **right to buy the asset** at the end of the agreed period. There are two types: **finance leasing** and **operating leasing**.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
- **Accounts payable (trade credit):** financing from suppliers that arises when goods are paid for some time after they are received; suppliers allow the company to defer the payment.
- **Bank financing:** short-term **loans and credits**, with the same features as the long-term ones, and **trade discounts**, in which the financial institution advances to the customer the amount of a note (bill of exchange, promissory note, etc.) before it falls due, after deducting some expenses (interest, commission, etc.).
- **Factoring:** the company sells a credit it holds against a customer to a factoring company before it expires; the factoring company collects it and assumes the risk of insolvency.

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
The financial structure is the combination of the different financial resources. With $E$ for equity and $L$ for liabilities:

$$\%\,\text{Equity} = \frac{E}{E+L}, \qquad \%\,\text{Liabilities} = \frac{L}{E+L}, \qquad \text{Debt-to-equity ratio} = \frac{L}{E}$$

The **debt-to-equity ratio** evaluates the company's **financial leverage**: the degree to which it finances its operations through debt rather than its own funds. It reflects the ability of shareholders' equity to cover all outstanding debts in a business downturn, and **higher leverage ratios tend to indicate higher risk for shareholders**.

With total liabilities and equity of 1,000 M€, of which 700 M€ are equity and 300 M€ liabilities:

$$\%\,\text{Equity} = \frac{700}{1{,}000} = 70\%, \qquad \%\,\text{Liabilities} = \frac{300}{1{,}000} = 30\%, \qquad \frac{L}{E} = \frac{300}{700} = 0.43$$

chunks.t: Topic 3 - Financial Management I - Financial Statements
chunks.x:
Every financial resource has a cost: **equity** has an **implicit (opportunity) cost**, and **liabilities** an **explicit cost**. The **capital cost** $K$ is the weighted average of the costs of all the financial resources the company obtains:

$$K_{WACC} = K_{EQ} \cdot \frac{E}{E+L} + K_L \cdot \frac{L}{E+L}$$

where $K_{EQ}$ is the cost of equity and $K_L$ the cost of liabilities, weighted by the shares of equity and liabilities in the financial structure. With the structure of the leverage example (70% equity, 30% liabilities), $K_{WACC} = 0.70\,K_{EQ} + 0.30\,K_L$.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** a production system converts inputs into outputs, and production (operations) management plans, designs, staffs and controls it. Its objectives — cost, quality, time of delivery and flexibility — partly contradict each other, so firms choose between rigid, flexible and Just in Time systems and between three plant layouts. Production is then planned (Gantt charts) and controlled for efficiency, a posteriori with productivity indexes and a priori with cost analysis: the break-even point $Q_0 = FC/(P - VC) = FC/m$, the operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ and the margin of safety.

The topic has three parts [Slide 2]: the function of production (concept, objectives and types of production systems: rigid, flexible and Just in Time), production planning and control with the Gantt chart, and the control of efficiency.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
A **production system** is a method for converting inputs into outputs. **Production management** (operations management) is the set of activities aimed at planning, designing, staffing and controlling a firm's production system [Slide 3].

The system has four elements [Slide 4]: the **factors of production** (creative, basic and managerial), the **transformation process** (tasks, flows and storage), the **outputs**, and the **feedback** that returns information from the outputs to the inputs. The whole system sits inside the generic and specific **environment** of Topic 2.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
The function of production pursues four objectives [Slide 5]: **cost**, **quality**, **time of delivery** and **flexibility**. They can contradict each other [Slide 6]:

| Pair of objectives | Why they conflict |
|---|---|
| Cost - quality | higher quality usually needs better materials, processes and controls, which cost more |
| Flexibility - cost | producing many different products in small amounts loses the savings of standard, large-scale production |
| Time of delivery - cost | delivering faster needs spare capacity, stocks or overtime, which cost more |

The right-hand column explains the pairs in plain words; the slide names only the pairs.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.h: 3. Five generic types in three categories [Slides 7-9, 23]
chunks.x:
Production systems are placed on the **product-process matrix** [Slide 7]: from **project** (civil engineering), **craft** (product under demand), **batch** (bakery) and **mass** (automobiles) to **continuous** production (petrochemistry). Towards the project end variability and flexibility grow; towards the continuous end volume grows.

The five generic types are grouped in three categories [Slides 8-9]: **rigid or continuous** (mass and continuous), **flexible or intermittent** (craft and batch) and **Just in Time**. The project type stands apart, with individualized products. Slide 23 summarises them:

| Type | Products and resources | Plant layout |
|---|---|---|
| Project | individualized products: high cost, qualified workers, equipment for general use, difficult planning and control | fixed |
| Craft and batch | a low quantity of a great variety of products; craft: more adaptability, less quantity; batch: more uniformity, more quantity (batch size) | functional |
| Mass and continuous | standard products for mass markets, division of labour; mass: more dependent on workers than on machines; continuous: more dependent on machines than on workers | product |

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
**Characteristics** [Slide 10]: big volumes of production, commercialization at a low price, standard products, capital intensive.

**Advantages of job specialization** [Slide 11]: less time to learn a task; the simplicity of the task makes learning cheaper; no time lost changing from one task to another; the worker acquires expertise; a better fit between worker and job position; easy replacement of workers (and mechanization).

**Organization of the factory** [Slide 12]: division of labour into different job positions, assigned by seniority, which leads to the **bureaucratization** of the company. Its two types are **mass production** and **continuous or process production** [Slide 13].

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
**Characteristics** [Slide 14]: flexible volumes of production, more complex and differentiated products, more highly qualified workers, equipment for general use.

**Organization** [Slide 15]: plant layout based on teamwork, workers with more responsibility, fewer hierarchical levels, employee rotation, and remuneration that depends on qualification. Its two types are **craft** and **batch** production [Slide 16].

**Flexible versus rigid** [Slide 17]: drawn against the volume of production, the total cost of the rigid system starts higher (more fixed cost) but grows more slowly (less variable cost per unit). Below the volume where the two lines cross (zone A) the flexible system is cheaper; above it (zone B) the rigid one is.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
Just in Time arose from the need to manufacture many types of automobiles, in small batches but under the same production process. It is **based on requests and eliminates inventories** [Slide 18]. Its competitive advantages are to manufacture high-quality products and to reduce the whole production cycle [Slide 19].

| Element [Slides 20-21] | Tool |
|---|---|
| Internal organization | job cells |
| Plant distribution | U shape |
| Mechanisms to support quality | Jidoka, Poka Yoke |
| Mechanisms of visual control | Andon, control panels, work sheets, Kanban |

The slides only name these tools.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
There are three plant layouts [Slide 22]: **functional or process**, **product** and **fixed**.

| Layout | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Functional or process [Slide 24] | high use of the machines; machines easily replaced; operators of similar, nearby machines can train and supervise themselves; a specific incentive system for each worker | distance between functions; handling wastes when transporting materials; the flow of materials and the operators' work are difficult to standardize and to plan; activities are difficult to plan; lines are not balanced (some saturated, others free) |
| Product [Slide 25] | little work in process; less space for transport and temporary storage; simpler planning and control; operators need little preparation; the flow of materials is easy to anticipate | inflexible; the time is set by the slowest machine (bottlenecks must be avoided); a problem in one machine affects the whole process; high investment; incentive programmes per employee are difficult to define |
| Fixed [Slide 26] | the product stays in one place and machinery, materials and labour are brought to it | — |

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
**Production planning** is the determination of what products to produce and where, when and how to produce them. **Production control** is the effort to ensure that production plans or schedules are met [Slide 27]. The basic process has six steps [Slide 28]:

1. Receiving the orders from customers.
2. Developing a list of required materials.
3. Developing a route sheet.
4. Developing production schedules.
5. Dispatching notices to operators to begin work.
6. Following up to see that the schedule is being met.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x: The **Gantt chart**, named after Henry Gantt, who developed it in the early 1900s, represents the phases and activities of a project work breakdown structure [Slide 30]. It is a bar chart that shows the scheduled start and stop dates of each production step; it is a visual illustration of times, used for non-complex projects; it normally does not show the dependency relationships between activities; and it shows the current schedule status with percent-complete shading and a vertical "TODAY" line [Slide 31].

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
The production system is controlled for **efficiency**, which is not the same as **efficacy** [Slide 33]. Two kinds of index are used: **productivity**, measured a posteriori, and **cost analysis**, a priori.

**Total productivity** relates everything produced to all the factors used, and a **partial productivity** to one factor only [Slide 34]:

$$\text{Total productivity} = \frac{\text{Goods and services}}{\text{Labour} + \text{Capital} + \text{Raw materials} + \text{Energy}} \qquad \text{Labour productivity} = \frac{\text{Goods and services}}{\text{Labour}}$$

Productivity depends on external factors, factors of capacity, product factors, factors of process design, factors of human resources and quality factors [Slide 35].

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
The **break-even point** (BEP) is the volume of sales or production at which the company covers its total costs, and from which it starts to make profits; it depends on the cost structure [Slide 36].

With price $P$ per unit, variable cost $VC$ per unit, fixed costs $FC$ and volume $Q$, revenue is $R = P\,Q$ and total cost $TC = FC + VC\,Q$, so

$$\text{Profit} = P\,Q - (VC\,Q + FC) = Q\,(P - VC) - FC$$

The **unit margin** is $m = P - VC$. At the break-even point the profit is zero, $Q_0\,m - FC = 0$ [Slide 37]:

$$Q_0 = \frac{FC}{P - VC} = \frac{FC}{m}$$

Slide 38 compares two cost structures with the same revenue line: case A, with higher fixed costs and a steeper profit line, and case B, with lower fixed costs and a flatter one. The break-even point moves with the cost structure.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
The **operating leverage** measures how a change in sales translates into a change in operating income (profit or loss) [Slide 40]. It is the relative change of the profit divided by the relative change of the volume [Slide 39]:

$$OL = \frac{\Delta \text{Profit} / \text{Profit}}{\Delta Q / Q}$$

Since $\text{Profit} = Q\,(P - VC) - FC$ and $FC$ does not change with $Q$, $\Delta\text{Profit} = \Delta Q\,(P - VC)$. Substituting,

$$OL = \frac{\dfrac{\Delta Q\,(P - VC)}{Q\,(P - VC) - FC}}{\dfrac{\Delta Q}{Q}} = \frac{Q\,(P - VC)}{Q\,(P - VC) - FC} = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - FC} = \frac{Q\,m}{\text{Profit}}$$

**Interpretation** [Slide 40]: with $OL = 3$, a 1% increase in sales raises profit by 3%, and a 10% fall in sales lowers profit by 30%.

**Comments** [Slide 41]: the OL captures the sensitivity of operating income to sales; it is an index of **economic (operating) risk**; it is used to compare businesses of the same sector; and, ceteris paribus, the higher the fixed costs, the higher the OL.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.h: 13. Relationship between break-even point and operating leverage [Slide 42]
chunks.x:
Since $FC = Q^*\,m$ (with $Q^*$ the break-even point), the leverage depends only on how far the volume is from the break-even point:

$$OL = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - Q^*\,m} = \frac{Q}{Q - Q^*}$$

- **Profits** ($Q > Q^*$): $OL > 1$, a more than proportional effect; the closer to the break-even point, the larger the leverage.
- **Losses** ($Q < Q^*$): $OL \le 0$; for $OL < -1$ an amplifier (more than proportional) effect, for $-1 < OL < 0$ a less than proportional effect.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
The **margin of safety** represents the strength of the business: the amount the company is above (or below) the break-even point.

| Measured in | Formula |
|---|---|
| units | $MS = Q - Q^*$ |
| monetary units | $MS = (Q - Q^*)\,m$ |
| percentage | $MS = (Q - Q^*)/Q^*$ |

The percentage form of the slide divides by the break-even volume $Q^*$.

chunks.t: Topic 4 - The Production Function
chunks.x:
| Magnitude | Formula | Slide |
|---|---|---|
| Unit margin | $m = P - VC$ | 37 |
| Profit | $\text{Profit} = Q\,m - FC$ | 39 |
| Break-even point | $Q_0 = FC/m$ | 37 |
| Operating leverage | $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC) = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ | 40, 42 |
| Margin of safety | $Q - Q^*$; $(Q - Q^*)\,m$; $(Q - Q^*)/Q^*$ | 43 |
| Labour productivity | goods and services / labour | 34 |

The eight exercises of the break-even and operating leverage sheet are solved one by one in Problem Set - T4 Break-Even Point and Operating Leverage.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** marketing is the process of planning and executing the conception, pricing, promotion and distribution of ideas, goods and services to create exchanges that satisfy individual and organizational objectives. Strategic marketing analyses the market, segments it and positions the product; operative marketing builds the marketing mix of the 4 Ps (product, price, place and promotion). Demand analysis measures how the demand reacts to those variables through elasticities, above all the price elasticity $E_d = (\%\Delta Q_d)/(\%\Delta P)$: elastic demand ($|E_d| > 1$) makes revenue fall when the price rises, inelastic demand ($|E_d| < 1$) makes it rise.

The topic has three parts [Slide 2]: the role of marketing in the company, market segmentation and positioning of the product, and the marketing-mix decisions on product, price, place and promotion. The supplementary notes topic 5.2.2.pdf develop the price elasticity of demand.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x: The concept of **exchange** is crucial in marketing: exchange is the process by which two or more persons give and receive something of value. **Marketing** is the process of planning and executing the conception, pricing, promotion and distribution of ideas, goods and services to create exchanges that satisfy individual and organizational objectives.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
| Stage | Era | Features |
|---|---|---|
| Passive marketing | production era | producers are production-oriented; seller's market (demand greater than supply); marketing is not important; usually mass production |
| Organizational marketing | sales era | producers are sales-oriented; buyer's market (supply greater than demand); result: consumerism (high consumer power) |
| Active marketing | marketing era | producers turn to a market or customer orientation and produce what potential customers want; market segmentation arises |
| Social marketing | — | main objective: finding out the needs and wants of the target market and contributing to a better welfare state |

The **sale** is a one-way process: the company puts goods and services in front of the customer. **Marketing** is a two-way process: the goods and services go to the customer and information about what is desired comes back to the company [Slide 5].

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
Marketing management has two systems [Slide 6]:

- **Strategic marketing** (the analysis system): analysing the potential demand, identifying the customers' needs, and setting the marketing objectives and strategies.
- **Operative marketing** (the action system): creating and maintaining a marketing mix that satisfies the target market, combining four variables, the **4 Ps**: product, place, price and promotion.

**Strategic marketing** analyses the current situation of the company's products and the customers' needs and wants, selects and analyses a target market, and identifies the threats and opportunities that, combined with the resources and capabilities of the company, may create a **competitive advantage** [Slide 7]. Its phases:

1. Analysis of the situation: market, competitors, environment and internal analysis.
2. Diagnosis of the situation: SWOT analysis.
3. Definition of the marketing objective.
4. Formulation of the strategies: market segmentation and positioning of the product.

**Operative marketing** develops and coordinates product, place, promotion and price strategies so that the target market is satisfied and the firm makes a profit [Slide 8]. Its phases:

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
1. Define the action plan for the marketing mix: identify the sales objectives, define the activities to achieve them (the 4 Ps) and establish the marketing budget.
2. Execute the marketing-mix strategies.
3. Control and assessment.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Market segmentation** is the process of identifying smaller markets, the **market segments**, that exist within a larger market. It helps marketers tailor marketing mixes for the target segment, and it requires knowledge of potential customers' wants and behaviour, of changes in the market and of competitors [Slide 9].

Segmentation criteria [Slide 10]:

| Criterion | Examples |
|---|---|
| Geographical | national, international, regional; different areas (coast or not) |
| Demographic | age, sex, family size, level of income, type of job |
| Psychological and purchase behaviour | personality, lifestyle; frequency of purchase (regular, temporary); type of use of the product (low, medium, high) |

Segmentation identifies the market needs that are not being satisfied, gives a better adjustment of supply and demand, and identifies the competitors [Slide 11].

Three segmentation strategies [Slide 12]:

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
- **Undifferentiated (mass) marketing:** the company appeals to the whole market with a single product or service and marketing strategy; a single marketing mix is offered to the total market.
- **Wide differentiated (multisegment) marketing:** the firm targets two or more segments and develops distinct products or services with a separate marketing mix for each.
- **Differentiated concentrated (niche) marketing:** the product and the marketing message are aimed at a single, well-defined segment.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Positioning** is the technique by which marketers try to create an image or identity for a product, brand or company in the perception of the target market [Slide 13]. It has two phases: the marketing manager uses the marketing-mix strategy to position the product in the mind of the customer, and the customer creates a perception of the product, how buyers see it.

A successful positioning strategy is usually based on a **sustainable competitive advantage** of the company. Positioning can be based on product characteristics, benefits of the product, user characteristics, placing and comparing it relative to another product, or the price-quality relationship [Slide 14].

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.h: 6. Analysis and forecast of the demand [Slides 15-16]
chunks.x:
Demand analysis measures and quantifies the real demand, identifies the variables that affect it and forecasts it [Slide 15]. One measure is the market share:

$$\text{Brand's market share} = \frac{\text{Brand sales}}{\text{Total sales of the market of reference}}$$

Techniques include pilot markets, the Delphi technique and purchasing intention surveys.

**Demand** is the volume of sales of a certain product for a specific group of customers, at a set time and place, given some environment conditions and a marketing programme. It is quantified along three dimensions (product, group of customers and time), and the **real** demand is distinguished from the **potential** market demand [Slide 16].

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
A main objective of demand analysis is to forecast and measure the variations of the demand due to changes in the factors related to it, mainly the marketing-mix variables. The **elasticity** of the demand with respect to a factor $F$ is

$$E = \frac{\%\ \text{variation in the demand}}{\%\ \text{variation in the factor}} = \frac{\Delta D / D}{\Delta F / F} = \frac{(D_2 - D_1)/D_1}{(F_2 - F_1)/F_1}$$

| Value | Demand |
|---|---|
| $E > 1$ | elastic: sensitive to changes of the factor |
| $E = 1$ | unit elastic |
| $E < 1$ | inelastic: not sensitive to changes of the factor |

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
The **price elasticity of demand** $E_d$ measures how much the quantity demanded of a good changes when its price changes: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2). Written with differentials, for good $n$ with price $p_n$ and quantity demanded $q_n^d$:

$$E_d = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in price}} = \frac{dq_n^d / q_n^d}{dp_n / p_n} = \frac{dq_n^d}{dp_n}\cdot\frac{p_n}{q_n^d}$$

By the law of demand the coefficient is **negative** (price and quantity move in opposite directions), and its **absolute value** is used. It depends mainly on the availability of substitute goods, since then the quantity demanded depends a lot on the price (p. 2).

**Elasticity and income** (p. 3). Revenue (income) is $I = P \cdot Q$.

| Demand | Price rise | Price fall |
|---|---|---|
| Elastic, $\lvert E_d \rvert > 1$: a 1% price change moves $Q_d$ by more than 1% | demand falls even more, income falls | demand rises even more, income rises |
| Inelastic, $\lvert E_d \rvert < 1$: a 1% price change moves $Q_d$ by less than 1% | nearly the same quantity at a higher price, income rises | nearly the same quantity at a lower price, income falls |
| Unit elastic, $\lvert E_d \rvert = 1$ | the percentage price rise is offset by an equal fall in volume, income does not change | income does not change |

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Limiting cases** (p. 4): **perfectly inelastic** demand, $E_d = 0$, does not respond to price changes (a vertical demand curve); **perfectly elastic** demand, $E_d = \infty$, changes indefinitely for a tiny price change (a horizontal demand curve).

**Cross elasticity** (p. 5) relates the demand for one good to the price of another:

$$E_{XY} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in the quantity demanded of good } X}{\%\ \text{change in the price of good } Y}$$

It is **positive for substitute goods** and **negative for complementary goods**. If X and Y are complementary, a fall in the price of X increases the consumption of both; if they are substitutes, a fall in the price of X increases the consumption of X and decreases that of Y. The greater the substitutability or complementarity, the greater the reaction to any change in price.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
The marketing mix has four elements: **product, price, place and promotion** [Slide 18].

The **product** is a bundle of tangible and intangible attributes that may satisfy customer wants and is received in exchange for payment. The basic (core or generic) product is less than the total product people buy: customers also buy benefits such as quality, design, packaging, size, quantity, post-sale services and image. Customer satisfaction depends on the physical-technical characteristics and on psychosocial factors; the psychosocial attributes are brand, design, packaging and quality [Slide 19].

**Brand** [Slide 20]: a name, term, design, symbol or any other feature that identifies one seller's good or service as distinct from those of other sellers. It contains a **name** (the part that can be said) and a **logo** (design, symbol, graph and distinct colours). Strategic options: manufacturer brands or dealer brands (owned by a wholesaler or retailer); a corporate (unique) brand, multi-brands, individual brands, a family (umbrella) brand, or secondary brands. Slide 21 illustrates individual branding (the products of one soft-drink company, each with its own name) against umbrella branding (one name over many businesses), and dealer brands.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Design and packaging** [Slide 22]: design is the appropriate combination of physical appearance, colour, shape and ease of use, from an aesthetic (beauty) and a functional (ease of use) perspective. Packaging is the design and production of the container or wrapper of a product, including the label; it protects the content and eases transport, carries the compulsory label with information about the product, and can make the product more convenient and attractive.

**Quality** [Slide 23] measures whether the product satisfies the customers' needs; it depends on the intrinsic characteristics of the product and on what consumers expect of it. Other attributes are warranty, post-sale services, size, quantity and product line.

**Product lines** [Slide 24]: a range of products (assortment) is an offer of product lines and individual products, described by its **extension** (number of lines), **depth** (products per line), **length** (total number of individual products) and **consistency** (with the final use). Product strategies: add product lines (more range), extend the lines (more depth) or incorporate product variations (more length).

**Product life-cycle** [Slide 25]: it can apply to a product category, a product form or a brand, and has four stages: introduction (launching a new product), growth (sales take off), maturity (the longest part) and decline (obsolescence).

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x: Slide 26 asks which of three sales curves is a fashion product, an immediate failure and a product of a dilated life. Reading the curves: A, whose sales grow and then stay, is the product of a dilated life; B, which rises and falls, is the fashion product; C, which falls almost at once, is the immediate failure.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
**Price** is the marketing-mix element that sets the amount of money the seller seeks from the buyer in exchange for the product. It matters because it influences the demand, reinforces the image of the product and must be compatible with the other marketing-mix strategies. Pricing objectives are aligned with the marketing objectives and with the other objectives of the company: maximizing profit, maximizing sales or achieving a certain market share [Slide 27].

There are three approaches to pricing [Slide 28]: the **competition** approach, the **demand** approach and the **cost** approach. The cost approach uses **cost-plus pricing** (the mark-up is the difference between the cost of a good and its selling price) or **break-even analysis** (Topic 4).

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x: **Communication** is the process of influencing others' behaviour by sharing ideas, information or feelings; marketers' efforts to communicate with target audiences are called **promotion**. Its objectives are to gain attention, to teach, to remind, to persuade and to reassure. The promotion mix has five activities: advertising, sales promotion, public relations, direct marketing and personal selling [Slide 29].

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
| Activity | Definition | Decisions |
|---|---|---|
| Advertising [Slide 30] | any paid form of non-personal communication through the mass media about a product by an identified sponsor (magazines, direct mail, internet, TV, billboards, newspapers); informative or persuasive | 1. target audience; 2. objectives; 3. message; 4. media; 5. budget; 6. timing; 7. evaluating effectiveness (sales- or communication-oriented) |
| Sales promotion [Slide 31] | any activity that offers an incentive for a limited period to induce a desired response from customers, salespeople or intermediaries; it adds value because the incentive does not ordinarily come with the product | 1. objectives; 2. type of promotion; 3. programme; 4. advertising the plan; 5. evaluating the results |
| Public relations [Slide 32] | communication to build and maintain a favourable image of the firm, keep the goodwill of its stakeholders and explain its goals (relations with the media, sponsorship) | — |
| Direct marketing [Slide 32] | an interactive system that uses one or more media (telephone, internet, TV, direct mail, social media) to obtain a specific, measurable response or transaction at any location | — |
| Personal selling [Slide 33] | a person-to-person process in which the seller learns the prospective buyer's wants and seeks to satisfy them with a sale | planning and coordinating the sales force (size, re

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x:
The objective of **distribution** is getting the product to customers where and when they want it. A **distribution channel** is the series of interdependent firms that facilitate the transfer of title to a product as it moves from producer to final buyer; an **intermediary** (wholesaler, retailer) operates between the producer and the final buyer. Distribution is physical (logistics) or through distribution channels [Slide 34].

**Types of channel** [Slide 35]: **direct**, where the producer sells directly to the final buyers, and **indirect**, where independent intermediaries take some tasks: merchandise agents and brokers (bring buyers and sellers together, without owning title, for a commission), wholesalers (sell to intermediaries or organizational buyers, not to final consumers) and retailers (sell consumer goods and services to final consumers).

**Functions of intermediaries** [Slide 36]: improve exchange efficiency, help match supply and demand, offer a wide product mix from different producers, manage logistics, and perform other marketing functions such as financing, market information and storage.

chunks.t: Topic 5 - Marketing and Sales Management
chunks.x: **Selecting a channel** [Slide 37]: 1. set the objectives of the distribution, considering buying habits, customer characteristics, product characteristics and the characteristics of the company and its competitors; 2. establish a distribution strategy: **intensive**, **selective** or **exclusive** distribution; 3. define the distribution channel, considering the characteristics of each intermediary and the coordination among them.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** management is the process of setting and achieving goals through four managerial functions — planning, organizing, leading and controlling — that use human, financial and material resources. Managers take routine, adaptable or innovative decisions through an eight-step process, work at three levels of the management pyramid with different mixes of technical, interpersonal and conceptual skills, and play Mintzberg's ten roles. Organizing produces a structure, formal and informal, built from five common parts and shaped into five basic configurations, from the simple structure to the adhocracy.

The topic covers [Slide 2]: the managerial functions (decisions and their types, the decision-making process, management levels, managerial skills and roles), planning, organizing (formal and informal structures and the types of formal structure), leading (human resources management) and controlling.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: **Management** is the process of setting and achieving goals through the execution of four basic managerial functions that use human, financial and material resources. The **management functions** are the four broad activities managers perform to achieve organizational goals: **planning, organizing, leading and controlling** [Slides 3-4].

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
Managerial decisions are classified by two axes: the type of problem (from known and well defined to unusual and ambiguous) and the type of alternative solutions (from known to ambiguous and not planned).

| Type of decision | Problem | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|
| Routine (planned) | known and well defined | known |
| Adaptable | in between | in between |
| Innovative (not planned) | unusual and ambiguous | ambiguous and not planned |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: The decision-making process has eight steps: 1. recognizing the problem or opportunity; 2. gathering information; 3. identifying the critical factors; 4. considering alternative courses of action; 5. evaluating the results; 6. choosing an alternative; 7. implementing the decision; 8. implementing changes. The slide groups them into analyzing the alternatives and implementing the changes.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: The **management pyramid** has three levels: **top management**, **middle management** and **low management** (first-line supervisors). By the scope of their activities, top management is **strategic** and **general**; the lower levels are **tactical** and **functional**.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
Three skills are used in different proportions along the hierarchy:

| Skill | Meaning | Where it weighs most |
|---|---|---|
| Technical | the ability to understand how things operate | low management |
| Interpersonal | the ability to interact with people at work successfully | at every level |
| Conceptual | the ability to see the firm as a whole | top management |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
| Group | Roles |
|---|---|
| Interpersonal roles | figurehead, leader, liaison |
| Informational roles | monitor, disseminator, spokesperson |
| Decisional roles | entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: **Planning** is the process of setting goals or objectives and deciding on the strategy to achieve them. A **goal** is a specific achievement to be attained at some future date. Its main steps are: 1. developing forecasts; 2. defining strategic objectives; 3. developing alternative courses of action; 4. deciding on a course of action.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: **Organizing** is the process of arranging the human resources of the firm so that their activities contribute to the firm's goals. Its purpose is to give each person a distinct task and to coordinate those tasks so that the firm achieves its goals. It is a double process of **differentiation** (dividing the work) and **integration** (coordinating it). The **organization chart** is the graphic representation of the organization structure.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: The **formal structure** is defined by management. The **informal structure** is the informal contacts, communications and ways of doing things that employees develop. The **real structure** combines both.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
| Factor | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Specialization | horizontal (number of tasks) and vertical (autonomy to organize one's job) |
| Standardization | how far the work is done by set rules and procedures |
| Formalization | how far the rules are written down |
| Centralization | centralized or decentralized decision-making |
| Structural configuration | departmentalization (types), number of layers (hierarchical levels), span of control, size of the administrative component |

The middle column of the standardization and formalization rows explains the terms in plain words; the slide only names them.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.h: 11. The parts of a formal structure [Slide 14]
chunks.x: Any formal structure has five common parts: the **strategic apex** (top management), the **middle line** (middle management), the **operating core** (employees), the **technostructure** (analysts who design systems and processes) and the **support staff** (outside the operating workflow).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
| Configuration | Features |
|---|---|
| Simple structure (entrepreneurial start-up) [Slide 15] | the strategic apex is the key part (direct supervision); only strategic apex and operating core; start-ups or very small businesses |
| Machine bureaucracy [Slide 16] | many rules, regulations and formal communications: standardization and very formal procedures in the operating core; highly specialized, routine tasks, horizontal and vertical (low-qualified employees); functional departmentalization; centralized decision-making; elaborate administrative structure with many layers and a low span of control; mature, big organizations in a stable and simple environment |
| Professional organization (professional bureaucracy) [Slide 18] | high horizontal specialization (highly qualified employees); standardization of outputs, skills and knowledge; decentralization; the staff mainly supports the operating core; all types of departmentalization; big organizations in a stable but complex environment |
| Division organization [Slide 20] | autonomous divisions; the middle line is the key part; top management coordinates their performance and outputs; each division is a bureaucracy; diversified businesses in more dynamic environments |
| Adhocracy (innovative organization) [Slide 22] | high horizontal and low vertical specialization; low standardization and formalization; decentralization is

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: key to flexibility; matrix departmentalization; the technostructure disappears and middle line, operating core and staff are mixed; used as a complementary structure for specific projects |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x: **Human resources** are the firm's employees, workers and managers. The problem is to **align individual interests with the objectives of the company**. **Human resources management** is the process of recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and compensating employees; it is a basic function of every manager. It involves **directing** (motivation, leadership and communication) and **staffing** (recruiting, selecting and training; performance appraisal systems, compensation and incentive programmes).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - The Management Function
chunks.x:
**Controlling** is the task of ensuring that activities are providing the planned results: managers must ensure that their workers perform as expected [Slide 24]. It involves establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations and taking corrective action if required. All control systems aim to influence employee behaviour, and **planning and controlling are inseparable**.

Types of control [Slide 25]: by **who** is controlled (top, middle or low management); by **what** area (the whole company, a unit, a department or an individual); by **when** (reactive, proactive or interactive control); and by **frequency** (constant, periodic or occasional control).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
**Central idea:** innovation comes from individuals, firms, universities, government-funded research and private nonprofits, and above all from the linkages between them. Innovations are classified in pairs — product or process, radical or incremental, competence-enhancing or competence-destroying, architectural or component — and follow technology trajectories: an S-curve of performance against effort, discontinuous jumps to new technologies, and diffusion through innovators, early adopters, the early and late majority and laggards. Industries usually settle on a dominant design, selected by learning effects and network externalities, which can lead to winner-take-all markets.

The topic deals with formulating and implementing a technological innovation strategy in three parts [Slide 2]: the sources of innovation, the types and patterns of innovation, and standards battles and design dominance. Its two tables of Part I quote E. Roberts, "Benchmarking Global Strategic Management of Technology", *Research Technology Management*, March-April 2001.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
Innovation can arise from many sources: individuals (the lone inventor, or users who design solutions for their own needs), the research of universities, government laboratories and incubators, and private non-profit organizations. Firms have strong incentives to develop differentiating new products and services, which may give them an advantage over non-profit or government-funded entities [Slide 3].

The most important source of innovation is the **linkages between these players**. Networks of innovators that leverage knowledge and other resources from multiple sources are one of the most powerful agents of technological advance, so the sources of innovation form a complex system in which an innovation may emerge from one or more of its components or from the linkages between them [Slide 4].

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
An individual's **creative ability** is a function of intellectual abilities, knowledge, style of thinking, personality, motivation and environment. The most important intellectual abilities are to look at problems in unconventional ways, to analyze which ideas are worth pursuing, and to articulate those ideas and convince others that they are worthwhile.

The **creativity of an organization** is a function of the creativity of its individuals and of the social processes and contextual factors that shape how they interact. It is not a simple aggregate of the individuals' creativity: the organization's structure, routines and incentives can thwart individual creativity or amplify it.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.h: 3. Firms' sources of research and development [Slides 6-7]
chunks.x:

| 2 | internal R&D within divisions | central corporate research |

Slide 7 gives the percentage of companies that report extensive collaboration with customers, suppliers and universities:

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
- **Universities:** to increase the degree to which their research leads to commercial innovation, many universities have set up technology transfer offices.
- **Government-funded research:** governments invest in research through their own laboratories, science parks and incubators, and grants to other public or private research entities.
- **Private non-profit organizations:** some perform their own R&D, some fund the R&D of other organizations without doing it themselves, and some do both.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
Collaborative research is especially important in high-technology sectors, where no single individual or organization is likely to have all the resources and capabilities needed to develop and implement a significant innovation.

- **Technology clusters:** regional clusters of firms connected to a common technology, which may have buyer, supplier and complementary relationships as well as research collaboration; geographical proximity seems to help the formation and activity of such networks (example: the semiconductor firms of Silicon Valley).
- **Technological spillovers:** a positive externality of R&D that results from the spread of knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x: The path a technology follows through time is its **technology trajectory**, most often used to represent its rate of performance improvement or its rate of adoption in the market. Many factors influence these trajectories, but some patterns appear consistently across industries and periods.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
| Pair | Definitions |
|---|---|
| Product vs process [Slide 11] | **product** innovations are embodied in the outputs of an organization, its goods or services (e.g. a carmaker's new hybrid electric vehicle); **process** innovations change the way an organization conducts its business, such as the techniques of producing or marketing goods or services, often to improve the effectiveness or efficiency of production (fewer defects, more output in a given time) |
| Radical vs incremental [Slide 12] | a **radical** innovation is very new and different from prior solutions; an **incremental** innovation makes a relatively minor change to existing practices |
| Competence-enhancing vs competence-destroying [Slide 12] | an innovation that builds on (or renders obsolete) existing knowledge and skills; it depends on whose perspective is taken: the same innovation can enhance one firm's competences and destroy another's |
| Architectural vs component [Slide 13] | an **architectural** innovation changes the overall design of a system or the way its components interact; a **component** (modular) innovation changes one or more components without significantly affecting the overall configuration |

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x: Plotted against the effort invested, the performance of a technology follows an **S-curve**: it improves slowly at first, then quickly, and finally flattens as it approaches the **limit of the technology**.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
A **discontinuous technology** fulfils a similar market need by building on an entirely new knowledge base. The slide draws the S-curves of a first and a second technology: the second may start below the first and then overtake it [Slide 15].

**Technology diffusion** is the spread of a technology through a population [Slide 15]. Its adopters fall into five categories [Slide 16]:

| Category | Share | Profile |
|---|---:|---|
| Innovators | 2.5% | risk-oriented, leading-edge individuals extremely interested in technological developments; a fraction of the population |
| Early adopters | 13.5% | larger but still small; risk-oriented and highly adaptable to new technology; tend to be young and well educated |
| Early majority | 34% | much larger and more careful; open to new ideas but wait to see how they are received before investing |
| Late majority | 34% | slightly conservative and risk-averse; need convincing before investing in something new |
| Laggards | 16% | extremely frugal, conservative and often technology-averse; invest only once an idea is extremely well established |

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x: The technology cycle almost always has a stage in which the industry selects a **dominant design** (Anderson and Tushman). Once it is selected, producers and customers focus on improving their efficiency in manufacturing, delivering, marketing or deploying that design instead of developing alternatives. A dominant design is a single product or process architecture that dominates a product category, usually 50% or more of the market; it is a **de facto standard**, a standard of the industry even if not officially enforced.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Entrepreneurship and Innovation
chunks.x:
**Learning effects** [Slide 18]: the more a technology is used, the more it is developed and the more effective and efficient it becomes. Adoption generates sales revenue that is reinvested in refining the technology, and firms accumulate experience that lets them use it more productively. **Absorptive capacity** is the ability of an organization to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge.

**Network externalities** [Slide 19], or positive consumption externalities, occur when the value of a good to a user increases with the number of other users of the same or a similar good. They act through the **installed base** (the number of users of a good, e.g. the consoles of a video game system installed in homes) and the **complementary goods** (goods and services that enable or enhance its value, e.g. the games, peripherals and online services of that console).

**The result: winner-take-all markets.** These forces push the market towards natural monopolies: some alternative platforms survive in niche markets, but most of the market may be dominated by a single design or a few.
